body: Welcome to the GitHub repository for Layer5’s documentation website! The docs website is hosted at https://docs.layer5.io. We use Hugo with the google/docsy theme for styling and site structure, and Netlify to manage the deployment of the site. Quickstart 🔗 Here’s a quick guide to updating the docs: Fork the layer5io/docs repository on GitHub. Make your changes and send a pull request (PR). If you’re not yet ready for a review, add “WIP” to the PR name to indicate it’s a work in progress. Wait for the automated PR workflow to do some checks. When it’s ready, you should see a comment like this: deploy/netlify — Deploy preview ready! Click Details to the right of “Deploy preview ready” to see a preview of your updates. Continue updating your doc and pushing your changes until you’re happy with the content. When you’re ready for a review, add a comment to the PR, remove any holds or “WIP” markers, and assign a reviewer/approver. See the Layer5 contributor guide. If you need more help with the GitHub workflow, follow this guide to a standard GitHub workflow. Local development 🔗 This section will show you how to develop the website locally, by running a local Hugo server. Install Hugo 🔗 To install Hugo, follow the instructions for your system type. NOTE: we recommend that you use Hugo version v0.140.2, as this is currently the version we deploy to Netlify. For example, using homebrew to install hugo on macOS or linux: # WARNING: this may install a newer version than `v0.140.2` brew install hugo Install Node Packages 🔗 If you plan to make changes to the site styling, you need to install some node libraries as well. (See the Docsy setup guide for more information) You can install the same versions we use in Netlify (defined in package.json) with the following command: npm install -D Run local hugo server 🔗 Follow the usual GitHub workflow of forking the repository on GitHub and then cloning your fork to your local machine. Fork the layer5io/docs repository in the GitHub UI. Clone your fork locally: git clone git@github.com:/docs.git cd website/ Initialize the Docsy submodule: git submodule update --init --recursive Install Docsy dependencies: # NOTE: ensure you have node 18 installed (cd themes/docsy/ && npm install) Start your local Hugo server: hugo server -D You can access your website at http://localhost:1313/ Useful docs 🔗 User guide for the Docsy theme Hugo installation guide Hugo basic usage Hugo site directory structure hugo server reference Menu structure 🔗 The site theme has one Hugo menu (main), which defines the top navigation bar. You can find and adjust the definition of the menu in the site configuration file. The left-hand navigation panel is defined by the directory structure under the content/en directory. A weight property in the front matter of each page determines the position of the page relative to the others in the same directory. The lower the weight, the earlier the page appears in the section. Here is an example _index.md file: +++ title = "Getting Started with Layer5" description = "Overview" weight = 1 +++ Docsy Theme 🔗 We use the Docsy theme for the website. The theme files are managed with a git submodule in the themes/docsy directory. Do not change these files, they are not actually inside this repo, but are part of the google/docsy repo. To update referenced docsy commit, run the following command at the root of the repo: # for example, to update docsy to v0.6.0 # WARNING: updating the docsy version will require you to update our overrides # check under: `layouts/partials` and `assets/scss` git -C themes/docsy fetch --tags git -C themes/docsy checkout tags/v0.6.0 Documentation style guide 🔗 For guidance on writing effective documentation, see the style guide for the Layer5 docs. Overriding theme styles 🔗 The theme holds its styles in the assets/scss directory. Do not change these files, they are not actually inside this repo, but are part of the google/docsy repo. These files are managed as a Git submodule and may be updated or replaced when the theme is upgraded. Any changes made directly to the theme files will be lost during updates and are not preserved in version control. You can override the default styles and add new ones: In general, put your files in the project directory structure under website rather than in the theme directory. Use the same file name as the theme does, and put the file in the same relative position. Hugo looks first at the file in the main project directories, if present, then at the files under the theme directory. For example, the Layer5 website’s layouts/partials/navbar.html overrides the theme’s layouts/partials/navbar.html You can update the Layer5 website’s project variables in the _variables_project.scss file. Values in that file override the Docsy variables. You can also use _variables_project.scss to specify your own values for any of the default Bootstrap 4 variables. For adding custom CSS rules, use the _styles_project.scss file in the same assets/scss/ directory. Image styling 🔗 Link and asset paths 🔗 Use Hugo ref when linking from one documentation page to another documentation page: [About]({{< ref "about.md" >}}) For images and other assets that live next to index.md or _index.md, or inside that page bundle, use a normal relative path: ![Alt text](images/example.png) If you need HTML for custom sizing, keep the same relative path: For global shared assets that physically live under static/, use the static shortcode: ![Layer5 logo]({{< static "images/logo.svg" >}}) Do not use the static shortcode for assets under content/. By default, Markdown images are rendered with: max-width: 70% of the viewport max-height: 80vh of the viewport height centered block layout This default styling works well for most landscape (horizontal) images. Note In Hugo, a section is a directory containing an _index.md file. Overview 🔗 Contributing videos involves either:
Creating a category → subcategory → adding video markdown files, or Adding video markdown files directly under a category (these will automatically be assigned to an “ALL” subcategory) 1. Creating a Category 🔗 To create a top-level category:
Create a directory under content/en/videos (e.g., getting-started) Add an _index.md file inside this directory with the following frontmatter: title: Getting Started # Category text appearing in the /videos category tab and left sidebar description: > Getting started videos on Cloud and Kanvas weight: 2 # Order in which this category appears in the /videos page and left sidebar icon: bi-rocket-takeoff-fill # Icon for the category (supports Bootstrap icons and local/remote assets) videoGrid: true # When true, shows all child / nested videos as a grid of cards on this section's index page # When false, presents a hyperlinked list of videos/sub-sections instead draft: true # When true, previews this section on local dev server but hides from left sidebar and /videos landing page on published site 2. Adding Videos to Your Category 🔗 There are two approaches for adding videos:
Approach A: Create a Subcategory with Videos 🔗 Create a subdirectory under your category (e.g., getting-started/onboarding) Add an _index.md file with the following frontmatter: title: Onboarding # Subcategory text in the /videos subcategory tab and left sidebar videoGrid: true # Same functionality as in the category _index.md weight: 2 # Order in which this subcategory appears Create video markdown files (e.g., video1.md, video2.md) in this subdirectory with the following frontmatter: --- title: "Design Reviews: Adding Comments" # Required: title of the video card/list description: > # Required: description of the video Add comments to your designs in Kanvas's Designer Mode to enhance collaboration and streamline design reviews. videoId: "" # Required: YouTube video ID, example: bb6J--aApk8 videoType: youtube # Required: currently supports "youtube" (support for "local" is present, though currently disabled) # Categories and tags help match videos with documentation pages by scoring relevance, # see the guide at bottom to know how categories: [designer] tags: [review, collaboration, comments] # available as hyperlinked tags in the video card and individual video page duration: 2:30 # Optional: duration in minutes:seconds format ("min" is automatically added) --- # the following youtube shortcode is used for individual video page # Example: {{< youtube id=bb6J--aApk8 class="yt-embed-container" >}} # we can control the styling of resulting iframe and wrapping div by modify style of .yt-embed-container in assets/scss/_videos_project.scss {{< youtube id="videoId" class="yt-embed-container" >}} Approach B: Add Videos Directly Under a Category 🔗 Create video markdown files directly in the category directory with the same frontmatter format shown above. These videos will automatically be assigned to an “ALL” subcategory within the parent category.
Video and Documentation Page Matching 🔗 To display Related Videos carousel on documentation pages section pages and individual pages, videos are matched with the docs pages based on shared tags and categories:
Each matching tag contributes 1 point to the relevance score Each matching category contributes 2 points to the relevance score Videos with at least one matching tag or category appear in the “Related Videos” carousel Videos with higher scores appear first in the carousel Example 🔗 If a documentation page has:
categories: [designer] tags: [catalog, publishing] And there are two videos:
Video A:
categories: [designer] tags: [catalog, review] Video B:
categories: [designer] tags: [designs] Video A scores: 2 (category match) + 1 (tag ‘catalog’) = 3 Video B scores: 2 (category match) + 0 = 2 Video A will appear before Video B in the carousel on the documentation page.
Example Directory Structure 🔗 content/en/videos/ └── template-category/ # Top-level section (category) ├── _index.md # Defines the "Template Category" section └── sub-category/ # Sub-section inside the above category ├── _index.md # Defines the "Sub Category" sub-section └── video-1.md # file containing video specific data See content/en/videos/template-category/ for an example of a category with subcategories and videos. It is set to draft and is not published and is intended as a reference for adding videos.

Layer5 Cloud calls an HTTP endpoint you choose when three things happen: a person asks for help, a Provider Admin decides a signup request, and a person gains Kanvas access. On a self-hosted deployment you set the three endpoints in Helm. None is set by default, and an unset webhook does nothing. The three names are fixed. Adding a fourth webhook requires a change to Layer5 Cloud itself.
Customize and add your own custom webhook 🔗 Set the chart values. They are written into the server ConfigMap as environment variables. There is no .env file to edit in a Helm install.
Step 1: Locate the .env File 🔗 For a Helm deployment, the webhook URLs are env.webhookHelpAndSupport, env.webhookSignupRequest, and env.webhookKanvasEntitlement in your values file. See Helm Chart Values.
Step 2: Define Custom Webhooks in the .env file 🔗 env: webhookHelpAndSupport: "https://hooks.example.com/layer5/support" webhookSignupRequest: "https://hooks.example.com/layer5/signup" webhookKanvasEntitlement: "https://hooks.example.com/layer5/kanvas-access" Chart value Fires when Payload env.webhookHelpAndSupport Someone submits the Help and Support form in Layer5 Cloud, or a support request raised in Kanvas reaches your deployment memberFormOne env.webhookSignupRequest A Provider Admin approves or denies a signup request signupData and newUser env.webhookKanvasEntitlement A new user registers, a user completes a first brokered social sign-in, or a role assignment gives a user Kanvas access signupData and newUser webhookHelpAndSupport also receives Kanvas support requests Support requests raised inside Kanvas travel from the browser to Meshery Server, which forwards them to your Layer5 Cloud deployment, which fires the same webhook. Both sources deliver the same memberFormOne payload. Kanvas users must be connected to your deployment for Help and Support to work. Under Meshery’s local provider the request is refused as not implemented. Leave a webhook unset if you do not need it. Do not invent additional variable names. The server only calls these three.
Step 3: Applying the Configuration 🔗 Upgrade the release. The pods restart because the values land in the ConfigMap.
helm upgrade layer5-cloud layer5/layer5-cloud -n layer5-cloud --values values.yaml Step 4: Testing the Webhooks 🔗 Trigger each one through its real action: submit the Help and Support form, approve a test signup request, or register a test user. There is no signature and no shared secret header. Restrict the receiver by network policy, or put an unguessable token in the URL path.
Property Behavior Method and body POST with a JSON body and Content-Type: application/json; charset=UTF-8. Authentication None. Success A 200 or 202 response. Any other status counts as a failure. Timeout None. The server waits until the receiver answers. Retries None. Each event is sent once. The support and signup webhooks run inside the request of the person who triggered them, so a slow receiver makes that person wait.
Payloads 🔗 Help and support 🔗 { "memberFormOne": { "firstname": "Ada", "lastname": "Admin", "email": "ada@example.com", "message": "I cannot connect my cluster.", "form": "support", "scope": "Layer5 Cloud", "subject": "Connection problem" } } Layer5 Cloud rejects a request that carries any field other than these seven, with a 400 error that names the problem.
Signup decisions 🔗 A decision requires an email, a first name, a last name, and a valid taskLink URL. Otherwise Layer5 Cloud refuses it with a 400 error before any call is made. status is approved or the denial value your receiver should expect from the decision. When the webhook fails, the decision request returns a 500 error (unable to webhook) and an alert event is recorded.
Kanvas entitlement 🔗 newUser is true for a first registration and a first brokered sign-in. For a role assignment it reflects whether the person is new to Kanvas. The formType value is the literal meshmap, the internal name of the Kanvas entitlement. A failure here never blocks the person: Layer5 Cloud records an event and continues.
Failure behavior 🔗 Webhook When the receiver fails What the person sees Help and support The caller receives a 500 error. An error on the form. Signup decision The decision request returns 500. The decision fails with an error. Kanvas entitlement The call is dropped. Nothing. Nothing retries. Reconcile missed events from the signup request list and the audit events.

Layer5 Cloud gives you a home for your designs and the people who work on them: an account, an organization that holds your teams, and workspaces that hold shared resources. Sign up and you already have an organization, a team, and a workspace once the first sign-in succeeds. From there you can invite a teammate and clone a design from the public catalog.
Prerequisites 🔗 A Layer5 Cloud account. Browsing the catalog needs no account. Cloning a design does. Meshery, when you want Layer5 Cloud to act as Meshery’s remote provider. A Kubernetes cluster is something Meshery connects to. Layer5 Cloud does not require a cluster of your own to create an account, an organization, or a design. Installation and Setup 🔗 Layer5 Cloud is a remote provider for Meshery. When you choose Layer5 Cloud as the provider in a Meshery Server, the server sends your browser to Layer5 Cloud to sign in, and Layer5 Cloud returns you to the server with a token. If your browser already holds a live Layer5 Cloud session, Layer5 Cloud skips the sign-in page and hands the token straight back. Layer5 Cloud returns tokens only to callback addresses it trusts and refuses all others. The trust rules are described in How Layer5 Cloud works with Meshery and Kanvas.
Open Meshery. Navigate to your Meshery UI (usually http://localhost:9081). Select the provider. On the login screen, select Layer5 Cloud. Sign in. The server sends your browser to Layer5 Cloud. Sign in with your email and password, GitHub, or Google, or with an identity provider your organization configured. A Meshery Server registers itself with Layer5 Cloud as a connection owned by the signed-in user. Registering the same server again updates that connection in place instead of creating a new one. Because every new account holds the Kanvas role, the Meshery Server receives the Kanvas extension capabilities when it connects with your account. See Meshery Server registration.
Core Workflow 🔗 Everything in Layer5 Cloud sits inside this structure. Your first successful sign-in creates one of each for you.
Object What it is How it relates What you get by default User Your personal identity on Layer5 Cloud. One user can belong to many organizations and teams. Your account, plus the global Kanvas role. Organization The unit of tenancy. Membership in an organization decides who is in. Owns its teams and workspaces. Every user belongs to at least one. My Organization (description “Default Organization”), owned by you, with the Organization Admin role. Team A named group of organization members. Belongs to the organization it is created in. Can be assigned to several workspaces. My Team (description “Default Team”), attached to My Organization, with the Team Admin role. Workspace A group of shared resources such as environments, connections, credentials, and designs. Lives in one organization. Has zero or more teams. A design belongs to at most one workspace. My Workspace (description “Default Workspace”), in My Organization, owned by you. If you would rather start from your own repositories, GitHub integration imports Kubernetes manifests, Helm charts, and Docker Compose files as designs.
Try it out! 🔗 Clone a design from the public catalog into the workspace you have selected. Start from a catalog design walks through browsing, opening a design in the Playground (a preview that creates nothing in your account), and cloning. A clone is named with " (Copy)" appended, is owned by you, and is private.
Deploying that design to a cluster is a Meshery Server operation. Layer5 Cloud stores the design. It does not deploy it.
Need Help? 🔗 If you run into issues during setup, join the Layer5 Slack community. The support page lists email, the community forum, the in-product support form, and what each plan includes.
Follow Along with Five Throughout these docs you’ll follow Five, a Platform Engineer at Orbital Labs, and his colleagues as they set up organizations, configure workspaces, deploy designs, and navigate the occasional Friday-afternoon incident. Meet Five and the full cast Set up your organization 🔗 An organization becomes useful when more than one person works in it. Invite a teammate by email, create a team, create a workspace, give the team that workspace, and move one of your designs into it. The organization decides who is in, teams group people, and workspaces decide which shared resources those people reach.
Before you begin 🔗 You have a Layer5 Cloud account. If not, follow Setting up a Layer5 account. You work in My Organization, the organization Layer5 Cloud created for you, where you hold the Organization Admin role. Any organization where your role grants the permissions below works the same way. You own at least one design. If you do not, clone one first with Creating a design from a catalog template. Each step needs a specific permission. These built-in roles hold them:
Permission Roles that hold it Invite User to Organization Organization Billing Manager, Organization Admin, Provider Admin Create Team Team Admin, Organization Admin, Provider Admin Add User to Team Team Admin, Organization Admin, Provider Admin Create Workspace Workspace Admin, Organization Admin, Provider Admin Assign team to workspace Workspace Admin, Organization Admin, Provider Admin Assign Designs to Workspaces Workspace Admin, Organization Admin, Provider Admin 1. Invite a teammate by email 🔗 Invite your teammate to the organization by email address. Your teammate does not need a Layer5 Cloud account first. An email invitation does all of the following at once:
Creates a pending account for the address. Adds that account to the organization, and to any teams you choose. Assigns the organization and team roles you choose. Sends an invitation email that names you, the organization, and the teams. Its sign-up link pre-fills your teammate’s name and address and carries your organization’s identifier. Layer5 Cloud refuses two kinds of invitation:
Situation Result The address already belongs to a Layer5 Cloud account Refused with HTTP 409 (“invite existing user”). No email address given Refused with HTTP 400 (“email is required”). To bring in someone who already has an account, share your organization’s open invitation link instead. Layer5 Cloud accepts that link on every sign-in, not only the first. See Using the open organization invitation link.
2. Create a team 🔗 Create a team for the people who will share the workspace you build next. A new team belongs to the organization you create it in.
Creating a team and adding people to it are separate actions. Once the team exists, add your teammate to it. When you invite more people later, you can choose this team in the invitation so they join it directly.
3. Create a workspace 🔗 Create a workspace in the same organization. A workspace groups shared resources such as environments, connections, credentials, and designs. Your My Workspace stays as it is. The new workspace is where you and your team collaborate.
4. Assign the team to the workspace 🔗 Assign your new team to the new workspace. Assignment is its own action, separate from creating either object. The relationship is many-to-many:
A workspace has zero or more teams. A team can be assigned to several workspaces. You share access to a workspace’s resources through the teams assigned to it.
5. Move a design into the workspace 🔗 Assign one of your designs to the new workspace. You can assign only designs you own.
Assigning a design moves it. A design belongs to at most one workspace, so assigning it to the new workspace removes it from the workspace it was in before, such as My Workspace.
How the pieces fit together 🔗 Object What it controls What you did with it Organization Who is a member at all. Teams and workspaces belong to one organization. Invited a teammate into My Organization. Team A named group of organization members, each with a team role. Created a team and added your teammate. Workspace A set of shared resources, reached by the teams assigned to it. Created a workspace and assigned the team to it. Design A resource that lives in at most one workspace. Moved a design you own into the workspace. Check your result 🔗 Your organization is set up when all of the following are true:
Your teammate’s account appears in the organization. The new team lists your teammate. The new workspace lists the new team. The design you moved appears in the new workspace and no longer appears in its previous workspace. For the underlying objects, see Organizations, Teams, and Workspaces. Editing the organization, including invitations, is covered in Organization management. Editing and deleting workspaces is covered in Managing workspaces.

GitHub Actions is how Layer5 Cloud meets your pull-request workflow. The Kanvas Snapshot action renders the infrastructure file in a pull request as a Kanvas design and posts the picture as a comment, so reviewers see the resources and their connections before they read the YAML. It runs on GitHub-hosted runners and never touches your cluster.
The action reference, including inputs, the workflow the wizard installs, token handling, and troubleshooting, lives in one place: Kanvas Snapshot.
Kanvas Github Actions 🔗 Kanvas Snapshot Performance Testing with Kanvas Performance testing from a workflow is a Meshery capability, not a Layer5 Cloud one.
Kanvas Snapshot GitHub Action 🔗 Kanvas Snapshot lets you visualize infrastructure changes in pull requests.
See your deployment changes pull request to pull request. Get snapshots of your infrastructure directly in your pull requests. See action in GitHub Marketplace
Configuring Kanvas Snapshots 🔗 Path Use it when Layer5 GitHub App wizard You want Layer5 Cloud to commit the workflow and show you the API token to store as a secret. Start at Integrating GitHub with Meshery, then follow Kanvas Snapshot. Your own workflow You want to pick the triggers, run snapshots from a workflow you already maintain, or authenticate with a personal access token. Follow Kanvas Snapshot. Both paths produce the same pull request comment.
The Kanvas GitHub App requires authorization to interact with your repositories. If you would like to use your GitHub user’s personal access token instead, see Support.
Customizing Snapshot Workflow Triggers in Kanvas Snapshot 🔗 The workflow the wizard installs runs when a pull request is opened, synchronized, or reopened. In a workflow you own, you can use any GitHub event. Only pull request runs post a comment, because the comment needs a pull request number. Other runs still render the snapshot and expose its image URL as an output. See Customizing Snapshot Workflow Triggers.
About events that trigger workflows 🔗 GitHub Actions provides events that can trigger workflows, such as opening a pull request or pushing commits. The snapshot guide lists the events this action handles.
Using Kanvas’s Performance Testing GitHub Action 🔗 You can create performance profiles to run repeatable tests with Meshery. That action is documented in GitOps with Meshery. See action in GitHub Marketplace
What Layer5 Cloud provides 🔗 An API token that authenticates the action to Layer5 Cloud. You generate and revoke tokens in Layer5 Cloud. See Tokens. A GitHub App that installs the workflow file in the repositories you choose, through the GitHub integration wizard. A generated design. Each comment links to the design the action produced.

Understanding the Layer5 Ecosystem 🔗 Kanvas delivers a collaborative experience similar to how Google Workspace transforms the digital work environment and how Figma democratizes UX design tooling. Kanvas simplifies the complexity of Kubernetes and multi-cloud infrastructure management accessible to all. Kanvas provides a visual, multi-player experience that allows you to create, configure, deploy, and manage modern infrastructure with confidence. 5-light-bg Layer5 Cloud is an identity provider and global console for deployments with an extensible and highly flexible authorization framework, tenant entitlement services, service provider-grade organizational hierarchy, team workspace management and a content catalog for public and private hosting of cloud native architectures. Layer5 Cloud is available as a service or self-hosted. What is Kanvas? 🔗 Kanvas is like Google Workspace for DevOps, as it allows you to create, test, and deploy cloud native architectures collaboratively and easily.
Kanvas is a web-based application that allows you to create and share orchestratable diagrams of cloud native infrastructure for Kubernetes and public cloud services. You can draw shapes, lines, text, and icons to represent your infrastructure components and their relationships. Kanvas also supports freestyle design, meaning that you can customize the appearance and layout of your diagrams without any constraints. Kanvas enables real-time collaboration, meaning that you can invite others to join your sessions and edit the diagrams together. Kanvas is a simple and intuitive tool for designing and communicating cloud native infrastructure for Kubernetes and multi-cloud services.
Choose your mode 🔗 Choose your mode of operation for Kanvas.
Designer Designer mode is for those who want to create their own Kanvas, using the palette of components. Drag-and-drop your cloud native infrastructure using a palette of thousands of versioned Kubernetes components.
Use context-aware relationships configure your infrastructure intuitively.
Operator Operator mode is for operating your Kubernetes clusters and cloud native infrastructure. Bring all your Kubernetes clusters under a common management. Deploy designs, apply patterns, manage and operate your deployments and services in real-time.
Interactively connect to pods and containers to debug and troubleshoot.

This guide walks you through the practical steps of managing your Workspaces. Here, you’ll learn how to create, edit, and delete Workspaces, as well as how to manage access by assigning teams and resources like Environments, Designs, and Views to them.
If you’re new to the concept of Workspaces, we recommend starting with the Workspaces Overview to understand what a Workspace is and how it relates to key components like Environments, Designs, and Teams.
A Note on Permissions Every action described in this guide is governed by roles and permissions. To see a detailed breakdown of what your assigned role allows you to do, please refer to the Default Permissions documentation. View Workspaces 🔗 The Workspaces page is where you can see all of the workspaces within the currently selected organization.
To suit different workflows, you can switch between two distinct layouts: a visual grid view and a detailed table view.
Grid View 🔗 The grid view offers a card-based layout, perfect for quickly identifying workspaces at a glance. Each card displays essential information, and you can flip it to reveal management options like editing or deleting and get audit history. Table View 🔗 The table view provides a dense, list-based format that is ideal for managing a large number of workspaces. This view allows for sorting and gives you more control over the specific details you see.
To customize the information displayed, click the View Columns icon and select the attributes you want to see, such as Owner ID or Created Date.
Consistent Actions Across Views Both the grid and table views provide the same set of management capabilities. You can choose the layout that best fits your needs without losing any functionality. Create a Workspace 🔗 Creating a new workspace allows you to manage resources, and define team access.
Permissions Required Creating a workspace requires the Create Workspace key in the organization that will own it. Organization Admin and Workspace Admin hold it by default. A custom role can hold it too. See Default Permissions. To create a workspace:
Click the + Create button to open the creation Dialog. From the dropdown menu, select the Organization that will own the new workspace. The chosen Organization cannot be changed after the workspace is created. Please select carefully. Enter a descriptive Name and an optional Description, then click Save. Name and description are each limited to 255 characters. A longer value fails with Unable to create workspace. Names do not have to be unique. Your new workspace will now appear on the page. It has no teams and no environments. The workspace stays in the organization you chose. Edit a Workspace 🔗 You can modify a workspace’s name and description at any time after it has been created. An update changes only the fields you send. The organization never changes. A workspace that is not in one of your organizations answers workspace not found.
From the Grid View: Flip the workspace card, then click the pencil icon. From the Table View: Click the pencil icon in the row of the workspace you wish to modify. Delete a Workspace 🔗 You can delete a single workspace or multiple workspaces at once.
To delete a single workspace:
From the Grid View, flip the workspace card, then click the trash can icon. From the Table View, click the trash can icon in the row of the workspace you wish to delete. To delete multiple workspaces (Grid View only):
Select the checkboxes on the cards of the workspaces you want to delete. Click the Delete button that appears at the top of the page. Deletion Restrictions An organization must keep at least one workspace. Layer5 Cloud refuses to delete the last one with cannot delete workspace: at least one workspace must exist for the organization. The refusal arrives as HTTP 500. The check holds under concurrent requests, so two simultaneous deletes cannot empty an organization. Create the replacement workspace first, then delete the other. Workspace Deletion Behavior 🔗 What Happens When a Workspace is Deleted? Deleting a workspace ends every team, environment, design, and view assignment it holds. It does not delete those resources. Designs and views remain, with no workspace, until you assign them to another one. When a Workspace is deleted:
The workspace record is removed. Proceed with caution: the assignment list is not restored. Teams, environments, connections, designs, and views all remain. Designs and views that were in the workspace have no workspace afterwards. Move them to another workspace first if you want them to keep a home. Team members lose the read-only connection access that flowed through the deleted workspace. Assign Teams to a Workspace 🔗 Assigning a team grants its members read-only access to the connections, and their credentials, in every environment linked to the workspace. It does not grant access to private designs or views, and it does not decide who can see the workspace: every organization member can already list every workspace.
The team and the workspace must belong to the same organization. A team from another organization is refused with HTTP 403. Assigning a team that is already assigned changes nothing. Removing the team ends the connection access at once.
To give someone access to a private design, share the design with that person. See Sharing Designs and Sharing a Workspace.
You can open the team management Dialog from either the grid or table view.
From the Grid View: Click the Teams tile. From the Table View: Click the Teams icon in the workspace row. A list of currently assigned teams will appear. From there, click the Assign Team button to open the assignment Dialog. Inside the assignment Dialog, you will see two lists: Available Teams on the left and Assigned Teams on the right.
Select one or more teams from either list. Use the arrow buttons to move the selected teams between the lists: > Assigns a selected team. < Unassigns a selected team. » Assigns all available teams. « Unassigns all assigned teams. Click Save to apply your changes. Team and Workspace Relationships You can assign multiple teams to a single workspace, and a single team can also be a member of multiple workspaces. This provides flexible access control across your projects. For more restrictions, see Workspaces documentation. Link Environments to a Workspace 🔗 When you link an Environment to a Workspace, its connections become readable by every member of the workspace’s teams. The access is read-only. The environment and the workspace must belong to the same organization; a cross-organization attachment is refused with HTTP 403.
Some environments are provisioned by Layer5 Cloud itself to hold organization configuration such as the mail server or sign-in providers. Layer5 Cloud refuses to attach one to a workspace: this environment is provisioned by the platform and cannot be added to a workspace. Attaching an environment that is already attached returns the existing attachment. Detaching one that was never attached answers no such environment assignment.
The process of linking environments is almost the same as assigning teams. Opening the Environments tile is also how you see which Environments a Workspace currently draws on: the dialog’s assigned list is that Workspace’s Environments.
Many-to-Many Relationship An Environment can be linked to multiple Workspaces, and a Workspace can have multiple Environments. This allows you to share common environments across different projects. Managing the Environments Themselves Creating an Environment, editing it, and choosing which Connections belong to it are done on the Environments page rather than here. See Managing Environments. Move Designs and Views Between Workspaces 🔗 Unlike Environments, a Design or View belongs to at most one Workspace. Placing it in a workspace moves it: Layer5 Cloud removes every earlier workspace assignment, then adds the new one. There is no copy. Removing it leaves the design or view with no workspace. The resource and its owner are unaffected.
The permission is checked in the destination workspace’s organization only. Layer5 Cloud does not check that you can open the workspace the design leaves. The unassigned list shows only designs you own. The workspace decides the organization the design is listed under. A private design stays private wherever it sits.
How to Move a Design or View 🔗 Click the Designs/Views tile on the Workspace card (or the equivalent icon in the table view) to open the management Dialog. Inside the Dialog, select the Design(s) or View(s). Use the arrow buttons to move the selected Design(s) or View(s) to the target workspace. Click Save. Exclusive Ownership A Design or View can only exist in one Workspace at a time. Moving it to a new Workspace will automatically remove it from its original location. For more detailed information, see Workspaces documentation. View Recent Activity 🔗 Meshery keeps a detailed audit log for each workspace, allowing you to track all significant events. This is useful for maintaining security and troubleshooting issues.
The activity log captures a variety of events, including:
The creation, update, or deletion of the workspace. The assignment or unassignment of Teams, Environments, Designs, and Views. Every entry carries the email address of the person who acted. Failed attempts are recorded as error events. Reading the log requires the View Workspace permission. The log is paged and searchable.
Putting It All Together: A Hands-on Guide To see how managing a Workspace fits into a complete, end-to-end workflow, follow the Using Workspaces Effectively learning path. Common Workspace Usage Patterns 🔗 There isn’t a single “best” way to organize your workspaces, as structure depends heavily on team dynamics and project needs. Instead, we recommend a flexible, multi-layered approach to maximize workspace effectiveness. Below are common usage patterns:
1. The Project Hub
Dedicate a shared workspace to each project. It becomes a central hub where your team can co-develop designs, share reusable components, and align with specific environments (e.g., staging or production). This keeps all your environments, history, and resources in one place
2. Your Personal “My Drive”
Think of a workspace you keep for your own designs as a personal working area. You can use it for confidential designs or for trying ideas. Team assignment still does not open those designs to anyone else. Share a design when you are ready for someone else to open it.
3. Template Library
Create a separate, access-controlled Workspace to serve as your organization’s internal, private template library. This is for storing non-public, organization-specific, or sensitive patterns.
This practice complements the public Catalog, which is used for sharing generic, non-sensitive designs with the community. A dedicated Organization Catalog feature is also planned for the future.
4. The Team Space
You can also organize long-term workspaces around specific teams, such as a “Developer Hub” or “QA Workspace.” This simplifies resource management and makes it easy to monitor team-wide activity.
5. The Environment-Specific Space
For teams requiring strict separation between environments, give a production workspace only the production environment and the platform team. Members of other teams cannot read production connections through it. Moving a design into that workspace is the promotion. There is no separate approval step. See Promoting a Design from Staging to Prod.
FAQ 🔗 1. When a design is transferred from one Workspace to the next, is design ownership affected? Who has access? What if the Workspaces are in different orgs? 🔗 Ownership: A Design’s ownership is permanent. The user who created it stays its owner after any move. Ownership never transfers. Access: Workspace membership grants no design access. Only the owner, provider administrators, and users the design was shared with can open a private design. Cross-Organization Transfers: Moving a design into a workspace in another organization lists the design under that organization. The permission checked is Assign Designs to Workspaces in the destination organization. 2. What can other users of a Workspace do with my design? Can they delete my design? 🔗 Workspace membership grants no design access. People you shared the design with can read, edit, and clone it. Only the owner or a provider administrator can delete it.
3. Can Workspaces contain private, public, and published designs? 🔗 Yes. A Workspace can simultaneously contain Designs that are private, public, and published.
4. How will I know if another user made changes to my design? Will I be notified? Is there an edit history or audit trail? 🔗 Currently, it is not possible to receive direct notifications or see a collaborative audit trail of changes made by other users. While a Version History feature exists for Designs, it currently only tracks changes made by you, not changes from other collaborators.
5. If I share my private design with a user in a different org, can they share my design with other users? 🔗 Sharing onward depends on that person’s own Share Design permission, not on the grant. A collaborator who holds Share Design can share the design onward. A grant is for one person. A team grant is not honored, so grant each person. See Sharing Designs.
learn more about sharing designs.
6. Does a workspace have space limitations or file count limitations? 🔗 Layer5 Cloud enforces no space or file-count limit on workspaces, and no plan check on workspace actions.
7. How can I make my design publicly available, but read-only to other users? 🔗 To make a Design available to everyone but in a read-only state, you should Publish it. A Published design can be viewed and cloned by any user, but the original cannot be edited by others.
8. How do I share a private design with a specific team for collaboration? 🔗 Assigning a team to the workspace does not open the design. Share it with each person:
Open the design and click Share. Search for the person and add them. The dialog finds individual users only. There is no view-only or comment-only level: a person who can open the design can edit it. Confirm the person appears under People with Access. A private design stays private. To remove someone, open Share and remove them from People with Access. See Sharing a Workspace.

Layer5 Cloud is a Meshery remote provider. When a Meshery Server uses Layer5 Cloud, hosted or self-hosted, the server registers itself with Cloud on behalf of the signed-in user. Registration is what makes that Meshery Server known to Cloud: it appears as a meshery connection owned by that user. This page explains what the server sends, how Cloud tells a new server from one it already knows, what survives re-registration, and what each failure means.
For where registration fits between Cloud and Meshery, see How Layer5 Cloud works with Meshery and Kanvas.
Why Registration Exists 🔗 Registration answers two questions for Cloud:
Which Meshery Server is calling? Many Meshery deployments can work with the same Cloud deployment, and Cloud must keep them apart. Who owns it? Every registration is owned by exactly one user, the user whose session made the request. A registration record answers both. It ties a stable server identifier to an owner and survives Meshery Server restarts.
Identifying a Meshery Server 🔗 A Meshery Server generates a stable server identifier on its first start and keeps it locally. It sends that identifier as serverId inside the connection’s metadata. The key is camelCase.
Cloud recognizes an existing registration by three values together:
the connection kind, meshery the owner, which is the authenticated user metadata.serverId Each owner and serverId pair maps to exactly one connection. Cloud places no limit on either side of that pair: one user can register any number of Meshery Servers, and one Meshery Server can be registered by any number of users, with one connection per user.
Connections are owned by a user, not by an organization. Each user sees their own connections, including the Meshery Servers they registered.
Registration Endpoint 🔗 A Meshery Server registers by sending a connection to:
POST /api/integrations/connections The request must be authenticated with a Cloud session or a bearer token. Cloud takes the owner from that authentication, never from the request body.
Field Required Description kind Yes The connection kind. Case-insensitive. Accepted values are meshery, kubernetes, prometheus, and grafana. A Meshery Server registers itself with meshery. metadata.serverId Yes, for meshery The stable identifier the Meshery Server generated. The key is camelCase. name No A display name. When omitted, Cloud names the connection <kind>-<random>, for example meshery- followed by a random suffix. metadata (other keys) No Additional details about the server, such as its version. Cloud refreshes them on every registration. On success, Cloud responds with HTTP 201 and a one-item page of connections containing the registered connection. Every registration call, first or repeat, records a “registered” event for the connection in the account’s event log.
What Happens on First Registration 🔗 When no connection matches the owner and serverId, Cloud creates a new meshery connection owned by the authenticated user.
The request is rejected before anything is stored when authentication does not resolve to a user. The error is “cannot register meshery connection: missing owner in authenticated session”.
What Happens on Re-Registration 🔗 A re-registration is any later call from the same Meshery Server, carrying the same serverId, for the same user. It typically follows a Meshery Server restart, a new sign-in, or a reconnect.
Cloud updates the existing connection in place:
Kept from the stored connection Refreshed from the request ID, name, kind, type, sub-type, status, owner, and creation time Metadata and the last-updated time Two consequences follow:
Re-registering never renames a server. A request that omits name, and would otherwise get a random name, cannot replace the name the connection already has. Re-registering never resets status. A Meshery Server you disconnected or ignored stays disconnected or ignored when it registers again. Status changes through connection lifecycle actions Connection status changes through the dedicated connection lifecycle actions, such as connect, disconnect, ignore, and delete, not through registration. Registration carries the stored status forward, so a restarting server cannot undo a status you set. Validation and Error Cases 🔗 Condition Result The request carries no Cloud session or bearer token Rejected. The endpoint requires authentication. The authentication does not resolve to a user Rejected before anything is stored, with the error “cannot register meshery connection: missing owner in authenticated session”. kind is not one of the accepted values HTTP 500 with the error “connection kind: <kind>, not implemented yet”. metadata.serverId is missing or empty on a meshery registration HTTP 500 with the error “empty server id; cannot check for existence”. No connection is created. A missing or empty serverId does not fall back to creating an unidentified connection.
Operator Guidance 🔗 If you operate a self-hosted Layer5 Cloud, these symptoms map to the most common causes:
Registration fails with “missing owner in authenticated session”. The request reached Cloud with authentication that does not resolve to a user. Look at the request in your logs and confirm that it carries a valid session or bearer token for an existing account. Registration fails with “empty server id; cannot check for existence”. The client did not send serverId in metadata. Cloud does not fall back to creating an unidentified connection. Confirm that the client sends the identifier under the camelCase key serverId. Registration fails with “not implemented yet”. The client sent a kind other than meshery, kubernetes, prometheus, or grafana. A Meshery Server appears under the wrong user. The owner comes from the session, not from the request body. The server was registered while a different account was signed in. The same Meshery Server appears more than once. Each owner and serverId pair is a separate connection, so a server registered by two users appears once for each of them. If one user sees the same server twice, the server presented a different serverId, which happens when it loses the identifier it stored locally and generates a new one. A Meshery Server’s name or status in Cloud does not change when it reconnects. This is intended. Re-registration preserves the stored name and status. Change them through the connection’s own actions. Where the Code Lives 🔗 The behavior on this page is the contract for POST /api/integrations/connections. Identity is the triple of kind meshery, the authenticated owner, and metadata.serverId. Status changes go through the connection lifecycle actions (connect, disconnect, ignore, and delete), not through registration.
Other connection kinds 🔗 The same endpoint registers the other accepted kinds, with their own identity rules:
Kubernetes. Cloud derives the connection’s ID from the cluster and the owner, so registering the same cluster again updates the existing connection instead of creating another. Cloud stores the cluster’s credential once and keeps the stored status. Prometheus and Grafana. Cloud creates the connection or updates the existing one in place.

Metrics provide valuable insights into how users engage with the designs, allowing us to understand usage patterns, identify trends, and make data-driven decisions to improve the user experience.
The design catalog can be accessed from the Layer5 Cloud catalog page at Layer5 Cloud Catalog.
Design Capabilities Designs can be imported, exported, versioned, forked, merged, snapshotted, published, shared, embedded, templatized, and more. Learn more about Designs You can view the metrics of a Design in two ways:
Below each Design’s catalog card, you can see its metrics. By clicking on the catalog card, a modal will pop up displaying all the information about the Design, including its metrics. Here’s a detailed explanation of each metric we track:
1. Opens 🔗 This metric helps us understand how often users are viewing a particular design.
2. Downloads 🔗 Downloads provide insights into the popularity and demand for a design.
3. Deploys 🔗 This metric shows how often a design is implemented or put into action.
4. Clones 🔗 Cloning metrics indicate how often users are creating copies of a design for modification or personal use.
5. Shares 🔗 Shares measure how often a design is shared.
How to read the counters 🔗 The counters are lifetime totals.
No deduplication. One person opening a design ten times adds ten Opens. The counters measure activity, not distinct people. Signed-out activity counts. Opens from anonymous visitors are included. No time window and no reset. A counter only grows. An older design has had more time to accumulate counts than a newer one. Edits do not reset them. Changing a design keeps its counts. Best effort. If recording a count fails, the action itself still succeeds, so a counter can undercount slightly. The same five counters appear on catalog cards and drive the Leaderboard, which is the catalog sorted by one counter. By default that sort is Opens, highest first.

This guide covers creating new organizations, editing their details, inviting members, and deleting organizations when necessary.
Permissions Required Operations described on this page for managing your Organization typically require Organization Administrator or similar administrative roles. To understand the specific roles needed for each action, please refer to the Default Permissions reference. Creating an Organization 🔗 An Organization provides a way to structure your teams, users, and resource access for different projects or initiatives.
How to create an Organization 🔗 Go to the Organizations section, click the Add Organization button The “Create New Organization” modal will appear: Organization Name: Enter a name for your new Organization. This is a required field. The form keeps Create disabled until you enter a name. Layer5 Cloud does not require the name to be unique. Country (Optional): Select the country for your Organization. Region (Optional): Choose the time zone for your Organization. Add Organization Members (Optional): You can begin adding existing Layer5 Cloud users to your new Organization in this field. What creation does: you become the owner, you and any users you picked are added as members, and Layer5 Cloud creates a default workspace named My Workspace, owned by you. Ownership cannot be transferred. A new organization does not carry a domain. A Provider Admin assigns one afterward. Creating a child inside a parent also makes the creator a member and an Organization Admin of the child.
Unable to Create More Organizations? If the “Add Organization” button is disabled, your role lacks Create Organization. Organization Admin and Provider Admin hold it by default. Child Organizations 🔗 An Organization can have child Organizations of its own, to any depth. A child is created from the Child organizations section of the Organizations page, and an Organization Administrator or Owner of the parent can edit the child’s settings and membership, or delete it, without joining the child. Anything inside the child still requires membership in the child. Deleting an Organization that still has children is refused until the children are deleted. See Child Organizations for details.
Editing Your Organization 🔗 You can update your Organization’s name, location, associated teams, branding, and identity providers, as well as access its invitation link, by editing its details.
How to Edit Your Organization 🔗 Select the Organization you want to modify and click its “Edit” button. The “Edit Organization” modal will open: Add Team: Associate existing Teams with this Organization. Theme: Customize your Organization’s visual theme by selecting from the available color swatches. Logos: Upload specific logo versions for various display contexts by clicking the respective “Upload” buttons. Invitations: Access a shareable link to invite users to your Organization. Identity Providers: Configure which OAuth applications power your Organization’s sign-in (see Configuring Identity Providers below). Email: Send your Organization’s email through your own mail server, from your own domain (see Configuring Your Own Mail Server below). Configuring Identity Providers (Bring-Your-Own Credentials) 🔗 The Identity Providers tab controls which OAuth applications power sign-in for your Organization. This is most useful when your Organization uses a custom domain and you want your own brand, not Layer5’s, shown on the Google, GitHub, or OIDC consent screen.
By default, your Organization uses Layer5’s shared OAuth applications. To override them, add your own provider. There is no separate “enable” step:
Use Add Google, Add GitHub, or Add OIDC to register a provider. Each walkthrough displays the exact redirect URI to add to your OAuth application. Saving your first provider switches the Organization to its own identity providers automatically. Use Edit to rotate a provider’s credentials, or Remove to delete a single provider. Removing your last provider reverts the Organization to Layer5’s defaults. Use Delete All Identity Providers to remove every configured provider at once. This deletes the Environment that Layer5 Cloud provisioned to hold them, and the Organization reverts to Layer5’s default identity providers. Every removal asks you to confirm and explains the consequences before it proceeds.
Who can configure this Organization Administrators and Owners can add, rotate, and remove their Organization’s identity providers themselves. Provider Administrators can additionally manage the Identity Providers configuration (and the configuration of other aspects) of any Organization - whether or not they are members of it. Switching identity providers does not affect existing user accounts or login history. Users who signed in through a provider you later remove may need to re-authenticate.
Configuring Your Own Mail Server 🔗 The Email tab lets your Organization send application mail such as invitations and notifications through its own SMTP server, from its own domain, instead of through Layer5’s shared mail server. Nothing about the message then points to a shared provider.
Setting it up has three steps: register the server and its credentials, prove control of the sending domain by publishing a DNS TXT record, and pass a connection test. Completing them changes nothing on its own - mail keeps leaving through Layer5’s shared server until an administrator clicks Turn on, which is what switches routing over. The tab reports delivery health afterwards, and a fallback setting decides what happens to a message your server does not accept.
The full walkthrough, including a worked example for Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Amazon SES, SendGrid and Postmark, and a troubleshooting table for every failure the tab reports, is in Bring Your Own Mail Server.
Who can configure this Organization Administrators and Owners can configure, test, turn on, turn off, and remove their Organization’s mail server, under the same gate as the Identity Providers tab. Using the Open Organization Invitation Link 🔗 To invite multiple users to your organization at once, or to allow open sign-ups (for example, for a public community), you can use the “Open Organization Invitation Link.” This is a shareable link that lets users join directly.
When to Use This Link 🔗 Bulk Onboarding: To quickly onboard many users without sending individual emails. Public Sign-ups: To let people sign up openly, for instance, by posting the link on a community page or another public resource. Cross-Organizational Collaboration: To make it easy for collaborators from other organizations or external partners to join. Inviting users to specific teams Layer5 Cloud has no team invite link. To place people into teams, list the teams on an organization invitation. See Teams and User Invitations. How it Works 🔗 For New Users (without an existing Layer5 Cloud account):
When a new user clicks the invitation link, they will be directed to the sign-up page. After creating their account, they will be automatically added to the organization associated with the invite link. For Existing Users (with a Layer5 Cloud account):
An existing user who signs in through the organization’s address joins with their current account, if they are not already a member. Acceptance adds the organization, team, and role grants the invitation carries. It never removes anything. If acceptance fails, Layer5 Cloud logs the failure and the sign-in still succeeds. The organization record publishes the open invitation’s id, and the id is also its invitation code. Treat an open invitation as a shareable link, not a secret. You designate it in either of two places: the Open Org Invitation setting of the organization, or the open-signup option on the invitation itself. When both are set, the organization’s setting wins as long as it names a live invitation of that organization. Writing the organization setting needs Organization Admin in the organization or in its parent. Setting isDefault on the invitation needs Manage Invitations.
Deleting Your Organization 🔗 Deleting an organization retires it and every membership in it. The operation has no undo. The organization’s owner, a Provider Admin, or an Organization Admin or owner of the live parent can delete it. An Organization Admin who is not the owner cannot.
Deletion is Permanent and Unrecoverable Once an Organization is deleted, this action cannot be undone. There is no restore operation. Consequences of Deletion 🔗 Deleting is a soft delete. It does the following:
The organization is marked deleted and no longer appears in any list or switcher. Every user membership in the organization ends. User accounts are not deleted. Every mapping between the organization and its teams ends. The teams themselves are not removed. The organization’s domain stops routing. The deleted organization still holds the domain, so no other organization can use it. Clear the domain before you delete if the address needs to be reused. The request does not delete the organization’s workspaces, environments, or designs. Nothing reaches them through the organization afterwards.
Layer5 Cloud refuses the deletion when the organization still has child organizations (HTTP 409, nothing is changed) or when it is the last live organization the caller owns (HTTP 403, you can't delete your last organization). The last-organization check does not apply when a parent’s administrator deletes a child.
When NOT to Delete 🔗 Avoid deleting an Organization if:
You might need the Organization or its data later. Critical resources within it have not been backed up or migrated. Other users or services still depend on it. You only need to modify memberships or restructure parts of it. You are unsure about the full extent of its data or dependencies. When Deletion May Be Appropriate 🔗 The Organization was for a temporary project or test and is no longer needed. It was created in error or is now redundant due to consolidation. Permanent removal of all its data is required for compliance or data lifecycle management. You are certain all its resources are obsolete or migrated, and no dependencies remain. How to Delete Your Organization 🔗 Select the Organization you want to delete and click its “Delete” button. A confirmation modal will appear, requiring you to verify this action. Click the “Delete” button to permanently remove the Organization. To abort the deletion, click “Cancel”. Branding 🔗 Branding applies to the signed-in experience and, on an organization with its own domain, to the sign-in, sign-up, and error pages.
Theme colors. Every color must be a hex value (#rgb, #rgba, #rrggbb, or #rrggbbaa). Layer5 Cloud rejects any other value with a 400 error that names the color. Resetting the theme also clears the logos. Logos. Four slots: desktop, mobile, dark desktop, and dark mobile. Each image can be at most 500 KB. A larger file fails the update with image size exceeds the maximum limit. Links. Terms of Service and Privacy Policy accept an http or https URL, a mailto: or tel: link, or a root-relative path. Support entries accept the same forms plus plain text without a colon. LinkedIn, X, and YouTube accept an absolute http or https URL. Layer5 Cloud silently drops a value it considers unsafe, including javascript: and data: links, instead of rejecting the update. Clearing every link restores the defaults. Feature carousel. Whether sign-in pages show the feature carousel. On by default. Domain 🔗 Only a Provider Admin can set a domain to a new value. Any other caller receives a 403 error that says a domain requires a Provider Admin. Clearing the field removes the assignment and is open to the organization’s administrators. Keeping the stored value is also open to those administrators.
Layer5 Cloud checks a changed domain when you save: 3 to 253 characters, dot-separated labels of 1 to 63 ASCII letters, digits, or hyphens, a label not starting or ending with a hyphen, a hostname rather than an email address, not starting with http, https, or www, not one of the provider’s reserved hosts, and unique across organizations including deleted ones. Internationalized names are written in Punycode (xn--). The check is syntactic. Layer5 Cloud does not look the name up in DNS. Lookups are cached for five minutes, and every organization create, update, and delete clears the affected entry on the server that handled the change.
Teams in the organization 🔗 Adding a team maps the team into the organization. Removing a team ends that mapping only. The team itself is not deleted. Adding a team requires an Organization Admin or owner of the organization, or a Provider Admin. Removing a team also admits someone who is both Team Admin and team owner of that team. Removing a team that does not belong to the organization returns a 404 error.
Managing members 🔗 Adding a member attaches an existing Layer5 Cloud account. It does not create an account. Adding someone who is already a member changes nothing. The caller must be an Organization Admin or owner of the organization, a Provider Admin, or an Organization Admin or owner of its parent. Removal ends the person’s organization membership and their membership in every team of that organization. Their account stays. The owner cannot be removed (Organization owner cannot be removed). Removing someone with no membership returns no organization membership to remove. Repeating a removal is harmless. See User Management.
Assigning or removing an organization role requires an Organization Admin of that organization, a Provider Admin, or Assign User Roles in it. The target must be a member, except when a Provider Admin makes the change. A row the caller may not change is skipped and reported as unauthorized to assign org roles, and the rest of the request still applies. Only a Provider Admin can assign provider roles.
Switching Between Organizations 🔗 Your current organization decides which resources you see, where new resources land, and which permissions apply. The switcher lists only the organizations you are a member of. Members who hold View All Organizations, a Provider Admin by default, can also select All Organizations. If you need an organization you are not in, ask its administrator or use an invitation link. See Navigating Organizations for the same behavior in more detail.
Layer5 Cloud decides the organization for each request from these sources, first match wins:
Domain. If the address you reached maps to an organization, that organization applies. This outranks every selection you make. X-Current-Orgid request header. API clients set it per request. Saved preference. The organization you last selected is stored in your user preferences. Browser session. The organization saved in the session cookie. Layer5 Cloud ignores a header, preference, or session value that names an organization you do not belong to, and runs the request with no organization scope. Holders of View All Organizations are exempt and can name any organization. There is no query-string source.
Area Behavior Designs, workspaces, environments, connections Only the selected organization’s resources appear. New resources Created in the selected organization. Resources do not follow you between organizations. Roles and permissions Scoped to the organization. Administrative rights in one organization grant nothing in another. Team memberships The memberships and permissions of the selected organization apply. Limits today 🔗 These actions do not exist in Layer5 Cloud today:
Transfer ownership. The creator stays the owner. Leave an organization on your own. An administrator removes a member. Restore a deleted organization. Move a child organization to a different parent.
