body:
An organization is the tenant boundary in Layer5 Cloud. It decides whose resources a request can reach, whose billing it counts against, and which roles apply. The organization is the unit of multi-tenancy and the core security boundary. Teams and workspaces belong to one organization, and users hold roles in it. Roles, keychains, and keys are defined once for the whole provider, but resources, billing, and access control are isolated per organization, so a role held in one organization grants nothing in another.
The structure is flexible. An organization has any number of teams. A team has any number of users, and a user can belong to any number of teams. A user can belong to any number of organizations and holds an independent set of roles in each.
Teams group users inside an organization and control access to workspaces and to workspace resources such as environments and managed and unmanaged connections. See Teams and Workspaces.
Every deployment has one provider organization and any number of tenant organizations. The provider organization operates the deployment and owns its default identity providers, which tenants use unless they bring their own. It is never a child, and it cannot hold child organizations. A tenant is every other organization. A tenant is configured as Hosted, Branded, or White-Label, depending on the domain it uses and the identity provider that authenticates its users. For how to choose, see Organization Configuration Scenarios.
Example: The Orbital Labs Ecosystem 🔗 The following organizations illustrate how multi-tenancy works across provider, startup, and enterprise tiers. Follow along in the rest of the docs using Five and the cast at Orbital Labs.
Constellation Cloud, Provider Type: Managed Service Provider
Plan: Enterprise
Provider Admin: Dr. Aiko Sato
Constellation Cloud manages multiple tenant organizations, including Orbital Labs and Stellar Dynamics. As the provider, it controls the top-level entitlement configuration for all tenants.
“We keep the lights on so you don’t have to.”
Orbital Labs, Startup Tenant Type: Cloud-native startup
Plan: Team
Org Admin: Maya Chen
Orbital Labs is a tenant of Constellation Cloud. Users at Orbital Labs belong to one or more teams (Infrastructure, Development) and access workspaces within their organization.
“Moving fast and occasionally breaking staging.”
Stellar Dynamics, Enterprise Tenant Type: Enterprise client
Plan: Enterprise
Org Admin: Marcus Webb
Stellar Dynamics is a separate tenant of Constellation Cloud and an enterprise client of Orbital Labs. Users at Stellar Dynamics can be granted access to specific Orbital Labs workspaces and designs via cross-org access controls.
“Fortune 500, cloud-native ambitions, legacy everything.”
Cross-Organization Access 🔗 Users of one organization may be granted access to resources (workspaces, designs) in another organization. Entitlements are org-scoped: the permissions a user has in Orbital Labs do not automatically apply in Stellar Dynamics, and vice versa.
Cross-organization access works through resource-access mappings, a grant attached to an individual resource (such as a single design) that names the user it is shared with. These mappings deliberately cross the organization boundary: a user does not need to be a member of an organization to open a resource that has been shared with them there. For example, when Maya at Orbital Labs shares the stellar-saas-platform design with Marcus at Stellar Dynamics, Marcus can open that one design even though he is not a member of Orbital Labs. This is the mechanism that makes collaboration between organizations possible, and it is distinct from organization membership and from the organization-scoped roles described below. Sharing a single resource grants access to that resource only. It does not make the recipient a member of the organization, give them a role there, or reach any of the organization’s other resources.
Info Organization membership alone does not decide what a user can see and do. For how the connected identity provider, organization-scoped roles, and resource-access mappings fit together, and what counts as a security boundary, see Identity and Security: Security Boundaries. Info See Meet Five and the Cast for the full narrative reference, including team structure and workspace inventory. Child organizations 🔗 A child organization is a tenant created inside another tenant, its parent. See Child Organizations.
An organization can have any number of children, and children can have children of their own. There is no depth limit. A child has exactly one parent, fixed when the child is created. A child cannot be moved to a different parent. The Organization Admin or owner of a parent governs its direct children only: they can edit a child’s settings, add members to it, search its members, and delete it. Governing a grandchild belongs to the administrator of the intermediate organization. A parent administrator is not a member of the child. Workspaces, teams, connections, identity providers, and the mail server inside the child still require membership and a role in the child. An organization that still has live child organizations cannot be deleted. Delete the deepest children first. The provider organization cannot hold child organizations. The owner 🔗 The user who creates an organization is its owner. Ownership is a fixed attribute of the organization, separate from the Organization Admin role.
The owner cannot be removed from the organization. A removal request for the owner fails with “Organization owner cannot be removed”. Ownership cannot be transferred. Layer5 Cloud has no operation that reassigns the owner of an organization. No member can leave an organization on their own. Membership ends only when an authorized administrator removes the member. The owner can delete the organization. An Organization Admin who is not the owner cannot. Plan who creates each organization accordingly. For a shared or long-lived organization, have it created by the account that should remain its owner.
How a request or sign-in finds its organization 🔗 Every guarded request runs in one organization. Layer5 Cloud resolves that organization from these sources, in this order, and the first source that applies wins:
Domain. The request’s host matches an organization’s custom domain. X-Current-Orgid header. The organization an API client names. Saved preference. The default organization stored in the user’s preferences. Browser session. The organization the browser session last selected. The header, the saved preference, and the browser session must name an organization the user is a live member of. A value that names any other organization is ignored, and the request runs with no organization scope. Callers who hold View All Organizations (Provider Admin by default) are the exception: they can name any organization, or all to span every organization. Layer5 Cloud reads no organization from the query string.
Why the domain wins 🔗 A custom domain identifies the tenant before the user makes any choice. A sign-in page served on an organization’s domain shows that organization’s branding, authenticates through that organization’s identity provider, and applies its open invitation, so the request belongs to that organization regardless of the user’s saved preference. Resolving by domain does not check membership. Every guarded action still checks the permissions the user holds in that organization.
Domain matching follows these rules:
The host is matched exactly against organization domains, with the protocol and port removed. The deployment’s own base host, IP addresses, and the provider’s reserved domains are never treated as custom domains. A domain belongs to at most one organization. A deleted organization keeps its domain, so clear the domain before deleting if the address must be reused. Domain-to-organization lookups are cached for five minutes. Creating, editing, or deleting an organization clears its entry on the server that handled the change, so other server instances can serve the previous mapping until their entry expires. Assigning a new domain to an organization requires a Provider Admin. Organization administrators can keep the current domain or clear it. Layer5 Cloud validates the domain’s syntax when it is saved and does not perform a DNS lookup. See Organization Configuration Scenarios.
The organization switcher lists only the organizations the user is a member of. Holders of View All Organizations can also select All Organizations. See Navigating Organizations.
Lifecycle 🔗 Organization Management covers the procedures.
Create 🔗 An organization starts with a name (required), a country, and a region. Creating it does two things:
The creator becomes the owner. Layer5 Cloud creates a default workspace named “My Workspace”, owned by the creator. A domain is not set at creation. A Provider Admin assigns one afterward. Creating a child organization inside a parent requires Create Organization in the parent, and makes the creator a member and an Organization Admin of the child.
Edit 🔗 Administrators of the organization shape how it looks and how users join it:
Setting What it controls Name, country, region The organization’s identity in lists and the switcher. Branding Theme colors (hex values only) and four logos: desktop, mobile, dark desktop, and dark mobile, each up to 500 KB. Resetting the theme also clears the logos. Links Terms of service, privacy policy, support channels, and social links shown on the organization’s sign-in, sign-up, and error pages and in email footers. Unsafe values are dropped rather than rejected. Sign-in carousel Whether sign-in pages show the feature carousel. On by default. Domain The custom host that resolves to the organization. New values require a Provider Admin. Open invitation One invitation that admits any non-member who signs in through the organization’s host. The user gains the invitation’s organization, team, and role grants. The invitation’s ID is public and works as a shareable link. Teams Which teams belong to the organization. Removing a team ends the mapping. The team itself is not deleted. Identity providers The organization’s own sign-in providers, in place of the provider organization’s defaults. Mail server The organization’s own SMTP server for outgoing email. See Bring Your Own Mail Server. Delete 🔗 Deleting an organization is a soft delete:
The organization, every membership in it, and every team-to-organization mapping end. Teams, workspaces, environments, and designs are not deleted by the request, but nothing reaches them through the organization afterward. No restore operation exists. Layer5 Cloud refuses the deletion in two cases:
The organization still has live child organizations (HTTP 409). Nothing is changed. The organization is the last live organization the caller owns (HTTP 403). This check does not apply when a parent administrator deletes a child. The organization’s owner, a Provider Admin, or an Organization Admin or owner of the live parent can delete an organization.
Who can do what 🔗 Several organization actions check a role or ownership on the server rather than a single permission key:
Delete the organization. Allowed for the organization’s owner, a Provider Admin, or an Organization Admin or owner of the live parent. An Organization Admin who is not the owner cannot delete. Assign a new domain. Allowed for Provider Admins only. Any other caller receives HTTP 403 when saving the change. Edit the organization and add members. Allowed for an Organization Admin or the owner of the organization, a Provider Admin, or an Organization Admin or owner of the live parent. Holding Edit Organization or Add User to Organization through another role is not enough. Adding a member adds an existing account. It does not create one. Assign organization roles. Allowed for an Organization Admin of the organization, a Provider Admin, or a holder of Assign User Roles there. The target must be a member. Role rows the caller cannot write are skipped and reported in the response. The rest are applied. List every organization. Requires View All Organizations. Without it, the organization list shows only the organizations the caller is a member of. Layer5 Cloud does not block organization actions by plan today. See Roles and Permissions for the keys each default role holds.

Kanvas is designed to handle a wide range of infrastructure and application configurations. However, there are some performance limits that you should be aware of when working with Kanvas. This guide will help you understand these limits and provide tips for tuning your environment for optimal performance.
Performance Limits 🔗 Maximum Number of Components 🔗 Kanvas enforces a component cap set by the organization’s plan, checked whenever a design is saved or imported. The seeded limits are 100 for Personal, 200 for Team Designer, 100 for Team Operator, and 300 for Enterprise. A deployment can differ. There is no separate 1,000-component cap. A design over the plan limit is not saved.
Maximum Number of Annotation-only Components (non-semantically meaningful components) 🔗 What is a Non-Semantic Component? A non-semantic component is a component that does not represent a meaningful entity in your design. For example, a textbox, a shape, a line, or a comment are all examples of non-semantic components. These components are used for annotation purposes only and do not have a direct relationship to the underlying infrastructure or application that you are modeling. Kanvas does not enforce a separate cap on annotation-only components such as text boxes, shapes, lines, and comments. They still add to what the canvas draws and to what each save sends.
Maximum Number of Orchestrated Components (semantically meaningful components) 🔗 What is a Semantic Component? A semantic component is a component that represents a meaningful entity in your design. For example, a server, a database, or a network switch are all examples of semantic components. These components have a direct relationship to the underlying infrastructure or application that you are modeling. Maximum Number of Relationships 🔗 Kanvas enforces no cap on the number of relationships in a design. Large relationship counts still slow rendering, saving, and live editing.
Maximum Number of TagSet Relationships 🔗 Tags are indexed and searchable. However, the performance of design operations may degrade as the number of tags increases. To ensure an optimal user experience, we recommend using tags judiciously and limiting the number of tags used in a design.
TagSets are drawn only in Full mode, and at most 30 of them. Past 30, Kanvas skips the rest and shows “Skipped rendering of N matchlabels relationships due to limit of 30”. There is no Group Components control that turns grouping back on after that limit. See Working with Tags.
Maximum Number of Users 🔗 Kanvas does not enforce a fixed cap of 20 or 34 simultaneous collaborators. Live edits synchronize peer to peer after Layer5 Cloud introduces the participants. Large designs and embedded images still slow that synchronization because each change is sent to every participant. See Layer5 Cloud Networking Services for the network path.
Impact of Images 🔗 Be aware that designs are self-contained documents and that all artifacts, like any images (e.g. SVG, PNG, GIF, WEBP, etc.) that are added to your design are embedded into your design document, adding to the overall size of your design file. The embedding of images into your design file ensures portability of your design. You can export your design with the assurity that your images will remain in your design upon (re-)import.
As the number and size of images contained in your design grows, images can significantly increase file size, potentially causing performance issues. With each change made to your design, the entire design file is uploaded to Layer5 Cloud. This same performance consideration applies during collaborative editing sessions with multiple users viewing/editing the same design. Each change to your design made by any user in the collaboration session will be propagated to every other currently collaborating user. If your design contains a large number of images, this can lead to slow performance and increased bandwidth usage.
An image or text file added to a design is limited to 512,000 bytes (about 500 KB) each. The limit is the same on every plan. The rejection message says “Your current plan allows files up to 500 KB”, but the cap is not plan-specific. Kanvas enforces no separate 10 MB total for images. Embedded images still enlarge every save.
Performance Tuning 🔗 Optimize Your Design using the Layers Panel 🔗 To improve the performance of your design, consider optimizing by disabling one or more layers.
Control which layers of your design are visible using the Layers panel. Some layers specifically offer control of visibility of components, while other layers offer control over the ongoing evaluation of relationships between components.
Depending on the type of layer disabled, either specific components or all components by type will display or not be displayed, allowing you to finely tune the performance of you design rendering experience by saving design resources and improving the performance of Kanvas as you adjust both the number and type of components in view.
Even though you might hide components, those components are not deleted or removed from your design. These components are simply hidden from current view.
In the same way, as you toggle the evaluation of different types of relationships, understand that these relationships between your components still exist. Those relationships are simply temporarily hidden from view and the overhead of their evaluation eliminated while the respective type of relationship is disabled.
Using the Layers panel you control the level of sophistication or simplicity of the rendering of components and relationships in your designs. You can both simplify your design layout by removing unnecessary elements and improve performance simultaneously. Alternatively, you can increase the level of detail in your design by enabling additional layers and relationships, while controlling the balance between detail and performance.
Keep It Lightweight Hide layers you don’t need at the moment to keep your workspace lightweight and responsive. Optimize use of Images in your Design 🔗 To optimize performance, consider the following:
Use vector images (SVG) instead of raster images (PNG, JPG, etc.) as they are typically smaller in size and scale without pixelation. Prioritize using smaller file sizes whenever possible. Use the webp image format over png, jpg, or gif as it generally provides significantly better compression, resulting in faster design save times without sacrificing much image quality. Remove any unnecessary images from your design. Use image compression tools to reduce the size of your images before adding them to your design. What Affects Performance 🔗 As your designs grow in complexity, certain design patterns can impact how smoothly Kanvas responds. Understanding these factors helps you create designs that remain fast and responsive.
Related performance controls This page covers the design patterns and tuning levers that affect Kanvas performance. For the per-mode rendering ladder (Full, Medium, Wireframe, View-Only) and automatic fidelity management, see Render Modes. For the drag-to-edge viewport pan and its per-render-mode size thresholds, see Auto-pan on Drag. Working with Grouped Components 🔗 When you create groups of components (placing multiple components inside a parent container), you might notice performance differences as the number of grouped items increases. Here’s what you might experience:
Signs of Performance Impact:
Dragging groups feels laggy or choppy Design takes longer to load and display Moving or resizing groups shows delayed response Screen updates appear slower during interactions Large Groups Groups containing 100 or more components may experience noticeable lag during drag operations. Consider breaking large groups into smaller, logical subgroups for better performance. If dragging across a design that extends past your viewport feels slow, see Auto-pan on Drag for the per-render-mode thresholds that gate the drag-to-edge pan. How Kanvas Optimizes Your Design 🔗 Kanvas automatically works behind the scenes to keep your designs running smoothly:
Smart Rendering:
Kanvas only updates the parts of your design that actually change, not the entire canvas Components outside your current view aren’t fully rendered, saving resources Information badges and labels are displayed efficiently to prevent unnecessary redraws What This Means for You: The table below shows typical performance improvements you’ll experience:
Design Scenario Without Optimization With Optimization Your Experience Dragging a group of 100 components Laggy and slow Smooth and responsive 90% improvement Moving grouped components Choppy interactions Fluid movement Significantly better Overall responsiveness Delayed reactions Immediate feedback Much more responsive Automatic Optimization These optimizations work automatically. You don’t need to configure anything to benefit from better performance. Managing Design Complexity 🔗 Kanvas provides many interactive features that enhance your design experience. Understanding how these features work together helps you maintain optimal performance.
Features That Impact Performance 🔗 Your design experience includes several interactive capabilities that all work together:
Interactive Features:
Alignment guides help you position components precisely as you drag them Automatic relationship management keeps connections between components updated Tooltips and information displays show helpful context as you work Resize handles and controls let you adjust component sizes smoothly Visual grouping indicators show which components belong together When you’re working with many components simultaneously, these features all activate together, which can sometimes slow down interactions like dragging.
Performance Tip If dragging feels slow, try these strategies:
Hide unnecessary layers temporarily using the Layers panel Break your design into smaller, focused sections Work on one area of your design at a time Zoom in to focus on specific components Practical Tips for Better Performance 🔗 When Creating Large Designs:
Use the Layers panel to hide components you’re not actively editing Break complex designs into multiple smaller designs that you can link together Group related components thoughtfully rather than creating very large groups Remove old comments and annotations you no longer need When Experiencing Slowness:
Check if you have many layers enabled that you’re not using Consider whether the design is near your plan’s component limit (100, 200, or 300, depending on the plan) Try hiding relationship layers temporarily while arranging components Close and reopen your design to refresh the canvas How Kanvas Keeps Things Fast 🔗 Kanvas includes built-in intelligence to maintain smooth performance as you work on your designs. You don’t need to manage these features manually—they work automatically in the background.
Efficient Updates 🔗 What Happens When You Make Changes: Think of your design like a document. When you edit a single paragraph, you wouldn’t want your word processor to reformat the entire document. Similarly, Kanvas only updates the specific components you’re changing, not your entire design.
Benefits You’ll Notice:
Quick response when you move or edit components Smooth interactions even in large designs Consistent performance throughout your work session Better experience when multiple people collaborate on the same design Smart Performance Kanvas is designed to only update what needs updating, keeping your design responsive without requiring any configuration from you. Smooth Interactions During Continuous Operations 🔗 When you’re actively dragging components, resizing groups, or panning around your design, Kanvas automatically manages how often the screen updates to ensure smooth, responsive interactions.
What This Means:
Dragging feels fluid, not jerky Your cursor stays synchronized with the component you’re moving Multiple simultaneous operations remain responsive The interface doesn’t freeze or stutter during intensive operations Working with Different Zoom Levels 🔗 The zoom level you choose affects both what you see and how your design performs. Kanvas adapts its rendering based on your current zoom level to provide the best experience.
Progressive Detail Display 🔗 Kanvas automatically adjusts the level of detail based on how far you’re zoomed in or out:
Zoomed Out (Overview Mode):
Shows component shapes and primary names Displays main relationships between components Provides a fast, high-level view of your entire design Perfect for understanding overall structure Medium Zoom (Working Mode):
Adds relationship details and secondary information Shows more component metadata Good balance between detail and performance Zoomed In (Detail Mode):
Displays all badges, annotations, and detailed information Shows validation messages and warnings Reveals complete component properties Best for detailed configuration work Use Zoom Strategically Take advantage of zoom levels: zoom out to get an overview and rearrange major sections, then zoom in when you need to configure specific components in detail. Performance Benefits: When you’re zoomed out, Kanvas doesn’t spend resources rendering details you can’t see anyway. This keeps panning and navigation fast even in large designs. As you zoom in, more information progressively appears, giving you the detail you need without overwhelming the display.
Zoom Limits 🔗 Kanvas sets reasonable minimum and maximum zoom levels to ensure everything remains usable:
Text stays readable without becoming pixelated Interactive handles remain large enough to click Badges and indicators maintain appropriate sizes The design looks good on all devices (desktop, tablet, mobile) Zoom Boundaries If you try to zoom beyond the minimum or maximum limits, Kanvas won’t zoom further. These limits are in place to maintain usability and performance. Testing Your Design’s Performance 🔗 As you build larger designs, it’s helpful to evaluate how well they perform. Here are practical ways to test your design’s responsiveness.
Practical Test Scenarios 🔗 Try these scenarios to understand how your design performs:
Small Group Test (10-20 components in a group)
Does dragging feel instant and smooth? Do components respond immediately to your actions? This is the baseline—everything should feel effortless Medium Design Test (50-100 components total)
Can you drag groups without noticeable delay? Does panning around the canvas feel fluid? Are minor delays acceptable for your workflow? Large Design Test (200+ components)
How does dragging large groups feel? Is there lag when you first load the design? Does zooming in and out remain responsive? Complex Nesting Test (groups within groups, 3+ levels deep)
Can you still move parent groups smoothly? Do nested relationships display correctly? Is the design still manageable? Testing Approach Start simple and add complexity gradually. This helps you identify exactly when performance starts to degrade, making it easier to adjust your design approach. Simple Performance Checks 🔗 You don’t need specialized tools to evaluate performance. Just ask yourself:
Responsiveness Check:
Does dragging components feel smooth or choppy? Do components respond immediately when you click them? Can you pan around the design without lag? Loading Time Check:
Does your design load within a few seconds? Are badges and indicators visible quickly? Does the design feel “ready” when it first appears? Interaction Check:
Can you resize components smoothly? Do relationships update without delay? Does the interface feel responsive or sluggish? Using Browser Developer Tools (Optional) 🔗 For more detailed performance analysis, you can use your browser’s built-in developer tools:
Open Developer Tools: Press F12 (Windows/Linux) or Cmd+Option+I (Mac) Navigate to Performance Tab: Look for the “Performance” or “Profiler” tab Record an Interaction: Click the record button, perform an action (like dragging), then stop recording Review Results: Look for long operations or frame drops that indicate performance issues Browser Differences Performance can vary between browsers. If your design feels slow, try testing in Chrome, Firefox, or Safari to see if performance differs. Future Improvements 🔗 We’re continuously working to make Kanvas even faster and more responsive. Future updates will bring additional performance enhancements, including:
Improved rendering techniques for even smoother interactions Smarter optimization of complex designs Better handling of very large designs Enhanced performance on lower-powered devices These improvements will happen automatically through Kanvas updates—you won’t need to change your designs or workflows to benefit from them.
Continuous Improvement Performance optimization is an ongoing priority. As Kanvas evolves, your existing designs will automatically benefit from new performance enhancements. Render Modes and URL Overrides 🔗 Kanvas can paint the same design at four distinct fidelity levels — Full, Medium, Wireframe, and View-Only — and can switch between them automatically via Adaptive Render Mode based on live render and interaction latency. The lower-fidelity modes suppress badges, overlays, and texture work, so they stay fast on large designs while keeping the same underlying components, relationships, and metadata.
Render modes are the primary performance lever once a design grows past a few hundred components. Rather than duplicate the details here, see:
Render Modes — what each mode renders, the per-mode feature-size gates, and how Adaptive mode decides when to upshift or downshift. Auto-pan on Drag: auto-pan is off by default, and Kanvas turns it off past 100 components and relationships in Full, 500 in Medium, and 1,000 in Wireframe and View-only. Design Render Quality: URL parameters (render=full|medium|wireframe|view-only, adaptive=true). The read-only value is view-only, with a hyphen. Gates, Adaptive mode, and zoom 🔗 Feature Gate Auto-pan on Drag Your setting must be on, and the canvas must draw at most 100 components and 100 relationships in Full, 500 in Medium, and 1,000 in Wireframe and View-only. Designer only. Animated layout Full mode only, and only while the design has no more than 50 components, 50 relationships, and 100 edges drawn. Past that, a layout still applies its positions without the animation. TagSets Full mode only, at most 30 drawn. Feasibility evaluation and the component style toolbar Zoom above 0.5 divided by the display pixel ratio. That is 0.5 on a standard display and 0.25 on a display with a pixel ratio of 2. Canvas zoom in the Options dialog has a minimum of 0.1 (adjustable from 0.1 to 5) and a maximum of 30 (adjustable from 0.1 to 30). Each person sets their own.
Adaptive mode is off by default. It samples only while you pan or zoom, using the 95th percentile of the last 20 frame times. It steps down when that percentile exceeds 80 ms, then ignores samples for 3 seconds. It steps up when the percentile stays under 30 ms for 10 consecutive samples, more than 5 seconds after the last change, and the next mode is not above the ceiling. The ladder is Full, Medium, Wireframe. View-only is never entered or left automatically. After a step down, Adaptive recovers at most one step on its own. Turning Adaptive on sets the canvas to the ceiling at once (Full, unless you chose another). Changing the ceiling while Adaptive is already on does not change the running behavior until you turn Adaptive off and on. Turning it off keeps the mode Adaptive last chose. Notifications read “Switched to mode mode for better performance” and “Performance improved - switched to mode mode”.
Experimental WebGL renderer 🔗 Kanvas can draw the canvas with WebGL instead of the standard 2D canvas. It is off by default and available only from the Debug Mode panel, which appears when Enable Debugger is on in the Options dialog. The choice is stored in the browser, not the account, and applies the next time a canvas loads. The WebGL path draws dashed and dotted relationship lines as solid lines, draws every arrowhead as a triangle, and does not hide labels at low zoom. Above a zoom of 7.99 Kanvas uses the standard canvas. After the browser loses its WebGL context, Kanvas uses the standard canvas for the rest of the session.

This guide will walk you through setting up your Layer5 account, and through the profile, password, linked sign-in, account deletion, and subscription settings that belong to that account.
Configuring your Layer5 account 🔗 The first steps in starting with Layer5 are to create an account, verify your email, sign in, and view your profile. You do not name an organization or a workspace yourself. Layer5 Cloud creates an organization, a team, and a workspace the first time the new account signs in successfully. Submitting the sign-up form alone does not create them. An email sign-up signs you in immediately, so that first sign-in happens as part of registration. The Check your email page and the Import from GitHub first-run page described below arrived in Layer5 Cloud v1.0.278.
Every person who uses Layer5 Cloud has their own personal account, which can be part of multiple organizations and teams. Your personal account is your identity on Layer5 Cloud and represents you as an individual.
1. Creating an account 🔗 Sign up at https://cloud.layer5.io/signup. The registration page offers these sign-up methods:
Method What happens next Email and password You fill in one form. Layer5 Cloud signs you in right away and sends a verification email. Opening its link verifies your address and takes you back to where you started. GitHub You authorize with GitHub and are signed in straight after registration. Layer5 Cloud treats the email address GitHub reports as verified, so no verification email is sent. Google You authorize with Google and are signed in straight after registration. Layer5 Cloud treats the email address Google reports as verified, so no verification email is sent. Your organization’s identity provider An organization that brings its own identity provider credentials, including a generic OIDC provider, shows that provider on its own sign-up page. What the email sign-up form checks 🔗 The email sign-up form is a single screen that asks for your first name, last name, email address, and password. Layer5 Cloud validates each field and keeps what you typed when it shows an error, so you only correct the field at fault.
Field Rule First and last name 1 to 50 characters. Letters, combining marks, and spaces only. A spam filter also rejects blocked keywords in names. An invalid name shows “Invalid first name.” or “Invalid last name.” Email address A syntactically valid address. The spam filter also rejects disposable-email domains. An invalid or rejected address shows “Invalid email address or domain not allowed.” Password At least 8 characters. Must not appear in the Have I Been Pwned breach corpus. Must not be too similar to your email address. When the deployment has a reCAPTCHA check enabled, the submit button stays disabled until you solve it. A field-level validation failure keeps your solved captcha. If the server rejects the whole submission after the captcha was sent, the captcha resets and asks you to “Please complete the verification again.” If the network fails, the page shows “We couldn’t submit your sign-up. Check your connection and try again.”
GitHub and Google sign-up skip the spam filter and the captcha.
The sign-up form stays valid for 24 hours. If you leave it open longer, it restarts and you fill it in again.
Open Design 2. Verifying your email address 🔗 After an email sign-up, Layer5 Cloud signs you in and sends a verification email that contains both a verification link and a verification code. Either one completes verification. Both stay valid for 720 hours (30 days). You cannot use your account, or sign in again with your password, until you verify your address.
Opening the link verifies your address at once. You do not need to type the code or press a button. Layer5 Cloud then takes you back to the page you started signing up from, or to your dashboard if you opened the sign-up page directly. If the link has expired or was already used, the verification page says so and lets you request a new email.
Your browser lands on a Check your email page that says you are signed in and names the address the verification email went to. You can wait on this page:
Resend email sends a new verification email without leaving the page. Once it is sent, the page also offers a form where you type the code from the new email instead of opening its link. Sign out and use a different email signs you out so you can sign up again with the correct address. Use it if you mistyped your address. An account cannot change its email address before that address is verified, so signing up again with the correct address is the fix. The page remembers your address only in the browser tab you signed up in. If you open Check your email in a different tab, or your browser blocks site storage, the page shows generic text instead of your address. Resend email then opens the verification page, which asks for your address before it sends a new email.
If your organization uses a custom domain, the verification link, the page it opens, and the return afterward all stay on your organization’s domain, with your organization’s name and logo.
If your link has expired, request a new verification email and use the latest link.
3. Signing in to Layer5 Cloud 🔗 Sign in at https://cloud.layer5.io/login with the method you signed up with. If you signed up with GitHub or Google, Layer5 Cloud sends you to that provider to authenticate. The sign-in form stays valid for 12 hours. An expired form restarts.
You are not asked to name an organization or a workspace. Layer5 Cloud creates both, and your default team, on your first successful sign-in, as described in the next steps.
Where your first sign-in takes you 🔗 Your first sign-in normally opens your dashboard. One exception applies: if you started signing up from Kanvas, or from a Meshery Server on your organization’s custom domain, and you registered in this browser, your first sign-in opens the Import from GitHub page (titled “Get started”) once. If the sign-in carries an explicit return address, Layer5 Cloud sends you there instead.
The Import from GitHub page holds one card. It explains that connecting GitHub lets you pick repositories and import Kubernetes manifests, Helm charts, and Docker Compose files as designs. It also names your organization and workspace: “Organizations own workspaces. You’re in My Organization, working in My Workspace. Rename either anytime.” Select Import from GitHub to start the GitHub integration wizard, or skip to your dashboard.
Info Layer5 Cloud remembers where you started only for the browser session you signed up in. If you sign in from a different browser, or after closing the browser you signed up in, you land on your dashboard. The Import from GitHub page is always available at https://cloud.layer5.io/register/choose-start. 4. Your default organization 🔗 Organizations are the unit of tenancy in Layer5 Cloud, and every user belongs to at least one. On your first sign-in, Layer5 Cloud creates an organization named My Organization (description “Default Organization”), makes you its owner, and gives you the Organization Admin role in it. You can create more organizations and join existing ones.
Layer5 Cloud also creates a team named My Team (description “Default Team”), attaches it to My Organization, and gives you the Team Admin role on it.
Layer5 Cloud records your primary email address so that one person signing in by a different method reuses the same account instead of creating a second one. Layer5 Cloud accepts open organization invitation links on every sign-in, not only the first. See Using the open organization invitation link.
Info For more information, see Organizations. You can rename My Organization and change its description at any time. See Editing your organization.
5. Your default workspace 🔗 Workspaces are logical groups of shared resources such as environments, connections, credentials, and designs. On your first sign-in, Layer5 Cloud creates a workspace named My Workspace (description “Default Workspace”) in My Organization, owned by you. You can create more workspaces and share access to their resources through teams. If any of your organizations ever has no workspace, Layer5 Cloud re-creates My Workspace in it.
Info For more information, see Workspaces. You can rename My Workspace and change its description at any time. See Edit a Workspace.
Everything your first sign-in sets up 🔗 Created for you Name Your access Organization My Organization Owner, Organization Admin role Team My Team, attached to My Organization Team Admin role Workspace My Workspace, in My Organization Owner Global role Kanvas Grants the Kanvas extension capabilities when a Meshery Server connects with your account Your account is ready when you can sign in at https://cloud.layer5.io/login (for an email account, a successful password sign-in also proves your address is verified), your dashboard loads, and My Organization contains My Workspace.
6. Dashboard 🔗 The dashboard is your normal landing page after sign-in, except for the first sign-in described in step 3, which can open the Import from GitHub page. It is a grid of widgets whose layout you can edit. Layer5 Cloud prompts you before you leave with unsaved layout changes. Available widgets include Getting Started, Workspace Activity, Explore Playground, My Academy, Learn by Video, Help Center, Meshery Instances, Kubernetes Clusters Count, Catalog Content Count, Invite Friends, Badges, My Designs, System Version, Catalog Leaderboard, and Catalog Metrics. Academy administrators see additional widgets for Academy content statistics, metrics, test analytics, and registrations.
7. Viewing your Layer5 profile 🔗 Your Layer5 profile tells people the story of your work through recent activities and designs you have published to the catalog. Your avatar, tagline, and social links appear on your public profile. The next sections cover editing that profile, your password, linked sign-in providers, deleting the account, and the organization’s subscription.
Your account settings 🔗 Your profile belongs to you, not to an organization. A change applies in every organization you belong to.
The account area has four tabs: Profile, Preferences, Subscription, and Plans. Each tab opens only for a user who holds its permission. Without the permission, the tab shows a permission-denied view. When the account page is shown inside a Meshery UI that uses Layer5 Cloud as its provider, only the Profile tab appears.
I want to Where Permission needed Update my name, email, avatar, tagline, or social links Edit your profile View Profile Change my password Change your password Reset Password Sign in with GitHub or Google as well as my password Link or unlink a sign-in provider View Profile Delete my account Delete your account Delete Account Choose which emails I receive Notification preferences View Profile See, start, upgrade, or cancel my organization’s subscription Subscriptions and billing View Subcription, plus Organization Owner or Organization Admin The default user role holds View Profile, Reset Password, and Delete Account, so every member can manage their own account. The subscription permission is spelled View Subcription in the permission list. Use that spelling when you search for it.
Layer5 Cloud signs you in through an identity service. Password changes and account deletion need a live browser sign-in. A script that holds only an API token cannot do either. Changing a password or linking a provider is a privileged action. If your sign-in is older than the privileged-session window, Layer5 Cloud asks you to sign in again first. The window is 24 hours on hosted Layer5 Cloud and 15 minutes by default in the self-hosted chart. A user’s profile can also be edited by an administrator who holds Update User Profile in an organization you share with them. Only a Provider Admin can change another user’s email address. Edit your profile 🔗 The profile form saves itself. About one second after you stop typing, Layer5 Cloud saves the change and confirms it with a short message. There is no Save button, and edits made during a save are queued, not lost.
Field Behavior First Name, Last Name Free text. An empty value never overwrites the stored name. Username Read-only. It is the identifier assigned to the account and cannot be edited. E-mail Must look like an address (name@host.domain). An invalid value blocks saving and shows “Please enter a valid email address”. Country, Region Optional. Pick a country, then a region of that country. Avatar URL Optional. A public URL to a JPEG, PNG, GIF, SVG, or WEBP image. Layer5 Cloud loads the image before it saves. An address that does not load as an image is rejected. Avatar color The background color shown when you have no avatar image. Saved as a user preference. Tagline A short public line about you. Social Links Up to 5 links, each with a type (GitHub, LinkedIn, X, Company or Organization, or Personal Website) and a URL. An empty URL is allowed. A malformed one is rejected. Change your email address 🔗 Changing the email address changes the identifier you sign in with. Layer5 Cloud marks the new address as unverified and sends it a verification message. The confirmation reads “Profile updated. Please check your new email address to verify it.” Verify the new address before you rely on it. If the verification message cannot be sent, the change still completes.
Layer5 Cloud writes the change to the identity service first and to your profile second, so a rejected address never leaves the two out of step.
Change your password 🔗 Use the Reset Password control on the profile. Enter the new password twice. The two entries must match, or the form reports “Your new passwords do not match”.
The identity service enforces the password policy:
At least 8 characters. Not a password found in known breaches. Not too similar to your email address. A strength bar (Very weak to Strong) shows how guessable the password is. It is advice only and does not block you. The policy above does. A rejected password returns the identity service’s reason. A successful change shows “Password updated”.
Changing your password does not end your other sessions or revoke your API tokens. To cut off a device or script, end the session or revoke the token yourself. See Sessions and Tokens.
If you forgot your password, use the recovery flow from the sign-in page instead. It emails a one-time code and link that stay valid for 30 days. See Support.
Link or unlink a sign-in provider 🔗 Link GitHub or Google to sign in with whichever you prefer. Either method opens the same account, with the same organizations, designs, and roles. GitHub and Google are the only supported providers for linking.
The profile lists a Link option for each provider you have not linked and an Unlink option for each provider you have linked. The provider you used to create the account appears in neither list: you cannot unlink it, and it is already linked.
Linking sends you to the provider to approve access, then returns you to Layer5 Cloud. Layer5 Cloud asks GitHub for your profile and email address and Google for your email and profile. Unlinking removes the provider from your account. Your password and the other linked provider keep working.
A provider account can be linked to one Layer5 Cloud account only. Linking depends on the provider reporting a verified email address. For how Layer5 Cloud resolves sign-ins that share an email address, read Account Consolidation and the Account Linking rules.
Linking a provider is a privileged action, with the same 24 hour hosted window and 15 minute self-hosted default described above.
Delete your account 🔗 Deletion is permanent. Layer5 Cloud asks you to confirm, and then does not offer recovery. You need the Delete Account permission, which the default user role holds, and a live browser sign-in.
What deletion does, in one step that either completes or changes nothing:
Hands on every organization and team you own (see Organizations and teams you own). Hands any credential you hold on behalf of an organization to that organization’s owner, or else its longest-standing Organization Admin, so the organization keeps working. For an organization you owned, that is its new owner. Marks your account as deleted and ends your memberships in every organization and team, which removes your roles with them, along with any provider-wide role. Each membership is kept as an ended record, so organization history shows when your access ended. Revokes every API token you created, so none of them works afterwards. Releases your email address, so it can be used to sign up again. Records the deletion, and each organization or team handed on or deleted, in the audit trail. Removes your sign-in identity, including linked GitHub and Google sign-in, and signs you out. What deletion leaves behind:
Published content, such as items you published to the catalog, stays public. The audit trail keeps its entries. Organizations and teams you own 🔗 Each organization you own passes to someone who still belongs to it:
Its longest-standing Organization Admin, if it has one. Otherwise its longest-standing member. Otherwise, when nobody else belongs to it, the organization is deleted. “Longest-standing” means the membership that was created first. Members whose own accounts are deleted, and guest (anonymous) accounts, are never chosen. The new owner keeps the roles they already had. Ownership does not change anyone’s roles.
Teams you own follow the same rule, with Team Admin in place of Organization Admin.
An organization that is the parent of another live organization is never deleted this way, because child organizations are never deleted or moved along with their parent. If such an organization has nobody else in it, it keeps you as its owner and the audit trail records why. Your account is still deleted.
When deletion is refused 🔗 Because organizations you own are handed on first, a refusal is rare. Layer5 Cloud refuses the deletion, and changes nothing, when you hold credentials designated to an organization you do not own and that organization has no live owner or Organization Admin to receive them. The message begins “Refusing to delete your account” and names the organization. Without a successor, those credentials would be orphaned.
Resolve it, then retry:
Ask that organization’s members to promote someone to Organization Admin. Or release the credentials from the organization, or delete them. Signing up again 🔗 Signing up again with the same email address, by email and password or with GitHub or Google, on Layer5 Cloud or on an organization’s custom domain, creates a new, empty account with a new account ID and its own personal organization (or the placement an organization’s open invitation gives any new account). It inherits nothing from the deleted one: no profile, preferences, memberships, roles, or ownership, and no linked sign-in providers. An account is identified by its account ID, not by its email address, so the deleted account cannot be restored this way. To regain access to an organization, ask one of its administrators to invite you again.
Subscriptions and billing 🔗 A subscription connects an organization to a Layer5 plan and bills for it. A subscription belongs to an organization, not to a person. Layer5 Cloud checks the caller against the subscription’s own organization, so administering one organization gives you no access to another organization’s billing. Current prices are on the pricing page.
Who can manage a subscription 🔗 Action Organization Owner Organization Admin Provider Admin Other members See the organization’s subscriptions Yes Yes Yes No Start a paid subscription Yes Yes Yes No Upgrade a subscription Yes Yes Yes No Cancel a subscription Yes Yes Yes No The Subscription and Plans tabs open for any user who holds View Subcription or View Plans. The default user role holds both. A member who is not an owner or Organization Admin can open the tab, but Layer5 Cloud refuses the data behind it, so the subscription table cannot load. For subscriptions that belong to another organization, Layer5 Cloud answers “subscription not found”, the same answer it gives for an id that does not exist.
Read your subscriptions 🔗 The Subscription tab lists each subscription with these columns:
Column Meaning Plan The plan the subscription is on. Cadence Monthly or annual billing. Status The subscription’s state, from the table below. Users Billable The number of billable users counted for the subscription. Forecasted Amount Users Billable multiplied by the plan’s price per user, in US dollars. Start Date, Created At, Updated At When the subscription started, was created, and last changed. Three summary cards sit above the table: your current plan, the forecasted bill (“Based on current usage”, or “No billable usage” when the amount is zero), and the next payment due.
Status Meaning active Paid and in good standing. trialing In a trial period. Layer5 Cloud’s own checkout starts no trial. incomplete Created, but the first payment has not completed. past_due A payment failed. unpaid Payment attempts for the period have been exhausted. canceled Ended. expired, inactive No longer in effect. incomplete_expired The first payment never completed. The row is hidden from the list. Layer5 Cloud takes the status from the payment processor. Status changes arrive when the processor reports them, so the tab can trail a payment by a short time. Use the refresh control to reload.
Start a paid subscription 🔗 The Plans tab lists the Personal plan (“Free Forever”), Team Designer, Team Operator, and Enterprise, each with monthly and annual prices and a currency selector.
Personal is free and needs no subscription step. In entitlement records this plan is named Personal. The Free name is the same plan. Team Designer and Team Operator start in the tab. Review the plan, apply a coupon if you have one, and enter your billing address and payment details. The payment form is hosted by the payment processor, and Layer5 Cloud does not store card details. Enterprise does not use self-service checkout. Its subscribe action opens a contact form, and the Layer5 team arranges the subscription. Layer5 Cloud creates the subscription as incomplete, counts your billable users, and asks the payment processor to start billing. The status becomes active when the first payment succeeds. Checkout starts no free trial.
Upgrade a subscription 🔗 Upgrade moves a subscription to a higher plan on the same ladder. Each ladder is separate:
Monthly core plans, in order: Team Designer, Team Operator, Enterprise. Annual core plans, in the same order. Academy theory and lab bundles, each with its own monthly and annual ladder. You cannot move down a ladder, and you cannot switch between monthly and annual billing on an existing subscription. To change cadence or move to a lower plan, contact Support.
Before you confirm, the upgrade shows an invoice preview with the prorated line items. Layer5 Cloud prorates the change: you pay for the new plan’s price for the rest of the current period, less credit for the unused part of the old plan. The confirmation reads “Subscription upgraded to” followed by the plan name.
Upgrade is unavailable for subscriptions that are canceled, inactive, incomplete, or on the free plan.
Cancel a subscription 🔗 Cancel asks you to confirm and then tells the payment processor to end the subscription at the end of the current billing period. The plan stays in force until the period ends. Because the plan runs to the end of the period, canceling issues no refund.
Cancel is unavailable for subscriptions that are already canceled or inactive, that never completed, or that are on the free plan.
How the billable user count works 🔗 Plans bill per user. The count is the number of distinct people who are members of the organization, with these rules:
The account must be active. A person who has been invited but has not accepted is not counted. A deleted account is not counted. A member whose only role is academy learner is not counted. A member added without any role is not counted. The count never falls below the plan’s minimum number of users. Academy plans that bill per learner count active learners instead of organization members. Layer5 Cloud recalculates the count when it creates a subscription, and then every 2 hours for subscriptions that are active, trialing, past due, incomplete, or unpaid. It sends the new count to the payment processor each time. No plan blocks you from adding users: the count changes what you pay, never what you can do.
What a change in the count costs:
The count rises mid-period. The payment processor charges a prorated amount for the added users for the rest of the period. At renewal, the full amount reflects the new count. The count falls mid-period. The processor issues a prorated credit for the unused part. The credit stays on the organization’s account balance, does not expire, and reduces future invoices. It is not refunded automatically. Renewal date. A change in the count never moves the renewal date. At renewal, the organization pays for the count as of that date. Removing a user from the organization, or deleting their account, lowers the count at the next recalculation.
What a plan enforces 🔗 Plans record several limits. Layer5 Cloud enforces only the number of components in a design.
Entitlement Free (Personal) Team Designer Team Operator Enterprise Components per design 100 200 100 300 Relationships per design 100 200 100 300 Image size in a design 250 KB 1 MiB 1 MiB 10 MiB Designs per workspace Unlimited Unlimited Unlimited Unlimited Workspaces per organization See note 10 10 Unlimited For workspaces per organization on the Free plan, the plan records disagree: the monthly billing record sets 1 and the annual billing record sets 10.
When you save or import a design, Layer5 Cloud compares its component count with the limit of your organization’s active plan. A design that exceeds the limit is refused with the error Design exeeds maximum limit of N components supported by your current plan, where N is the limit. Reduce the number of components or upgrade the plan. When an organization holds more than one active subscription, the highest component limit among them applies. An organization with no active subscription cannot save or import a design. The request fails with HTTP 500 and the error Org is not entitled to adding components to a design.
Layer5 Cloud records every other quantity in the table and lists it through GET /api/entitlement/features, but it does not refuse an action because of any of them. See the API reference.
Only Provider Admins create custom roles. Layer5 Cloud refuses a role creation request from anyone else with HTTP 403. On hosted Layer5 Cloud, an organization cannot create a custom role itself. On a self-hosted deployment, the operator’s Provider Admins can. Roles are defined for the whole deployment, not per organization. Layer5 Cloud does not check your plan when a custom role is created.
Failure modes 🔗 What you see Cause What to do The subscription table does not load You are not an Organization Owner or Organization Admin of the selected organization Ask an owner or Organization Admin to manage billing, or switch to the right organization. “Payment Error” during checkout The payment processor declined the payment Correct the payment details and retry. Status stays incomplete The first payment has not completed Complete the payment. An incomplete subscription that never completes becomes incomplete_expired. Cancel and Upgrade are disabled The status or plan rules above Check the status column. Organization owners and Organization Admins are described in Organizations.

body:
Share designs from Workspaces 🔗 Five has been working in the orbital-dev workspace, a development sandbox with a local Kubernetes environment (kind) and LocalStack for AWS service emulation. Rex Park needs to open the microservices-baseline design.
Assigning the Development team to orbital-dev does not do that. Team assignment grants read-only access to the connections in the workspace’s environments. It does not open designs. Every member of the organization can already see the workspace.
Here is how Five shares the design itself with Rex.
Share a single design from orbital-dev 🔗 In your browser, go to Layer5 Cloud.
Open microservices-baseline. Click Share. Share is hidden while the design is empty or published, and while it is still loading. Search for Rex and add him. The search finds individual users only. There is no permission level to set: a grant has no view-only or comment-only option. A person who can open a private design can edit it, clone it, and download it. Confirm Rex appears under People with Access. Treat that list as the source of truth after every share. Sharing one design gives Rex that design only, not the other designs in orbital-dev, and not the right to modify its connections. To let Rex read the workspace’s connections, an organization administrator assigns Rex’s team to the workspace. That assignment is still read-only for connections, and it still does not open any design.
A private design’s link does not grant access by itself. The recipient must also be added in Share.
Stop, limit, or change Workspace sharing 🔗 You stop connection access by removing the team from the workspace. You stop design access by removing the person from People with Access. Those are different controls.
If Five later wants to remove Rex’s access to the design:
Open the design and click Share Find Rex in People with Access Remove Rex There is no comment-only setting and no separate edit setting on the grant.
Share and collaborate on a design with many people 🔗 The Share dialog finds individual users only. Layer5 Cloud accepts a grant for a team through its API, but no access check honors it, so team members gain nothing from a team grant. Grant each person.
You cannot give a whole team access to a private design by placing the design in a workspace and assigning the team.
Share without publishing 🔗 Keep the design Private and add each person in Share. Copy Link is a pointer. For a private design, the link alone does not open it.
Publish the design 🔗 When a design is Published Publishing lists the design in the catalog. Anyone can read it, and any signed-in user with Clone Design can clone it. Published is not the same as Public. A public design is readable by anyone with the link and is not listed in the catalog. A design saved for the first time is public. Designs imported from GitHub start private. Unpublishing returns the design to private, not public. If many people need to open a design without a catalog entry, share it with each person, or set it to public. Share is hidden while a design is published. To remove a design from the catalog, unpublish it. See Publishing Designs. Stop sharing a design 🔗 The owner, and anyone who holds Share Design, can change who is listed under People with Access.
Deleting a design you own removes it. There is no trash. Collaborators cannot delete a design. Only the owner or a provider administrator can.
Anonymous or unknown users in a design 🔗 A public design can be opened by anyone with the link, including someone who is not signed in. A private design cannot. If someone you did not add can open a private design, check People with Access: another person who holds Share Design may have added them.
Info See Meet Five and the Cast for the full Orbital Labs workspace and character reference. The same sharing steps are summarized on Managing Workspaces.

At Layer5 Cloud, we’re here to help you every step of the way. If you have any questions, encounter any issues, or need assistance with anything related to our platform, please don’t hesitate to reach out to us. Our dedicated support team is committed to providing you with the help and guidance you need.
Contacting Support 🔗 You can contact Layer5 support in the following ways:
Channel Use it for Available on Email, support@layer5.io Questions and problems with Layer5 Cloud Every plan Community forum Questions, shared experience, and help from other users and moderators Every plan Slack Real-time conversation with the community Every plan Support form in Layer5 Cloud A written request routed to Layer5 Every plan FAQs Answers to common questions Everyone Our support team responds to email as soon as they can.
Account Recovery 🔗 If you’ve forgotten your Layer5 Cloud account password, you can recover your account from the sign-in page. Layer5 Cloud sends a recovery link and a code to the address on the account. Both are valid for 30 days. Password sign-in is refused until the address on the account is verified, so verify your address before you rely on password sign-in. See Setting up a Layer5 account.
Go to the Layer5 Cloud login page.
On the login page, click on the “Forgot Password” link below the login form.
Enter the email address associated with your Layer5 Cloud account and click “Submit.”
You’ll receive an email with instructions on how to reset your password. Follow the instructions provided in the email to reset your password. The link and the code in that email stay valid for 30 days.
Once you’ve clicked the password reset link in the email, you’ll be directed to a page where you can create a new password for your account. Enter your new password and confirm it, then click “Submit” to save your changes.
After successfully resetting your password, you can now login to your Layer5 Cloud account using your new password.
Open Design The support form 🔗 Layer5 Cloud has a Support page with cards for the documentation, the discussion forum, Slack, and the FAQs, and a contact form. The form takes these fields:
Field Rule Subject Required. At least 5 characters. Issue Description Required. At least 5 characters. Type of inquiry One of Account/Billing, Sales, Support, Partnership, Extension Points, or Community. Layer5 Cloud validates the request and delivers it to the support endpoint configured for the deployment. It rejects a request that carries fields it does not recognize with HTTP 400, and it answers HTTP 500 when delivery to the endpoint fails. The page shows a confirmation message after you submit, whatever the server answers, so confirm delivery by email if the request is urgent.
On a self-hosted deployment, your operator configures where the form delivers requests. See Self-hosted deployment.
Support by plan 🔗 Support Free Team Designer Team Operator Enterprise Community Support Included Included Included Included Standard Support Not included Included Included Included Premium Support Not included Not included Not included Included Community Support is help from the community forum. Standard Support adds troubleshooting help from Layer5 over the web (email). Premium Support adds a 2-hour response-time agreement and 24/7 web and phone support. Terms are part of your order. Current plan details are at layer5.io/pricing. These are commercial entitlements. Layer5 Cloud does not check your plan when you submit the support form.

body:
When you’re designing and visualizing in Kanvas, you’ll encounter a rich library of components. This guide will help you understand what these components mean and how they behave in your designs.
Core Component Categories 🔗 Components in Kanvas fall into two fundamental categories, distinguished by whether they can be orchestrated (managed) during deployment.
Semantic Components (Orchestratable) 🔗 These components represent actual infrastructure resources that Kanvas can understand and manage during deployment. They are “meaningful” because they map directly to real infrastructure elements. Examples include:
Kubernetes resources (Pods, Services, Deployments) Cloud provider resources (AWS S3 buckets, Azure Functions) Infrastructure components (Load Balancers, Databases) These components are orchestratable because Kanvas can create, configure, and manage their lifecycle during deployment.
Visual Distinction Rule To help users quickly distinguish between component types, Kanvas follows a clear visual design rule:
Semantic (Configurable) Components: Have a background to represent their status as “real” infrastructure resources Non-semantic (Annotation) Components: Have transparent backgrounds, as they are purely visual aids Non-semantic Components (Annotation-Only) 🔗 These components are visual and organizational elements that help document and organize your designs. They are “meaningless” in terms of infrastructure because they don’t represent deployable resources. Examples include:
Text boxes and comments Shapes and containers for grouping Arrows and lines for relationships Labels and tags Kanvas ignores these components during deployment as they are purely visual/organizational elements.
Visual Customization All components, whether semantic or non-semantic, support rich visual customization. For example, you can change a Kubernetes Pod’s color from blue to green, modify its shape, or replace its background logo - it’s all configurable! Semantic Components 🔗 These components represent real infrastructure that Kanvas can manage. They can be either built-in (like Kubernetes components) or custom components that you create.
Kanvas provides a rich ecosystem of semantic components through various integrations. While Kubernetes is a commonly used example, all integration models (like KEDA, Istio, AWS, etc.) provide components with the same orchestratable capabilities. To help you navigate this ecosystem, Kanvas organizes these components in a clear hierarchy:
Integration Hierarchy Kanvas organizes integrated components in a clear hierarchy:
Categories: High-level groups (e.g., “Cloud Native Network”, “Database”) Integration Models: Specific technologies (e.g., “AWS App Mesh”, “Prometheus”, “Kubernetes”) Semantic Components: Functional building blocks that can be deployed and managed Kubernetes Components Example 🔗 To illustrate how semantic components work in practice, let’s examine Kubernetes components. As one of the most widely used integration models, Kubernetes components demonstrate how Kanvas implements its design principles while maintaining a distinct visual style:
For Kubernetes resources, Kanvas employs a thoughtful design system built on these key principles:
Principle 1: Color and Structure
Uniform Color Scheme: Kubernetes component icons typically use a distinctive blue background as a standard identifier Standardized Icon Structure: The fundamental structure is consistent: an outer container shape with the blue background, encompassing a unique inner white symbol Meaningful Inner Symbols: The white symbol inside each icon is the crucial unique identifier for that specific Kubernetes Kind Principle 2: Shape as an Indicator
The blue background is framed by different outer shapes that help identify the component’s role:
Triangles: Used for core networking resources like Service and API Service Hexagons: Used for foundational workload controllers like StatefulSet Unique Polygons: Used for specialized resources like Endpoints, PriorityClass, or ValidatingWebhookConfiguration Exploring All Integrations This guide covers the visual style of components. For a complete catalog of all technologies that Kanvas integrates, visit the integrations directory. Non-semantic Components 🔗 These components help you document and organize your designs without affecting the actual infrastructure. They include:
Generic Shapes 🔗 The “Shapes” palette offers a diverse collection of annotation-only components for general-purpose diagramming. These are purely visual elements that won’t be deployed.
Arrows 🔗 Arrows are annotation-only components for showing direction or creating simple visual annotations. They are static shapes intended for illustration.
Looking for Dynamic Connections? The arrows shown here are static visual aids. To represent actual, functional relationships between semantic components (like network traffic or dependencies), you should use the Edge system instead. Learn more Flowchart Shapes 🔗 Kanvas includes a dedicated palette of standard flowchart shapes. These are annotation-only components that help document your design’s logic and flow.
Simple Line Icons 🔗 Kanvas provides a comprehensive library of Simple Line Icons as annotation-only components. These icons are intended for user-driven annotations and visual enhancement.
Component Visuals in Different Contexts 🔗 A single semantic component will be visually represented differently depending on where you encounter it in Kanvas. Let’s take the Deployment component as an example:
Deployment component with its distinctive shape and badge: Deployment icon as it appears in a component selection panel: Deployment component as seen in a cluster resource overview: Learn More About Interpreting Designs To learn how to interpret and understand designs in practice, including how components work together in a design, visit our comprehensive guide in the Layer5 Academy. Limits and deployed identity 🔗 Kanvas saves a new design only when it has at least one component, or a name that is not empty and not “Untitled Design”. You cannot create a design while the organization scope is set to all organizations.
Plan Components per design Personal 100 Team Designer 200 Team Operator 100 Enterprise 300 When a design exceeds the limit, the save or import is rejected with HTTP 403. The server message is “Design exeeds maximum limit of N components supported by your current plan” (the misspelling ships). The canvas shows “Unable to save. Retrying…”. If the organization is not entitled to add components, the save fails with HTTP 500 and “Org is not entitled to adding components to a design”.
Image and text files dropped on the canvas are limited to 500 KB on every plan. The rejection says “Your current plan allows files up to 500 KB”.
Every resource Kanvas deploys carries the label design.meshery.io/id and the annotations design.meshery.io/version and component.meshery.io/id. A new design starts public. Unpublishing sets visibility back to private. Other members need View Designs to read private designs that are not shared with them.
