You can change the logo, color scheme, domain name, and other aspects of the user interface to match your own identity. Branding is set per organization. You do not need to self-host to white-label: a hosted organization can use the same theme, logos, links, domain, and mail settings. Self-hosting adds the provider-level defaults that every organization inherits.
Customizing Themes 🔗 The Layer5 Cloud dashboard can be customized with your own branding. An organization sets theme colors and four logos: desktop, mobile, dark desktop, and dark mobile. Theme colors accept only hexadecimal values. Each logo can be at most 500 KB. Layer5 Cloud rejects a color or an oversized logo with an error that names it. The signed-in product, and the sign-in, sign-up, and error pages on the organization’s own domain, use that theme.
Dashboard Example This example includes a custom branding with colors and full-sized logo. Example: Cloudfire branding on Dashboard Dashboard Mobile Example This example includes a custom branding with colors and logo mark. Example: Cloudfire branding in Catalog Dashboard Mobile This example includes a custom branding with colors and full-sized logo. Example: CNCF branding on Dashboard Catalog Example This example includes a custom branding with colors and full-sized logo. Example: CNCF branding on Catalog Enable White Labeling: Organization Preferences 🔗 Layer5 Cloud supports customizing themes on a per organization basis. This includes the ability to upload your own logo and define your own color scheme. Your logo will be displayed in the top left corner of the dashboard. Both a full-sized logo and a logo mark are supported.
As an Organization Administrator, you can add your organization’s logo to the global navigation bar, which supports a large, horizontal logo for desktop users and a small, square logo for mobile users. The logo appears at the top of each user’s window for all Layer5 Cloud pages within your organization.
Preference Example This example shows how to customize through different themes Example: Selection of theme Custom Logos 🔗 You can upload your own logo for your organization. Logo appears in upper left corner of all Layer5 Cloud pages. All teams, workspaces, and users in your organization will use these custom logos.
Your custom logos will optionally be visible to external users if you choose to customize your login screen. Otherwise, your custom logos will only be visible to users within your organization.
If you use a mobile device, the logo mark will be visible.
Logo Image Requirements 🔗 Logo images must be either in SVG, PNG or GIF format. GIF images can be animated, but are not recommended given their distraction to users. The maximum file size for each image is 500 KB.
Horizontal logo: 389 width x 32 height pixels If you upload a smaller or larger image, the image is resized to exactly 389 x 32 pixels. If the aspect ratio does not match, then the image will be distorted. For example, a 132 x 132 pixel image expands to 389 x 32 pixels, causing distortion.
Square logo (mark): 32 width x 32 height pixels Full-sized Logo Example Logo Mark Example When users register through the Open Organization Invitation Link, they will see the full-sized logo.
When logging into Layer5 Cloud on mobile devices, the small logo mark will be displayed.
Uploading Your Logo 🔗 On the Organizations page, you can upload your custom logo for your organization.
Go to Menu and then [Identity > Organization]. To open the Edit window, click the pencil icon next to the organization name. Click Select file to upload and select the logo image on your computer. You’ll see a preview of your logo. Click Save, if satisfied. You may change your custom logo images at any time. Contact Information in Email Notifications 🔗 White-labeling extends past the browser: the footer shared by every transactional email Layer5 Cloud sends - invitations, welcome mail, role changes, catalog publish decisions, design comment mentions, email verification and password recovery codes - is built from your organization’s own contact information rather than Layer5’s.
That covers what the message says. The address it arrives from is a separate setting: by default every message leaves through Layer5’s shared mail server, so a fully branded email still arrives from a Layer5 address. An organization can instead register its own mail server on the Email tab of Edit Organization. Once the sending domain is verified, a connection test has passed and the server is turned on, application mail such as invitations and notifications leaves through that server from the organization’s own domain, subject to its fallback setting. See Bring Your Own Mail Server.
The same five link fields drive both your sign-in pages and your email footers. Set them as an Organization Administrator on the Organizations page: click the pencil icon next to your organization name, then fill in the fields under Login page links.
Field Where it appears in email Support Email The “email” contact link in the footer Discussion Forum URL The “forum” contact link and the forum icon Slack URL The “slack” contact link and the Slack icon Privacy Policy URL The “privacy policy” link in the footer’s legal line Terms of Service URL The “terms of service” link in the footer’s legal line How each field is resolved 🔗 Resolution is per field, not all-or-nothing. Each of the five fields is resolved independently, in this order:
Your organization’s value, when you have set that field. Otherwise, the Provider Organization’s value for that field - the contact details configured on the provider organization that owns the deployment. Otherwise, the Layer5 default baked into the email template (support@layer5.io, discuss.meshery.io, slack.layer5.io, and the Layer5 Cloud legal pages). Because the fallback is per field, filling in one field never blanks the others. An organization that publishes only its own support inbox keeps the Provider Organization’s forum, Slack, privacy policy, and terms of service alongside that inbox. A field left blank - or containing only whitespace - counts as unset and does not shadow the value it would otherwise fall back to.
Self-hosted deployments: configure the Provider Organization On a self-hosted deployment, the second tier of this fallback is your Provider Organization, not Layer5. Setting the five link fields on your Provider Organization gives every organization in your deployment a sensible branded default, so a member organization that has not filled in its own contact details still never surfaces Layer5’s support channels to your users. See Configuring a subdomain for how to reach your Provider Organization. Value formats 🔗 Values are normalized before they are rendered into an email, so the link is always followable from a mail client:
A root-relative value such as /legal/privacy-policy.html is resolved against your organization’s own host - your custom domain when you have configured one, and the deployment’s base URL otherwise. Recipients therefore stay on your domain rather than being sent to the canonical Layer5 Cloud host. A bare email address such as support@example.com is turned into a mailto: link. Absolute http://, https://, mailto:, and tel: values are used as given. As on the sign-in pages, values are sanitized server-side. javascript:, data:, and protocol-relative (//host) values are dropped, and the field then falls back as though it were unset.
Organization Dashboard Customization 🔗 Layer5 Cloud supports customizing dashboard layouts on a per organization basis. As an administrator of your organization, you can customize the dashboard experience for all members of your organization. To customize your organization’s dashboard, select from a collection of widgets to include or exclude.
To customize your organization’s dashboard, follow the steps in this video or the steps outlined in the screenshots below.
Edit your Org’s Dashboard Click ‘Edit’ to enter into customization mode. Add and Remove Widgets Pick and choose which widgets to include. Reposition and resize each as you like. Save and Publish Dashboard Make your customized layout available to all members of your org or reset your changes to revert to the default layout. Widget Limitations Each of the prebuilt widgets can be added to a dashboard only once. If you find that a particular widget that you would like to have is not available, please let us know. Custom Domain Name and Login Screen 🔗 Info Not sure whether you want a subdomain of the platform or your own separate custom domain - and whether you’ll need your own identity provider? The Organization Configuration Scenarios guide names each combination (Hosted, Branded, White-Label) and explains when to choose one over the next. Layer5 Cloud supports customizing the login screen based on custom domain name. Redirect your users to your own domain name. For example, if your domain name is mycompany.com, you can redirect users to meshery.mycompany.com.
Example: Layer5 Cloud custom branding on login screen with CNCF branding. Live example: https://cloud.layer5.io/signup?program=cncf
A subdomain is the part of a URL before the root domain. You can configure your subdomain as www or as a distinct section of your site, like hub.cncf.io.
Subdomains are configured with a CNAME record through your DNS provider.
Changing Custom Domain May Break Academy Integration Changing your custom domain name after configuring an external Academy can break the content integration. If you change your domain, you must also update the organizational folder name (/content/learning-paths/<your-org-name>) in your Academy content repository to match. Configuring a subdomain 🔗 To set up a hostname such as hub.example.org:
A Provider Admin enters the domain in the organization’s settings. Only a Provider Admin can set a new domain. An organization administrator can only clear one. Layer5 Cloud checks the format and uniqueness when you save, and does not look the name up in DNS. Saving does not reboot the server. Create a CNAME record that points the custom hostname at your deployment’s hostname. Use an internationalized name in its Punycode form. Add the custom hostname to ingress.hosts with the same paths as your main host, and add it to ingress.tls with a certificate that covers it. The chart routes only the hosts you list. Set env.proto to https. The server builds redirects to the custom domain from that value. If you cannot edit the organization, verify that you are a Provider Administrator.
Internationalized Domain Names If your custom domain is an internationalized domain name, you must enter the Punycode encoded version. Create one CNAME per hostname. Point it at your deployment’s hostname. On the hosted service that hostname is cloud.layer5.io. Do not rely on a wildcard record.
Risks of Using Wildcard DNS Records Warning: We strongly recommend that you do not use wildcard DNS records, such as *.example.com. These records put you at an immediate risk of domain takeovers, even if you verify the domain. For example, if you verify example.com this prevents someone from using a.example.com, but they could still take over b.a.example.com (which is covered by the wildcard DNS record). Domain Format Requirements 🔗 Uniqueness: The domain must be unique across organizations, including deleted ones.
Format: 3 to 253 characters. Dot-separated labels of 1 to 63 ASCII letters, digits, or hyphens. A label cannot start or end with a hyphen. Do not include a protocol or a www. prefix. Enter the hostname, for example meshery.mycompany.com. Internationalized names are written in Punycode (xn--).
Who can set it: Only a Provider Admin can set a new domain. An organization administrator can clear one. Clearing the field removes the assignment.
DNS: Layer5 Cloud does not look the name up when you save. Lookups are cached for five minutes, and an organization change clears the affected entry.
Verifying your custom domain 🔗 Open Terminal.
To confirm that your DNS record is configured correctly, use the dig command, replacing hub.cncf.io with your subdomain.
$ dig WWW.EXAMPLE.COM +nostats +nocomments +nocmd > ;hub.cncf.io. IN A > hub.cncf.io. 3592 IN CNAME . > meshery.layer5.io. 43192 IN CNAME meshery.layer5.io . > meshery.layer5.io . 22 IN A 192.0.2.1 Social sign-in on a custom domain 🔗 Social sign-in (Google and GitHub) works on any custom domain - whether it is a subdomain of your deployment’s base domain (its registrable domain, technically the eTLD+1, for example layer5.io or example.com) or a fully-custom domain on a different base domain. In every case, the Google and GitHub buttons appear and complete sign-in using the deployment’s default identity providers. No per-organization setup is required, and bringing your own identity provider is not a prerequisite for social sign-in.
Same base domain. If the custom domain is a subdomain of your deployment’s base domain - for example a deployment at cloud.example.com with a meshery.example.com custom domain (or, on the hosted service, a Layer5-provisioned partner subdomain such as partner.layer5.io) - Google and GitHub sign-in work out of the box with the deployment’s default identity providers.
Different base domain (fully-custom). If the custom domain sits on a different base domain - for example you CNAME meshery.yourcompany.com to the hosted cloud.layer5.io, where yourcompany.com and layer5.io are different base domains - Google and GitHub sign-in still work out of the box, again using the deployment’s default identity providers. You only need to bring your own identity provider credentials (BYOC) if you want your own brand on the consent screen, your own OAuth rate limits and audit trail, corporate single sign-on, or a distinct authentication boundary - never merely to enable social sign-in.
Social sign-in works without bringing your own identity providers On any custom domain, the Google and GitHub buttons are shown and fully functional alongside email-and-password sign-in, using the deployment’s default identity providers - no per-organization configuration is required. Bringing your own identity providers (BYOC) remains optional and changes whose OAuth apps and consent screen are used, not whether social sign-in is available. See Identity Services for what BYOC is and when you might want it. The same base domain / different base domain split above still marks an authentication boundary. Organizations that share an identity provider (the canonical host and custom domains that use the shared, central provider) sit within the same authentication boundary, while an organization that brings its own (BYOC) provider is a distinct authentication boundary: same identity provider source means the same security boundary, regardless of how the host is named. See Identity Services → The identity provider is the security boundary and Identity and Security → Security Boundaries.
Frequently asked questions about white labeling 🔗 Do I need to self-host Layer5 Cloud in order to white-label it? No, you can access and use all the same custom theming, custom dashboards, and organization preferences from the hosted version of Layer5 Cloud as well.
Do users have to use my custom URL to access the Organization? No. Users can always sign in through the deployment’s own address and reach the organization. On the hosted service that address is https://cloud.layer5.io. On a self-hosted deployment it is the hostname you configured.
When I send someone a link that includes my custom URL, do they need to be logged in? Yes. Users will need to be signed in through your custom URL (not through cloud.layer5.io) in order to open links that include your custom URL. Users who are not logged in can quickly do so, and subsequently, be redirected to the link you have shared.
Why does the custom domain work for my colleagues but not for me? This issue could potentially be related to your local network environment. It’s possible that a local proxy client, VPN, or network accelerator on your computer might be intercepting the network request before it can reach the public internet.

body:
Layer5 Cloud organizes people, infrastructure, and designs into a small set of building blocks. Permission checks, sharing, and the rest of this documentation depend on how those blocks fit together.
Core Entities 🔗 User. One person’s account and identity. A user exists independently of any organization, can own resources such as workspaces, designs, connections, and tokens, and is the actor every action is attributed to. Organization. The unit of tenancy and the core security boundary. Teams and workspaces belong to an organization, and resources, billing, and access control are isolated per organization. Team. A group of users inside one organization. Teams are how you grant a set of people access to workspaces and to the resources in them. Workspace. A shared space inside an organization where teams collaborate. A workspace groups designs and environments. A design belongs to at most one workspace at a time. Environment. A named group of connections, such as Kubernetes clusters or Prometheus instances, and the credentials they use. Assigning an environment to a workspace makes its connections available to that workspace. Design. A description of infrastructure that you author in Kanvas and deploy through Meshery. A design is owned by a user and lives in at most one workspace. Catalog. The public collection of published designs. Anyone can browse it. Signed-in users with the Clone Design permission can clone a published or public design from it. Connection. A resource that Meshery Server registers with Cloud, including the Meshery Server itself. A connection is owned by the user who registered it. Each user sees their own connections. Spaces explains workspaces, environments, and workspace management. Identity and Security explains organizations, teams, users, access control, roles, keychains, keys, tokens, and sessions. Catalog explains how designs are published, discovered, and cloned. Meshery Server Registration explains how a Meshery Server registers with Cloud. Cloud recognizes an existing registration by kind meshery, the authenticated owner, and metadata.serverId. Understanding Relationships 🔗 Relationship Cardinality What it means User and organization Many-to-many A user can belong to any number of organizations, and an organization has any number of users. Organization to team One-to-many A team belongs to the organization it is created in. An organization can have any number of teams. User and team Many-to-many A team can have any number of users, and a user can belong to any number of teams. Organization to workspace One-to-many Organizations own workspaces. Each workspace belongs to one organization. Team and workspace Many-to-many A workspace can have zero or more teams, and a team can have access to several workspaces. Workspace and environment Many-to-many A workspace can have zero or more environments, and the same environment can be assigned to several workspaces. Environment and connection Many-to-many An environment groups any number of connections, and the same connection can be assigned to several environments. Workspace to design One-to-many A design belongs to at most one workspace at a time. Assigning a design to a workspace moves it out of its previous workspace. User to connection One-to-many Connections, including registered Meshery Servers, are owned by a user. Each user sees their own connections. Design to catalog Many-to-one Published designs appear in the one public catalog, where others can view them and clone them. Team membership grants access through workspaces. A user who does not own a connection reaches it through a team that has access to a workspace, which has an environment, which contains the connection. That path grants read-only access to the connection.
Next Steps 🔗 The sections below describe how roles attach to these blocks, what a new account receives, and how Layer5 Cloud works as a Meshery remote provider. Meshery’s own component layout is documented at docs.meshery.io/architecture.
How roles, keys, and keychains attach 🔗 Keys are the atomic permissions. Each key names one operation, such as creating a workspace or cloning a design. Keychains group related keys. Roles carry keychains and are assigned to users. Roles are evaluated per organization, so the same person can hold different roles, and therefore different capabilities, in each organization they belong to. Roles are assigned at the provider, organization, team, and workspace levels. The built-in roles are Provider Admin, Organization Admin, Organization User, Team Admin, Workspace Admin, Workspace Manager, Environment Management, Curator, and Kanvas. The Kanvas role is global rather than scoped to an organization: it grants the Kanvas extension capabilities when a Meshery Server connects to Cloud on your behalf.
An individual resource such as a single design can be shared with a specific user. That grant covers only that resource and works across organization boundaries.
What every new account gets 🔗 Cloud provisions a default organization, team, and workspace the first time a new account signs in successfully. Submitting the sign-up form alone does not create them. Email sign-up signs you in immediately, so that first sign-in happens as part of registration. You can rename the organization and the workspace at any time.
Created Name and description Your relationship to it Organization My Organization, “Default Organization” Owner, with the Organization Admin role Team My Team, “Default Team”, attached to My Organization Team Admin role Workspace My Workspace, “Default Workspace”, in My Organization Owner Global role Kanvas Assigned to every new user If any of your organizations has no workspace, Cloud creates My Workspace in it for you.
How Layer5 Cloud works with Meshery and Kanvas 🔗 Layer5 Cloud is a Meshery remote provider. Meshery Server delegates identity, tenancy, and persistence to it, and Kanvas, which runs inside Meshery, reaches it through Meshery Server.
Read the diagram from left to right. Providers sit on the left: Meshery runs with either a remote provider, which is the role Layer5 Cloud plays, or a local provider. The remote provider handles identity, tenancy, and the storage and sharing of designs. Meshery sits in the middle and mediates every request between the provider and your infrastructure. Your clusters sit on the right, where Meshery Operator runs MeshSync and Meshery Broker to report live state back to Meshery. Meshery, not the provider, is drawn connecting to the clusters and adapters on the right. What Cloud provides to a connected Meshery Server 🔗 When a Meshery Server uses Layer5 Cloud as its provider, Cloud supplies four things:
Identity and sign-in. Cloud authenticates the user and hands Meshery Server a token. Cloud publishes the keys that verify its tokens, as a JSON Web Key Set, at its unauthenticated /keys endpoint. Tenancy. Cloud holds the organizations, teams, workspaces, environments, and roles that decide what a user can see and do. Persistence. Cloud stores designs and their versions, records who each design is shared with, hosts the catalog, and keeps the event log. A capabilities document. Cloud tells Meshery Server which features the provider offers to the current caller, and Meshery and Kanvas enable only those features. Meshery Server also registers itself with Cloud as a connection owned by the signed-in user. See Meshery Server Registration.
The sign-in handoff 🔗 A Meshery Server, or Kanvas, does not collect credentials itself. It hands the browser to Cloud and waits for a token to come back:
The client sends the browser to Cloud’s sign-in with a source: the address of its own token callback, encoded in base64url. The user signs in to Cloud. If the browser already holds a live Cloud session, Cloud skips the sign-in page. Cloud returns the browser to the source’s token endpoint with a token and the original reference in the query string. The token callback path is /api/user/token or /api/token. Older Meshery Servers send /user/login or /login, and Cloud rewrites those to the current paths, so older servers keep working.
If the user was working anonymously and the handoff carries the anonymous identity, Cloud moves the designs created under that anonymous identity to the signed-in account.
Which sources Cloud returns a token to 🔗 Cloud issues a token only to a source it trusts. A source must use https, name a host, and carry no port and no user information. Its host must then be one of three kinds:
Source host Accepted when Cloud’s own host The source uses the same scheme as Cloud’s configured base URL. A custom domain of an organization The domain is configured on a live organization and the source uses https. A loopback host The deployment runs in development mode. Outside development mode, loopback sources are refused. Every other source is refused with an error and no token is issued. That includes other schemes and any host that is not Cloud’s own host or a configured organization domain. There is no built-in list of trusted hosts beyond these rules. If Cloud cannot complete the lookup of an organization’s custom domain, it refuses the source rather than accepting it. Cloud never applies the live-session shortcut in step 2 to a source on its own host.
What a Meshery Server gets from Cloud, by caller 🔗 Meshery Server requests the capabilities document with GET /<meshery-version>/capabilities, optionally adding os and playground query parameters. The older unversioned /capabilities path is deprecated. The document Cloud returns depends on who is asking:
Caller Capabilities returned Anonymous, or no valid token Default capabilities only. Signed-in user Account capabilities: overview, profile, and tokens. Signed-in user with the Kanvas role Account capabilities, plus the Kanvas extension capabilities and the latest Kanvas extension package version for the connecting Meshery version. Provider Admin Account capabilities, plus administrative capabilities (user management, statistics, and events) and the Kanvas extension capabilities. Playground (playground=true) Playground capabilities, added to the set the caller would otherwise receive. Every new user receives the Kanvas role when their account is created, so a typical signed-in user gets Kanvas in Meshery without any extra setup. A user without that role still signs in but does not receive the Kanvas extension from Cloud.
The provider name 🔗 Meshery shows the provider’s name in its interface. When Cloud resolves the caller’s organization, the provider name is that organization’s name, which is how branded organizations appear under their own name. Otherwise Meshery shows the default provider name.
What Cloud stores and what stays with you 🔗 Held by Layer5 Cloud Held by your Meshery Server and clusters User accounts, organizations, teams, workspaces, environments, and roles The live state of each cluster, which MeshSync records in Meshery Server Designs, their versions, and who each is shared with The workloads and resources a deployed design produces The catalog and the event log The connections from Meshery Server to your Kubernetes clusters, through Meshery Operator, MeshSync, and Meshery Broker Connection registrations, including each registered Meshery Server and its metadata Meshery Server, not your browser, talks to your Kubernetes clusters, through the components it deploys into each one. Deploying, dry-running, and undeploying a design are operations Meshery Server performs against the contexts you select. When Meshery Server registers a Kubernetes connection with Cloud, Cloud records that connection and its credential.
Real-time collaboration is the one path from the browser straight to Cloud: Cloud hosts the signaling service that introduces collaborators, and edits then synchronize directly between their browsers. Kanvas is documented under Kanvas.
Remote provider versus local provider 🔗 Meshery runs with either a remote provider or the local provider. In both cases, requests about your connected clusters and their resources stay within Meshery. The difference is what happens to provider-bound requests:
With Layer5 Cloud as a remote provider, Meshery Server forwards provider-bound requests, such as designs, views, the catalog, sharing, and support, to Cloud and relays the answers back. With the local provider, there is no remote service behind Meshery, so every provider-bound feature returns HTTP 501 Not Implemented. Choose a remote provider for any feature that depends on accounts, sharing, or stored designs.
SaaS versus self-hosted 🔗 Layer5 Cloud runs as a hosted service and as a self-hosted deployment, and both act as a remote provider in the same way. The trusted-source rules above are relative to each deployment: a self-hosted Cloud trusts its own configured base URL and the custom domains of its own organizations, not those of the hosted service. To run your own deployment, see Self-Hosted.

body:
Welcome, content creators and instructors!
This guide provides all the necessary documentation for building high-quality educational content on the Layer5 Academy. We leverage a Git-native workflow, allowing you to use simple Markdown to create powerful, interactive learning experiences.
This section covers the entire content creation lifecycle, including:
Structuring your first Learning Path from scratch. Writing course materials and embedding interactive labs. Designing effective quizzes and assessments. Managing and publishing your content. Each content type also has a dedicated build guide:
Creating Content for the Academy - repository setup and learning paths. Building Challenges - hands-on, scenario-based tasks. Building Certifications - formal assessments and certificates. Instructor Console - registrations, completion, and pass rates. Integrating Assessments - quiz, test, and exam files, question types, scoring, and attempt limits. Using the Content Template Creator - the registration flow, the front matter it generates, and the invitation behind each content item. Extending the Academy - HTML, CSS, custom shortcodes, embedded designs, and award emails. Platform Development - local preview, theme development, and end-to-end builds. Register content in the console 🔗 The content creation flow creates the content record and generates the identifiers and front matter you paste into your repository. Only the content type is required to create the record. The record starts with status not ready, public visibility, and beginner level. Cloud generates the slug from the content type plus three random words.
Step Field Behavior Basic Information Content Type Learning path, challenge, or certification. Basic Information Title, Description Appear on the catalog card. Content Details Difficulty Level beginner, intermediate, or advanced. Content Details Categories, Tags Used for discovery in the catalog. Content Details Banner Image Optional. A path to an image in the same folder as the content’s index file. Content Access Workspace An existing workspace, or a new one. Content Access Team One existing team. Learners join it when they enroll. Content Access Status Enabled or Disabled. Disabled blocks new enrollment. Content Access Content Access End Date When the invitation behind the content expires. Empty means no expiry. Recognition Badge The badge awarded when a learner completes the content. Generate Template Front matter The YAML to place at the top of the content’s index file, including the content ID. Registering content also creates an invitation, except when the content is owned by the provider organization. When a learner registers, that invitation is accepted at the same time, which adds the learner to the content’s team and assigns the Academy Learner role if the learner does not already hold it.
You can change the team, access status, end date, workspace, and badge later from the Curricula view. Changing the content’s id in your repository after learners register orphans their progress, because progress is recorded against that identifier.
Opening the console requires the View Academy Metrics permission (Academy Admin, Organization Admin, or Provider Admin). The organization must already have the Academy configured, or the console stays in its “not configured” state.

body:
The catalog is a public collection of designs for cloud native infrastructure. Browsing it needs no account. Cloning does. This page walks through finding a design, trying it without changing anything, and cloning it into your workspace as a private copy.
Cloning a design from a template in the Meshery Catalog 🔗 Cloning needs the Clone Design permission. These built-in roles hold it, and they also hold View Designs: the User role, Team Admin, Workspace Admin, Organization Admin, and Provider Admin. If your role lacks Clone Design, the clone action is shown disabled.
Open the catalog. You can do this before you have an account. To clone, sign in to Layer5 Cloud first. If you do not have an account, follow Setting up a Layer5 account. Search by technology or type. Sort by Most Cloned or Most Downloaded to see what other people rely on most. Each design card shows a summary. Opening a design shows its full details. You can also download a design to work with it outside Layer5 Cloud. Pick the organization and the workspace the copy should land in, for example My Workspace in My Organization. A clone lands in the workspace you have selected, in the organization you have selected. You must have one specific organization selected. Cloning in the all-organizations scope is refused. Clone the design from its catalog entry. Layer5 Cloud then creates your copy:
Property of the clone Value Name The original name followed by " (Copy)", for example “My App (Copy)” Owner You Visibility Private to you Location Your selected workspace in your selected organization Content The original’s catalog data and file location, converted to the current design format Cloning also counts toward the original: Layer5 Cloud records a clone event on the original design, which feeds the catalog’s Most Cloned sort and the catalog leaderboard. If this is the first design you own, your profile earns the first-design badge.
You can also publish your own design to the catalog.
Open a design in the Playground 🔗 Before you commit to a copy, open the design in the Playground. Open in Playground opens the design in a new browser tab in Kanvas on the Meshery Playground, loaded straight from the catalog. Nothing is cloned and nothing lands in your workspace.
When cloning is refused 🔗 Situation Result The design is not Published or Public Refused with HTTP 403 (“unauthorized to clone design”). Only published or public designs can be cloned. The all-organizations scope is selected Refused with HTTP 400 (“Creating designs is not allowed for orgID all”). No organization is selected Refused with HTTP 400 (“orgID is not provided”). Your role lacks Clone Design The clone action is disabled. What a clone is 🔗 A clone is a separate, private design that you own. It starts from the original’s content and lives in your workspace, where you work on it like any other design you own. Opening a design in the Playground creates nothing in your account.
Your copy is ready when a design named after the original with " (Copy)" appended appears in the workspace you selected, owned by you and private.
To move that copy into a workspace your team shares, follow Set up your organization. To edit it, open Kanvas. How the catalog publishes and lists designs is covered in Catalog.

Requirements 🔗 The layer5-cloud chart installs the Layer5 Cloud server and, as subcharts, Kratos and Hydra. The defaults below are those of chart version 0.2.0, which ships with Layer5 Cloud v1.0.278. Run helm show values layer5/layer5-cloud to print the defaults of the version you install. For the install procedure, see Deploying Layer5 Cloud.
Values 🔗 The chart writes env.* values into one ConfigMap and one Secret, and the server pod reads both as environment variables. Sensitive values go to the Secret. Any change to either rolls the server pods.
Where it lands Values Secret env.githubappkeypath (the key file content), env.githubAppClientSecret, env.stripeWebhookSecret, env.githubWebhookSecret, env.kratosWebhookApiKey, env.cloudCredentialEncryptionKey, env.cloudOidcStateHmacKey, env.providerOrgGithubSecret, env.providerOrgGoogleSecret, and all four smtp.* values ConfigMap Every other env.* value Both the Secret and the Helm release still hold your values in plaintext.
Workload 🔗 Key Default Meaning replicaCount 1 Server replicas. Ignored when autoscaling is on. image.repository layer5/meshery-cloud Server image. image.tag latest Image tag. Pin it to a release. When empty, the chart uses its own appVersion. image.pullPolicy Always Image pull policy. resources.requests 256Mi memory, 250m CPU Requested resources. resources.limits {} No limits by default. autoscaling.enabled false Enables a HorizontalPodAutoscaler. autoscaling.minReplicas, .maxReplicas 1, 100 Autoscaler bounds. autoscaling.targetCPUUtilizationPercentage 80 Autoscaler target. serviceAccount.name meshery-cloud Service account. fullnameOverride meshery-cloud The Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, and Secret derive their names from this. The container has a liveness probe on /healthz and readiness and startup probes on /readyz.
Networking 🔗 Key Default Meaning service.type ClusterIP Service type. service.port 9876 Service port for the server. service.hydraAdminProxyPort 9879 Port of the internal proxy that sits between Kratos and the Hydra admin API. Set 0 to turn the proxy off. ingress.enabled true Creates the Ingress. ingress.className nginx Ingress class. ingress.hosts One empty host routing / to port 9876 You must set the host. Add /kratos and /hydra paths. ingress.tls [] TLS secret and hosts. The chart does not create certificates. Server settings (env) 🔗 Key Default Meaning proto "" http or https. Used to build redirects to organization custom domains. Set https on a TLS deployment. serverbaseurl http://localhost:9876 Public base URL. Also the base of the OAuth2 callback <serverbaseurl>/callback. serverHost localhost Public hostname. port 9876 Port the server listens on. environment cloud development connects to a local database at 127.0.0.1:5432, tolerates a failed migration, logs rendered email bodies, and skips reCAPTCHA. Use any other value in production. debug "false" Sets the DEBUG variable. loglevel 4 Log level: 4 info, 5 debug, 6 trace. Not in the default values; the server uses 4 when unset. db, hydradb, kratosdb In-cluster PostgreSQL URLs with sslmode=disable Connection strings. Change the user, password, host, and sslmode. minmesheryversion v1.0.55 Lowest Meshery Server version that can complete sign-in. initConfig "" Provider initialization document. See Provider initialization. otelConfig "" OpenTelemetry tracing configuration. See Monitoring. anonymousUserSessionsEnabled false Lets the deployment serve guest sessions. Leave off unless you operate that flow. ghtoken "" GitHub token the server uses to dispatch workflows. githubappid not set GitHub App identifier for the GitHub integration. githubappkeypath key.pem Path of the GitHub App private key file inside the chart. githubAppClientId, githubAppClientSecret "" OAuth client ID and a client secret from the settings page of the GitHub App that githubappid names. Layer5 Cloud v1.0.287 and later uses them to confirm which installations of the App the authorizing GitHub account can access. When either is empty, the server logs a warning at startup and no GitHub connection can be created or re-authorized. The App must also meet the Self-hosted GitHub App requirements. stripeSecretKey, stripePublicKey not set Stripe keys for payment processing. recaptchaSiteKey, recaptchaSecretKey not set Google reCAPTCHA keys. Signup verification runs only when both are set. Organizations on a custom domain with a different registrable domain are exempt. kratospublic none, required In-cluster address of the Kratos public service. The chart fails to render without it. kratosadmin not set In-cluster address of the Kratos admin service. kratosbrowser not set Address browsers use for Kratos, such as https://cloud.example.com/kratos. hydrapublic http://hydra-public:4444 Address of Hydra’s public API. The default name does not match the subchart service. hydrabrowser not set Address browsers use for Hydra. hydraadmin http://hydra-admin:4445 Address of Hydra’s admin API. The default name does not match the subchart service. oauthclientid meshery-cloud Id of the Hydra OAuth2 client the server uses. oauthsecret secret1234567890 Secret of that client. Replace it. kratosWebhookApiKey "" Key Kratos sends as X-API-Key on registration hooks. When empty, the server accepts the placeholder dev_token. providerOrgGithubKey, providerOrgGithubSecret "" Client id and secret of the default GitHub OAuth application. providerOrgGoogleKey, providerOrgGoogleSecret "" Client id and secret of the default Google OAuth application. cloudCredentialEncryptionKey not set Base64 of 32 bytes. Encrypts stored credentials. When empty, encrypting or decrypting a credential fails. cloudOidcStateHmacKey not set Base64 of 32 bytes. Signs brokered social sign-in. When empty, brokered sign-in fails. webhookHelpAndSupport not set URL that receives support requests. webhookKanvasEntitlement not set URL that receives Kanvas entitlement events. webhookSignupRequest not set URL that receives signup decisions. Mail (smtp) 🔗 Key Default Meaning smtp.smtphost "" Relay host. Must resolve to a public address. smtp.smtpport "" 25, 465, 587, or 2525. Port 465 uses implicit TLS; the others require STARTTLS. smtp.smtpusername "" Mailbox login. Must be a full email address, because it becomes the From address. smtp.smtppassword "" Mailbox password. Set all four or none. A partial configuration stops the server at startup. See Email / SMTP Troubleshooting.
Kratos (kratos) 🔗 The kratos.kratos.config tree is passed to Kratos unchanged. The values you must change for a real deployment:
Key Default Change to kratos.enabled true Keep true unless you bring your own Kratos. kratos.service.public.port, .admin.port 9010, 9011 Public and admin ports. kratos.kratos.config.dsn In-cluster URL for the kratos database Your connection string. kratos.kratos.config.secrets.cookie, .cipher [""] Long random strings. kratos.kratos.config.serve.public.base_url http://localhost:9010/ https://<host>/kratos. kratos.kratos.config.selfservice.flows.registration.after.*.hooks web_hook to http://localhost:9876/identity/users https://<host>/api/identity/users and your kratosWebhookApiKey. kratos.kratos.config.selfservice.methods.oidc.config.providers GitHub and Google with empty credentials Your client_id and client_secret. kratos.kratos.config.courier SMTP courier, empty connection string Your courier. Password sign-in is on with a minimum length of 8. Login flows last 720m, registration 24h, recovery and verification 720h. A list in a values file replaces the chart’s list as a whole.
Hydra (hydra) 🔗 Key Default Change to hydraPrefix cloud-hydra Services become <prefix>-public and <prefix>-admin. hydra.hydra.config.dsn In-cluster URL for the hydra database Your connection string. hydra.hydra.config.secrets.system [""] A long random string. hydra.hydra.config.urls.self.public, .self.issuer https://public.hydra.localhost/hydra/ https://<host>/hydra/. hydra.hydra.dangerousForceHttp true false once Hydra is reached over TLS. hydra.hydra.config.strategies.access_token jwt Keep jwt. hydra.hydra.config.ttl.access_token, .refresh_token, .id_token, .auth_code 24h, 1000h, 1h, 1h Token lifetimes.

Default Organization Roles Organization Administrators 🔗 What is the purpose of this role?
Administration of an organization (for each organization for which the user has this role assigned) Who can assign this role?
An Organization Admin of that organization, a holder of Assign User Roles there, or a Provider Admin. The person must already be a member, unless the caller is a Provider Admin. When this role first assigned?
When an authorized administrator assigns it. Creating a user does not assign Organization Admin. The creator of an organization is its owner and keeps administrator access through ownership, which is separate from this role. How many instances of these roles?
Any number, on every plan. Layer5 Cloud does not stop you removing the last Organization Admin. The owner keeps administrator access through ownership. Who can remove assignment of this role?
The same people who can assign it. The roles you submit replace the roles held in that organization. What permissions does this role have?
Check Permissions Reference Layer5 Cloud has no Organization Billing Manager role. The other organization-scoped roles are User, Workspace Admin, Workspace Manager, Academy Admin, and Academy Learner. Organization Admins assign them. Provider Admin can assign any of them. See Roles.
The owner of an organization is not a role. Ownership cannot be transferred. The owner can delete the organization. An Organization Admin who is not the owner cannot. A role write replaces the member’s roles in that scope. An empty list removes every organization role and keeps the membership. Provider roles cannot be granted in an organization row.

Workspace Administrator 🔗 What is the purpose of this role?
Managing workspaces, environments, teams, and lifecycle actions, and reviewing catalog requests, in each organization where the user holds the role. It is not limited to a single workspace, and there is no Workspace Owner role that assigns it. Who can assign this role?
An Organization Admin of that organization, a holder of Assign User Roles there, or a Provider Admin When this role first assigned?
When an authorized administrator assigns it. Creating a workspace does not assign Workspace Admin. How many instances of these roles?
Any number, on every plan Who can remove assignment of this role?
The same people who can assign it Workspace Manager
Workspace Manager is the other workspace role. It includes workspace, environment, team, and lifecycle management, plus management of designs, environments, and connections inside the workspaces where the user holds the role. It does not include catalog curation. Organization Admins assign it the same way they assign Workspace Admin. See Roles and Permissions.
What permissions does this role have?
Check Permissions Reference

High-level List of Deployment Tasks 🔗 Review the prerequisites for installing Layer5 Cloud on Kubernetes. (docs) Prepare INIT_CONFIG so the first start creates the provider organization and its Provider Admin. (docs) Install the layer5-cloud chart. (docs) Create the OAuth2 client in Hydra. The server does not create it. Deploy Meshery separately and point it at this deployment as its remote provider. (docs, registration) Kubernetes-based Installation with Helm 🔗 The layer5-cloud chart is in the Layer5 Helm repository. It deploys the Layer5 Cloud server together with Kratos and Hydra. It does not install PostgreSQL, an ingress controller, or a TLS certificate. Make the decisions in Planning first. The commands below use the release name layer5-cloud in the namespace layer5-cloud.
Prerequisites 🔗 A Kubernetes cluster and Helm 3. An ingress controller that supports WebSocket upgrades, and a TLS certificate for your hostname. The chart does not request a certificate. A PostgreSQL server you can create databases on. Any deployment works, including an operator such as CloudNativePG, a managed service, or a server outside the cluster. The chart reaches it only through the connection strings you set. An SMTP relay that satisfies the mail constraints, or the decision to run without mail. Set all four smtp values or none. The OAuth applications for Google and GitHub, if you offer social sign-in. The chart does not require a dedicated database namespace, a local-path provisioner, or cert-manager.
INIT_CONFIG 🔗 INIT_CONFIG is a YAML document, set in Helm as env.initConfig. It is not a JSON object and it is not a Docker run flag. When it is set and the provider organization does not exist yet, the server creates that organization and the first Provider Admin. See Provider initialization.
Purpose 🔗 INIT_CONFIG gives a new deployment an administrator who can sign in. Without it, the server starts with no provider administrator.
Usage 🔗 env: initConfig: | organization: name: "Example Corp" description: "The provider organization for Example Corp." country: "United States" region: "North America" user: first_name: "Ada" last_name: "Admin" email: "admin@example.com" username: "admin@example.com" password: "<initial password>" Or load the same YAML from a file:
helm install layer5-cloud layer5/layer5-cloud \ --namespace layer5-cloud \ --set-file env.initConfig=provider-init.yaml \ --values values.yaml Note The server evaluates INIT_CONFIG on every start. If the provider organization already exists, initialization is skipped and later edits are ignored. Configuration Schema 🔗 Field Required Meaning organization.name Yes Name of the provider organization. organization.description No Description. organization.country No Country. organization.region No Region. user.first_name Yes First name of the administrator. user.last_name Yes Last name of the administrator. user.email Yes Email address. It is the sign-in identifier. user.username No Defaults to the email address. user.password Yes Initial password. There is no provider.name or provider.settings field.
Installation 🔗 Create the databases, write a values file that replaces the chart’s localhost and placeholder secrets, install the chart, then create the Hydra client.
1. Prepare PostgreSQL 🔗 Create one role and three databases, then create the uuid-ossp extension in meshery. The server creates its own schema. CloudNativePG is one way to run PostgreSQL. It is not required, and this chart does not install it.
CREATE ROLE meshery LOGIN PASSWORD '<password>'; CREATE DATABASE meshery OWNER meshery; CREATE DATABASE kratos OWNER meshery; CREATE DATABASE hydra OWNER meshery; \c meshery CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS "uuid-ossp"; Give that user the rights to create tables in the public schema of meshery. Kratos and Hydra run their own migrations when the chart’s automatic migration setting is on, which is the default.
2. Deploy Layer5 cloud 🔗 kubectl create namespace layer5-cloud helm repo add layer5 https://docs.layer5.io/charts helm repo update helm show values layer5/layer5-cloud > values.yaml Edit values.yaml before you install. The chart defaults do not produce a working deployment: URLs point at localhost, secrets are placeholders, and the in-cluster Hydra addresses (hydra-admin, hydra-public) do not match the service names the subcharts create. Set at least env.proto, env.serverbaseurl, env.serverHost, the three database URLs, the Kratos and Hydra addresses, env.oauthclientid, env.oauthsecret, the two encryption keys, env.kratosWebhookApiKey, env.initConfig, ingress hosts for /, /kratos, and /hydra, and either all four smtp values or none. Point Kratos registration web hooks at https://<host>/api/identity/users. The chart default URL omits the /api prefix, which the server does not serve. The field-by-field list is Helm Chart Values.
helm install layer5-cloud layer5/layer5-cloud \ --namespace layer5-cloud \ --values values.yaml kubectl -n layer5-cloud rollout status deploy/meshery-cloud After the first install, run kubectl -n layer5-cloud get svc and correct env.kratospublic, env.kratosadmin, and env.hydraadmin if the service names differ, then upgrade.
3. Create an OAuth 2.0 client 🔗 Layer5 Cloud authenticates to Hydra as an OAuth2 client whose id and secret you set in env.oauthclientid and env.oauthsecret. Create that client with the matching values and the redirect address <serverbaseurl>/callback. Sign-in does not work until it exists.
kubectl -n layer5-cloud exec deploy/cloud-hydra -- hydra create client \ --endpoint http://127.0.0.1:4445 \ --id layer5-cloud \ --secret '<the value of env.oauthsecret>' \ --grant-type authorization_code,refresh_token,client_credentials,implicit \ --response-type token,code,id_token \ --scope openid,offline,offline_access \ --redirect-uri https://cloud.example.com/callback \ --skip-consent The command uses the flag names of the Hydra version in the chart’s subchart. If your Hydra is older, its command is hydra clients create with --grant-types, --response-types, and --callbacks.
Confirm the deployment works 🔗 GET https://<host>/readyz returns 200. The server log contains Server is up and running! and no Failed to initialize Provider Admin line. You can sign in as the administrator from env.initConfig. Send a test email. See Email / SMTP Troubleshooting. If you registered Google or GitHub, sign in with each. Once sign-in works, remove env.initConfig from your values file and run helm upgrade, so the initial password does not stay in the release history and logs.
Connect a Meshery Server 🔗 Meshery Server is a separate deployment. Install it from the Meshery documentation, then point it at your deployment as its remote provider. See Meshery Server registration. The server rejects sign-in from a Meshery Server older than env.minmesheryversion.
Upgrade 🔗 Run helm upgrade with the new chart version and your values file. The server applies pending database migrations when it starts, and exits if one fails. Take a database backup first.
Provider initialization 🔗 A new deployment has no users, so nobody can sign in to administer it. Provider initialization solves that: when the server starts with INIT_CONFIG set, it creates the provider organization and its first Provider Admin. The provider organization always has the fixed identifier 11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111.
What happens at startup 🔗 The server evaluates INIT_CONFIG on every start, after database migrations and before it reports ready.
Not set. Initialization is skipped. Set but invalid. A missing required field or YAML that does not parse is logged as an error. The server keeps starting, with no provider administrator. The provider organization already exists. Initialization is skipped, and any change to INIT_CONFIG is ignored. The provider organization does not exist. The server runs these steps in order: Creates a Kratos identity with the password and the email marked verified. Creates the user and marks the account active. Grants the user the Provider Admin role and the Kanvas role. Creates the provider organization with the fixed identifier, owned by that user. Adds the user to the organization with the Organization Admin role. The first administrator can sign in as soon as the server is ready. They never see an email verification step, because the address is created verified.
After the organization exists, the server also seeds the deployment’s default Google and GitHub sign-in credentials from env.providerOrg*. See Identity Services.
Failure modes 🔗 Condition Result A step fails after earlier steps succeeded The server logs the error and keeps starting. The steps are not wrapped in one transaction, so rows from earlier steps remain. Fix the cause and restart. A restart repeats the whole sequence for as long as the provider organization does not exist. Kratos rejects the identity (for example, the password is too weak or the identity exists) The server logs a warning and continues with the remaining steps. INIT_CONFIG removed after the first successful start No effect. The organization exists. INIT_CONFIG changed after the first successful start No effect. Change the administrator through the product. Handling the password 🔗 The initial password is stored in the Helm release, in the pod environment, and in the server log, because the server logs the configuration it reads. Treat all three as secret. After you have signed in and changed the password, remove env.initConfig and run helm upgrade. The administrator account is unaffected.

By default, Kanvas opens a design in Full render mode. Full already draws TagSets, badges, and animations. You do not add render=full to reveal them. Add a render value only when you want the canvas to draw less.
To learn more about defining relationships between components, including the detailed use and creation of TagSets, please see the Creating Relationships | Layer5 Documentation.
Enable Full Render Mode 🔗 Full is already the mode a link uses when it has no render parameter. A link such as https://kanvas.new/extension/meshmap?mode=design&design=xxxx opens in Full.
TagSets can still be hidden when the mode is not Full, when the TagSets layer is off, or when the design draws more than 30 of them. In that last case Kanvas skips the rest and shows “Skipped rendering of N matchlabels relationships due to limit of 30”. See Render Modes and Performance Limits and Tuning.
Advanced Usage Note This is an advanced feature primarily intended for power users, debugging scenarios, or system-level integrations. You will not need to manually adjust this parameter for everyday design work. Why Use Full Render Mode? 🔗 This capability is particularly valuable for:
Detailed Inspection & Debugging: When you need to meticulously review, debug, or verify all components, relationships, and intricate details within a design. Comprehensive Documentation: For creating thorough screenshots or technical documentation that requires all visual elements to be accurately represented. System & Integration Testing: During testing phases to ensure all parts of a design are processed and displayed by the rendering engine exactly as expected. Best Practices 🔗 To use full render mode effectively:
Use Selectively for Performance
Full is the default and draws the most. On a large design, set render=medium or render=wireframe, or turn on Adaptive mode, so the canvas draws less.
Promote Consistent Shared Views
When sharing a design link with render=full for review, advise collaborators to also enable the relevant toggles in their Layers panel. This helps prevent discrepancies caused by individual layer settings, ensuring everyone sees the same details.
Check the Layers Panel if Details Are Missing
If render=full is active in your URL but expected elements (like TagSets) are not visible, verify that their visibility is enabled in your Layers panel. Your Layers settings can hide elements even when full render is requested.
Additional Render Mode Parameters 🔗 You can specify render modes via the render parameter:
render=full – Full rendering with all details. This is the default when the parameter is omitted. render=medium – Style-only rendering without TagSets and most badges render=wireframe – Outline-only rendering render=view-only – Non-interactive view. Spell it with a hyphen. Kanvas does not validate the value, and any other spelling, including viewOnly, is unsupported. For example: https://kanvas.new/extension/meshmap?render=wireframe&mode=design&design=xxxx
See Render Modes for detailed descriptions of each mode.
Adaptive Mode Parameter 🔗 You can enable Adaptive mode via URL parameter:
https://kanvas.new/extension/meshmap?adaptive=true&mode=design&design=xxxx
When adaptive=true is set, Kanvas monitors how long the canvas takes to produce the next frame after a pan or zoom and switches modes as needed. A link cannot set the ceiling: adaptive=true always starts with a Full ceiling, and render only sets the starting mode. Choose a different ceiling in the render mode switcher after the canvas loads. Adaptive is off unless the link or the switcher turns it on. See Render Modes for details.
render=view-only locks components for that session. It does not change who may edit the design. Anyone with edit access can switch the mode back.
Other parameters Kanvas reads 🔗 Append parameters to the Kanvas route. On the hosted app that route is https://kanvas.new/extension/meshmap. On the Meshery Playground or a self-hosted Meshery it is /extension/meshmap on that host.
Parameters Result mode=design&design=<design-id> Opens the design in Designer. This is the form the Share dialog produces. name=<design-name> is optional. mode=design&type=design&id=<design-id>&name=<design-name> Older form that Kanvas still accepts. mode=design&type=catalog&id=<catalog-id>&name=<name> Clones the catalog design into the opener’s workspace and opens the copy. catalog-design=<catalog-id> Opens the catalog dialog focused on that design. mode=operator Opens Operator. mode=operator&type=view&id=<view-id>&name=<view-name> Opens Operator on a saved view. mode=operator&type=view&design_id=<design-id>&design_name=<design-name> Opens Operator on a view scoped to a design. viewport=<encoded> Restores the zoom and pan Copy Link recorded. Copy the value from a link rather than writing it by hand. A link to a private design opens only for people who can read it. For anyone else the load fails with “Failed to render design”, followed by the reason. Public designs open for anonymous visitors. Render mode and adaptive stay in the address when Kanvas rewrites it, and neither is saved in the design.

The Layer5 Cloud Academy is a modular learning management system (LMS) designed for building learning paths and interactive, hands-on challenges. It is deeply integrated into the Layer5 cloud ecosystem and Kanvas — a visual designer for cloud native infrastructure. This integration allows you to embed live visualizations, interactive designs, and contextual experiences directly into your courses. This approach transforms learning from passive reading into active, hands-on practice. Who Can Create Content 🔗 The ability to create, manage, and publish content is available to organizations on our Enterprise Plan. This plan includes full support for: Multi-tenancy: Your content, users, and data are securely isolated from all other organizations. White-labeling: You can brand the Academy with your own logo and color scheme. Customization: You choose the learning paths, challenges, and certifications you publish. You cannot replace the theme’s layouts, archetypes, or site-wide styles from a content repository. You can customize shortcodes only. Request theme changes through the theme’s issue tracker. You can learn more about our subscription plans on the Layer5 Pricing page. Content Creation Process 🔗 We believe you should always own your content. That’s why the Academy is designed around a Git-native workflow that avoids vendor lock-in. Instead of using a restrictive web UI, you manage all your learning content within your own Git repositories. This gives you the full power of version control, collaboration through pull requests, and a workflow that your developers are already comfortable with. The entire experience is powered by Hugo, a powerful static site engine, but we’ve abstracted away the complexity. You and your team only need to write in simple Markdown. No Web Development Skills Needed You don’t need to be a web developer to create beautiful and effective learning content. The provided theme handles all the layouts, styling, and complex components, letting you focus solely on the quality of your material. Organizing Your Learning Paths 🔗 Your content is structured hierarchically to create a clear and logical learning experience for your users. At the highest level, you have a Learning Path, which contains one or more Courses. Each Course is broken down into Modules, and each Module consists of individual learning activities like Pages (for text) and Labs (for hands-on practice). In addition, Tests can be integrated at various levels of this hierarchy. This modular structure makes your content easy to navigate, manage, and update. For example, a Learning Path named “Mastering Kubernetes” might contain: A Course on “Core Concepts”, which is broken down into multiple modules: Module 1: “Workload Fundamentals”, containing a Page on the “Anatomy of a Pod” and a hands-on Lab for “Scaling Deployments”. Module 2: “Networking Principles”, containing a Page that covers “Services and Ingress” and a Tests on networking concepts. Content Isolation To ensure security and isolation, all of your content files must be placed within a directory named for your organization UUID. You’ll learn the specifics of how to do this in our hands-on tutorial. Advanced Content Features 🔗 Create custom Hugo shortcodes, mix HTML with Markdown, and add custom CSS styling to enhance your Academy content. Content Format Support 🔗 The Academy platform supports Markdown + HTML mixing and custom CSS styling. HTML + Markdown Integration 🔗 Combine Markdown syntax with HTML elements in the same file. Leave a blank line between a raw HTML block and the Markdown that follows it. Without the blank line, Hugo does not parse the next Markdown element and it renders as literal text. Markdown inside an HTML element is parsed only when blank lines separate it from the tags, so write short content inside HTML elements in HTML. ## Markdown Heading This is **bold** text in markdown.

HTML Section

This is HTML. Write the wording inside the tags as HTML.

More **Markdown** follows the blank line after the div. Custom CSS Support 🔗 The platform supports CSS through multiple methods: Inline CSS (as shown above) CSS in shortcodes (demonstrated below) CSS classes in HTML elements Live Example: This example demonstrates custom CSS styling within the Academy platform. The styling includes custom colors, padding, borders, and typography. When properly rendered, you will see: Markdown after the HTML block, once a blank line separates them. Markdown jammed against a tag, or left inside a tag with no blank lines, stays literal text. Custom CSS styles applied (colors, spacing, borders) Seamless integration without layout conflicts Responsive behavior across different screen sizes Creating Custom Shortcodes 🔗 Custom shortcodes are reusable components that enhance Academy content. They function as templates that accept parameters and generate HTML output. Basic Shortcode 🔗 Step 1: Create the shortcode file in your organization’s directory: layouts/shortcodes//custom-org-shortcode.html Step 2: Define the shortcode template: {{ $names := .Get "names" }}
{{ $names }} Hey! This is a custom shortcode
Step 3: Use the shortcode in your content: Alex, Bob, Charely Hey! This is a custom shortcode How it works: {{ .Get "names" }} retrieves the “names” parameter The shortcode outputs: “Alex, Bob, Charely Hey! This is a custom shortcode” You can reuse this shortcode throughout your Academy content Shortcode with CSS 🔗 Add CSS styling to make shortcodes visually appealing. Example: layouts/shortcodes//styled-callout.html
{{ .Get "title" | default "Note" }}: {{ .Inner }}
Usage: {{< styled-callout title="Custom CSS Example" >}} This is a styled callout with custom CSS. {{< /styled-callout >}} Result: Custom CSS Example: This is a styled callout with custom CSS. How CSS works in shortcodes:

body:
Follow Along with Jordan and Five Throughout the Kanvas docs, you’ll follow Jordan Reyes — a developer and designer at Orbital Labs — as she creates, shares, and iterates on infrastructure designs. Five reviews her work and occasionally discovers that a design works better in practice than it does in theory. Their starting point is the microservices-baseline design in the orbital-dev workspace. Meet the full cast → Sign in 🔗 Anonymous users can author designs and save them into a guest account. Sharing or publishing opens a sign-in prompt. On kanvas.new, Validate, Dry run, Deploy, Undeploy, connecting a cluster, and Operator mode open a prompt that directs you to the Meshery Playground or a self-hosted Meshery, including when you are signed in.
Sign-in page: continue with GitHub or Google, or log in with email. Start here 🔗 Starting from scratch — open Designer and create your first design. Importing a Design — bring in Kubernetes, Helm, Compose, or existing Meshery designs. Working with Components — configure, copy, and arrange components on the canvas. Creating Relationships — connect components with context-aware edges. Choose Designer when you are authoring infrastructure; switch to Operator when you are inspecting live clusters. See the Kanvas overview for the mode chooser.
Use Kanvas for your diagrams 🔗 Dev Env Documentation The dev environment is an often overlooked but critical part of an organization’s infrastructure. Knowing what clusters and services are used, how to run and test services locally, and how to troubleshoot are critical parts for getting a team up and running quickly. With Kanvas, you can easily embed designs into your How To and Getting Started guides, making it easy to create, maintain and update concise documentation.
Migrations and Rollbacks Migrations and rollbacks are some of the most important things to get right when they’re needed. By making it easy to create, find, and reference these documents and diagrams, you can be confident that your processes will be understood and your knowledge up to date.
Deployment Pipeline Kanvas keyboard shortcuts and preset icons make it easy to create beautiful, informative designs that explain every aspect of your deploy, test, and monitor pipeline. Embed several designs in one document to cover all of your different services, vendors, and data stores.
From a saved design to a cluster 🔗 Validation checks every component against its schema and does not contact a cluster. A dry run sends the design to the target cluster without applying it. Deploy and undeploy apply to the Kubernetes contexts you select. If you select none, the action targets all connected clusters. Each resource Kanvas creates carries:
Metadata Key Value Label design.meshery.io/id The design’s ID Annotation design.meshery.io/version The design version that was deployed Annotation component.meshery.io/id The component the resource came from Validate Design permits both validation and dry runs. Deploy Design permits deploying. Undeploy Design permits undeploying. Those actions are disabled while the design is empty. Switching to Operator with unsaved changes asks “You have unsaved changes. Are you sure you want to leave?” A design’s Operator view is named after the design, with -View appended, and filters on design.meshery.io/id.
The steps live on Validating Designs, Dry Running a Design, Deploying Designs, and Undeploying Designs.
