body:
Ever wondered what those little icons in the corners of your components are? Think of them as your component’s real-time status display. These indicators, called badges, give you at-a-glance information about everything from configuration errors to live performance.
A Tale of Two Modes A badge’s meaning changes completely depending on your current mode. In Designer, badges help you build a valid blueprint. In Operator, they switch to providing real-time operational data from your live instances. What Each Corner Means 🔗 While the specific badges change depending on your mode, they all follow a consistent placement philosophy. Badges are organized into four quadrants around a component, with each corner reserved for a specific type of information.
Identity and Origin (Top-Left) This corner answers the question, “Where did this come from?”. It is used for primary metadata that identifies a component and traces its origin or management.
Contextual Actions (Top-Right) This corner provides helpful, non-critical actions or shortcuts, such as a link to relevant documentation.
Management and Control (Bottom-Right) This quadrant is for hands-on management, providing tools to either control a component’s internal composition or interact directly with its live instance.
The “Problem Corner” (Bottom-Left) This is your go-to spot for all status checks and issue reporting. If something needs attention, you’ll find it here.
Badges in Designer Mode 🔗 When you’re in Designer Mode, your main goal is to build a valid and deployable blueprint. The badges here act as your assistants, helping you catch issues early.
Validation and Deployment Errors 🔗 Displays the total count of configuration errors found through schema validation and dry-run checks. Clicking the badge reveals the specific errors.
For example, a badge showing “2” errors, which can be clicked to see details like “invalid image tag” or “missing required field”. If you see an error badge, you can often click on it to navigate directly to the configuration field that needs your attention.
Design Inventory 🔗 Shows the number of other components that are included or associated with this component in the design blueprint.
For example, a badge on a Deployment showing “2”, indicating it includes a ConfigMap and a Secret as part of its design. External Link 🔗 A clickable link to external documentation relevant to the component.
For example, a link to the official Kubernetes documentation for Deployments. Badges in Operator Mode 🔗 Once your design is deployed, you enter Operator Mode to monitor its live status. Here, the badges switch context to provide real-time operational data.
Design Link 🔗 Indicates the resource is managed by Meshery and provides a direct link back to the source design that was used for deployment.
For example, a Meshery logo that, when clicked, opens the original design file in the Designer Mode. Policy Violation / Health / Performance 🔗 Reports the real-time health, performance, and policy compliance status of the running instance.
For example, a yellow icon indicating a performance warning, or a red icon for a critical policy violation. Terminal 🔗 Provides direct, interactive shell access to the component’s runtime, specifically for containers.
For example, a terminal icon appears on a running Pod, which, when clicked, opens a live command-line shell to that container. Best Practices 🔗 Fix Errors First: Always resolve all validation errors in Designer before you deploy. A clean design is the best way to ensure a successful launch.
Find the Right Source File: When fixing a problem with a live service, use the Design Link in Operator Mode. It’s the fastest way to open the correct configuration file, saving you time while being clear and reliable.
Know Your Mode: Pay close attention to your current mode. A badge’s meaning is completely different in Designer than it is in Operator.

This guide shows how to manage profiles through the Layer5 Cloud API. Profiles have no page in the Layer5 Cloud UI yet. For the base URL and authentication, see the Cloud API. All paths below sit under /api.
A Note on Permissions Each action needs the permission named beside it. A profile you cannot see, one that was deleted, and one that belongs to another organization all answer the same 404. See Default Permissions. List profiles 🔗 GET /profiles (View Profiles) lists the profiles you can see in your current organization. Without View Profiles, it lists only the profiles you own. Pass orgId to choose another organization you belong to, userId to find the profile that represents a user, and search, order (name, createdAt or updatedAt), page and pagesize to page through the results.
GET /profiles/{profileId} (View Profiles, or the owner) returns one profile you can see. The owner can always read their own profile, even when it is in no workspace.
Create a profile 🔗 POST /profiles (Create Profile) with a JSON body:
{ "organizationId": "<organization id>", "name": "Release announcements", "description": "The accounts we announce releases through" } organizationId and name are required. You become the owner unless you send owner. owner and userId, when sent, must each be a signed-in member of the organization, or the request answers 400. A new profile is in no workspace, so only you and the organization’s admins can see it until you assign it.
Edit or transfer a profile 🔗 PUT /profiles/{profileId} (Edit Profile, or the owner) replaces name and description. metadata, owner and userId change only when you send them. Sending a new owner transfers the profile. The organization cannot change.
Delete a profile 🔗 DELETE /profiles/{profileId} (Delete Profile) deletes the profile and removes it from every workspace. The connections it linked to are not changed.
Link connections 🔗 GET /profiles/{profileId}/connections (View Profiles, or the owner) lists the linked connections. POST /profiles/{profileId}/connections/{connectionId} (Edit Profile, or the owner) links a connection you can access in the profile’s organization. Linking twice is harmless. DELETE /profiles/{profileId}/connections/{connectionId} (Edit Profile, or the owner) removes the link and leaves the connection in place. Share a profile through a workspace 🔗 POST /workspaces/{workspaceId}/profiles/{profileId} (Assign profile to workspace) assigns a profile you can see to a workspace in the same organization. A workspace in another organization answers 400. GET /workspaces/{workspaceId}/profiles (View Profiles) lists the workspace’s profiles. Without View Profiles, it lists only the ones you own. Add filter={"assigned":false} to list the profiles you could still assign. DELETE /workspaces/{workspaceId}/profiles/{profileId} (Remove profile from workspace) removes the assignment. Members of every team assigned to the workspace can then see the profile.

Kanvas Designer offers three modes: Default, Pencil, and Connector, which behave differently based on the context in which they are used. Understanding these modes is essential for effectively interacting with components and the canvas. You can switch between mouse modes using hotkeys or tool selection. Here are hotkeys that control your mode:
Hotkeys Description Spacebar Temporarily enables the alternative mouse mode (default mode vs pan mode) H Switches to pan mode (hand icon) Escape / V Switches to default mode irrespective of which mode you are currently using. Interacting with Components 🔗 Select Tool Pencil Tool Pen Tool Pan Tool Action Cursor Style Behavior Example Hover default (arrow) Nothing Click-and-drag move Moves component in the direction of the mouse Click default (arrow) Displays component toolbar, resize box, and connection handles Double-click (component) pointer Opens the component configurator Double-click (textbox) text Enables text editing inside the component Right-click default (arrow) Opens the circular component context menu Click-and-hold crosshair Initiates box selection for selecting multiple components Scroll wheel default (arrow) Pan up or down Scroll wheel + CMD/CTRL default (arrow) Zoom in/out Horizontal scroll wheel default (arrow) Pan left or right Pencil lines do not connect individual components, but offer annotating capability, allowing you to take notes and draw annotations to enhance your designs.
Action Cursor Style Behavior Example Hover custom(pencil) Nothing Mouse down + drag custom(pencil) Start drawing a freeform line Mouse down + SHIFT custom(pencil) Start drawing a straight vertical or horizontal line Mouse up custom(pencil) Complete the line and render into a styled component Click custom(pencil) Draws ink from the pencil Scroll wheel custom(pencil) Nothing Scroll wheel + CMD/CTRL custom(pencil) Nothing The Pen tool operates as a creator of annotation edges. Note that the pen tool has two behaviors depending upon the context in which you initiate the connection.
To Activate: (CMD/CTRL)+E
Connector Behaviors Component-connect Behavior: When you click an empty spot on the canvas, and drag to another empty spot on the canvas, you get a joint (aka a terminal node) from which you can create new connections as well as new edge relationships. Canvas-connect Behavior: When you click an empty spot on the canvas, and drag to an existing component, you get an annotation edge relationship. Phase Cursor Style Behavior Example 1. Click & release pen Initiate connection 2. Click-and-move pen Move the ghost edge around if a connection was initiated 3. Click while connecting pen Establish and render the connection The table below outlines the mouse interaction modes available in Kanvas while using, detailing cursor styles and their expected behavior.
Action Cursor Style Behavior Hover hand Nothing Click-and-hold grabbing-hand Grab the canvas and pan in the direction of mouse movement Scroll wheel + CMD/CTRL grabbing-hand Zoom in/out in the direction of the mouse Horizontal scroll wheel grabbing-hand Pan left or right in the direction of the mouse

body:
The invitation system gives you precise control over how members join your organization, allowing you to streamline onboarding and enhance security.
You can create highly customized invitations for any scenario, from onboarding specific individuals to launching large-scale community challenges. Each invitation can be configured with expiration dates, usage quotas, and pre-assigned roles, ensuring new members get the right access from the moment they join.
Required permission From Layer5 Cloud v1.0.293, creating, editing, and deleting invitations requires the Manage Invitations permission within your organization. That one permission also covers choosing the roles and teams an invitation grants, so anyone who can write an invitation, Academy Admins included, can specify its roles. Contact your organization administrator if you need access. Default organization state 🔗 By default, organizations are closed: there is no open registration. A user cannot join your organization simply by navigating to a URL. They must either open a valid invitation link or sign in through a page associated with an organization that has a default invitation configured.
When no default invitation is set, new users who arrive at your organization’s registration page are registered as platform users but are not automatically added to your organization. They will have no organization membership and no roles until an administrator adds them or they accept an invitation link.
Two ways to designate the open signup invitation An organization’s open signup invitation can be set in two places: the invitation picker in Edit Organization, or the isDefault setting on the invitation itself.
The Edit Organization selection takes precedence. The isDefault marker is used when no selection has been made there, or when the invitation that selection points at no longer exists.
Roles are not assigned automatically When a user joins an organization via invitation, they receive only the roles explicitly listed on that invitation. If the invitation has no roles configured, the user joins with no role. Use the roles field on each invitation to ensure new members receive the correct initial permissions. Key capabilities 🔗 The invitation system provides three main areas of control to help you manage access effectively.
Create custom invitations for any audience 🔗 Tailor each invitation to your specific needs with three flexible modes:
Precise invitation: Target a single user by specifying their full email address. Domain-wide invitation: Onboard an entire organization at once by allowing any email from a specific domain (e.g., @layer5.io). Public invitation: Leave the email field blank to create an open link for public events (e.g., Academy Challenge invitations). Use domain wildcards carefully Patterns like @company.com allow anyone with that domain. Verify ownership and pair with roles and teams that grant only necessary access. Control the invitation lifecycle 🔗 Manage access with settings that put you in control:
Expiration date: Set a specific date and time after which the invitation link can no longer be used to join. This prevents new signups but does not affect members who have already accepted the invitation. Usage quota: Limit the number of times an invitation can be used. The invitations table shows current acceptance count alongside the limit (e.g., 2 / 5). Blank means unlimited If expiresAt is not set, the invitation never expires. If quota is not set, the invitation has unlimited uses. Manage invitations dynamically 🔗 Instantly revoke access by switching an invitation’s status between enabled and disabled at any time. A disabled invitation can be re-enabled later without recreating it.
How to create an invitation 🔗 To create a new invitation, navigate to the Invitations page from the main menu. Click the Create New Invitation button to open the creation dialog.
Email notifications After an invitation is created, a notification email is sent only to addresses listed in the emails field that are exact email addresses. Domain-wide patterns (e.g., @layer5.io) and public invitations (empty emails field) do not trigger individual notification emails. Share the invitation link directly in those cases. The email is sent at creation only. Editing an invitation does not send it again, and there is no resend. A failed send does not fail the creation. Sending stops at the first failure, so addresses after it are not emailed. The subject reads <Inviter name> has invited you to <Organization name> Organization. The body names the organization and the teams you pre-assigned, and carries an Accept Invitation button. It does not list roles. The sender is your organization’s mail configuration when set, otherwise the deployment default. See Bring Your Own Mail Server. Address matching is exact and case-sensitive: User@Example.com does not match user@example.com. Invitation properties explained 🔗 Property Description emails List of email addresses or domain patterns allowed to use the invitation. Exact addresses (e.g., user@example.com) and domain patterns (e.g., @example.com) are both supported. If empty, the invitation is public: any email address can use it. roles List of roles automatically assigned to new members upon accepting the invitation. If empty, the user joins with no role. Each role must be an existing organization role. Provider-wide roles, such as Provider Admin, cannot be granted by an invitation, and an invitation listing one, or a role that does not exist, is refused when it is created or edited. teams List of teams new members are automatically added to upon accepting the invitation. If empty, the user joins no team. Each team must be an existing team of your organization; an invitation listing any other team is refused when it is created or edited. quota Number that limits how many users can accept the invitation. If not set, or set to 0, there is no usage limit. expiresAt Date after which the invitation link can no longer be used. Does not affect existing members. If not set, the invitation never expires. status Invitation status: enabled = active and usable; disabled = inactive (can be re-enabled later). name A human-readable name used to identify the invitation. Required in the form, up to 255 characters. description Additional information about the invitation’s purpose, for internal reference, up to 5000 characters. acceptanceOutcome What accepting does. direct_membership (the default) makes the person a member of the inviting organization. child_organization creates a new organization for the person beneath it. Creating or editing a child_organization invitation requires Create Organization in the inviting organization. childOrganizationBranding Branding copied onto a child organization created by a child_organization invitation. Ignored for direct_membership. See Branding of a child organization. isDefault When enabled, marks this invitation as the organization’s open signup invitation. Users who register through your organization’s registration page are automatically enrolled through this invitation, receiving the pre-configured roles and teams. Without a default invitation, the registration page does not automatically add users to the organization. Only one invitation can be designated as the default at a time. Designating a new one clears the previous. Turning this setting on or off requires the Manage Invitations permission. Editing any other property of an invitation does not, and leaves the setting as it was. An edit that omits this property leaves it unchanged. The Open Org Invitation selection on the organization wins when it names an invitation that exists in the same organization. A selection that points at a deleted invitation, or at another organization’s invitation, is ignored and the isDefault invitation is used. Managing existing invitations 🔗 All existing invitations are displayed in a table showing key details for each invitation: its name and description, a copyable acceptance link, the owner, expiration date, quota usage, assigned roles and teams, and current status.
You can filter the list using the filter control at the top right of the table. Available filters are:
Status: show only enabled or disabled invitations Roles: show invitations that grant a specific role Teams: show invitations that add members to a specific team From the table you can perform the following management actions on each invitation:
Copy Link: Click the copy icon next to the invitation URL to copy it for sharing. Edit Invitation: Click the pencil icon to open the edit dialog and modify any invitation properties. Delete Invitation: Click the trash icon to permanently remove the invitation. This action cannot be undone. If another administrator deletes an invitation while your edit dialog is open, saving reports that the invitation was not found rather than reporting success. Close the dialog and reload the invitations table to see the current list. Whenever an edit cannot be saved, the dialog reports the specific reason it was refused.
Tracking who has accepted an invitation 🔗 The Quota column in the invitations table always shows the number of users who have accepted an invitation alongside the configured limit, for example 2 / 5 if a quota is set, or 2 / Unlimited if no quota is configured. This lets you monitor uptake at a glance. Disabling or deleting an invitation never removes people who already accepted. Delete has no confirmation step. Expiry stops new people only.
To see the individual users who are now members of the organization, navigate to the User Management page. Members who joined via invitation appear there alongside their assigned roles.
What happens when a user accepts an invitation 🔗 When a user clicks an acceptance link and is logged in, the system performs the following steps in order. Steps 4 to 6 describe a direct_membership invitation, the default. A child_organization invitation replaces those steps, as described after the list.
Validates the invitation: confirms it exists, is enabled, has not passed its expiration date, and has not exceeded its quota. A person who already accepted is also refused once the quota is full. Checks email eligibility: verifies the user’s email matches the invitation’s emails list. An empty list allows any email (public invitation). Matching is exact and case-sensitive. Checks verification for a direct_membership invitation: an account whose email address is not yet verified is not placed. The invitation applies at the person’s first verified sign-in. A child_organization invitation is not held for email verification. Adds the user to the organization: the user becomes a member of the organization that owns the invitation. An existing member is not added twice. Assigns roles: listed roles the person lacks are assigned. If no roles are configured, a new member joins with no role. Existing roles are kept. Adds the user to teams: the user is added to listed teams they are not already in. The first failing check stops the acceptance and nothing is written. The person sees The invitation cannot be applied to this user with one of these reasons: invitation no longer exists, invitation is not enabled, invitation has expired, invitation has reached its quota, email is not on the invitation's allowlist, or account email address is not verified yet.
Assignments are additive. An existing member keeps what they have, gains any listed roles and teams they lack, and loses nothing. The first acceptance counts against the quota, including for someone who was already a member. Accepting again does not use more of the quota. Each acceptance writes one event, <email> accepted invitation "<name>". Creating, editing, and deleting invitations write no dedicated event.
For a direct_membership invitation, role and team assignment failures are non-blocking: the user is still added to the organization even if an individual role or team assignment fails. The page then shows an Error Accepting Invitation message with the probable cause and remediation, and offers Retry and Go to dashboard. Retrying is safe: it does not duplicate the membership or the acceptance. A stored team that has left the organization is skipped and recorded on the acceptance event, and the acceptance still succeeds.
For a child_organization invitation, the user is not added to the inviting organization. Instead, a child organization is created for them with the invitation’s roles and teams applied inside it, as described in Choosing what accepting an invitation does. That acceptance is all or nothing: if any part of it fails, including a single role or team, nothing is created and the acceptance is not counted against the quota.
Choosing what accepting an invitation does 🔗 Every invitation has an acceptanceOutcome that decides where the accepting user ends up.
In the Create New Invitation and Edit Invitation dialogs, choose it under When accepted. Direct membership is selected by default. Child organization appears only if you have the Create Organization permission in the current organization. If you lack that permission and edit an invitation that already uses Child organization, the option is shown selected but cannot be changed.
acceptanceOutcome Result of accepting direct_membership (default) The user joins the inviting organization with the invitation’s roles and teams, as described above. child_organization A new organization named My Organization is created as a child of the inviting organization. The user is its owner and Organization Admin, it gets the standard My Team and My Workspace, the invitation’s roles are granted in it, and teams with the same names and descriptions as the invitation’s teams are created in it with the user as a member. The user does not become a member of the inviting organization, and the inviting organization’s own teams are unchanged. A few things hold for both outcomes:
Every team listed on an invitation must belong to the inviting organization. An invitation that lists another organization’s team is refused when it is created, edited, or accepted. Accepting is counted once per person. Accepting the same invitation again does not create a second child organization or use more of the quota. When someone creates a new account through your organization’s open signup invitation, they do not also receive a separate personal organization; the invitation decides where they land. If the invitation turns out not to apply (for example, its quota is used up), a personal organization is created for them as usual. Branding of a child organization 🔗 A child organization created through a child_organization invitation starts with your organization’s branding by default. The invitation’s childOrganizationBranding, shown in the invitation dialogs as Child organization branding, can change that. It is ignored for direct_membership.
childOrganizationBranding The child organization starts with parent (default) A copy of your organization’s branding: theme (logos and colors), sign-in page branding, links (including social profiles), and the sign-in page carousel setting. provider A copy of the platform provider’s branding. none No branding of its own. The copy is taken once, when the child organization is created. Later changes to your branding are not carried over, and changes the child organization’s admins make do not affect yours. Organizations created directly, not through an invitation, are unaffected.
Email verification 🔗 Someone who signs up with email and password through your open signup invitation must verify their email address before a direct_membership invitation adds them to your organization. Until then they are not a member, and they cannot sign in. They join on their first sign-in after verifying. A child_organization invitation does not wait: the new account’s own child organization is created at sign-up, because it gives the person nothing of yours beyond a place beneath you. Either way the account becomes active once the address is verified.
How the open signup invitation is applied at sign-in 🔗 The open signup invitation is not limited to first-time registration. It is applied whenever someone signs in through your organization’s own address, such as its custom domain, on every sign-in method that address offers, including email and password as well as social sign-in. Someone who already has a Layer5 Cloud account and has never been a member of your organization becomes a member on that sign-in, with the roles and teams the invitation configures. When the open signup invitation is a child_organization invitation, that person instead receives their own child organization beneath yours, as described in Choosing what accepting an invitation does.
It is applied only to people who are not already members, which has two consequences worth knowing:
Roles and teams are never re-applied to an existing member. If you remove a role or a team from someone who joined this way, signing in again does not restore it. Each person is counted once. Repeated sign-ins by the same person do not increase the invitation’s acceptance count or add them to the organization a second time. When open signup adds nobody A person can sign in successfully and still not join your organization. The open signup invitation is applied only when all of the following hold:
Its status is enabled. Its expiration date has not passed. Its quota has not been reached. The person’s email address matches its emails list. An empty list matches everyone. For a direct membership invitation, the person’s email address is verified. When one of them does not hold, someone who is not already a member signs in as a platform user with no membership and no roles in your organization, and no error is shown to them. Existing members are unaffected: they keep the membership, roles, and teams they already have. Check these four properties first when people who sign in at your organization’s address are not appearing under User Management.
Use cases and examples 🔗 The invitation system offers flexible configurations to fit a variety of use cases.
How invitation links handle unauthenticated users When a user who is not logged in clicks an invitation link, the system saves the invitation ID in a short-lived 30-minute cookie and redirects them to the organization’s registration page. After a successful login or signup, the system reads the cookie and automatically completes the invitation acceptance with the outcome the invitation’s acceptanceOutcome selects: membership in the organization with the configured roles and teams, or a new child organization. Scenario 1: Inviting a single team member 🔗 Goal: Provide a new employee with a secure, single-use invitation that grants the correct initial permissions. Configuration: Email: Set to the new member’s specific email address. Roles: Assign their specific role (e.g., Developer). Teams: Add them directly to their project team (e.g., Frontend-Team). Quota: Set to 1 to ensure the link is only used once. Scenario 2: Opening registration for an entire organization 🔗 Goal: Allow all employees from your company to join using their corporate email without individual invitations. Configuration: Email: Use a domain pattern to cover all employees (e.g., @yourcompany.com). Roles: Assign a default role for all new members. Scenario 3: Launching a community challenge 🔗 Goal: Create a public signup link for a limited-time community event with a maximum number of participants. Configuration: Email: Leave blank for public access. Name: Give it a clear name like “Layer5 Challenge 2025”. Expiration date: Set to the date and time the challenge registration closes. Quota: Set to the maximum number of participants (e.g., 100). Roles: Assign Academy Learner if that is the access they should have. Learners and billing Invitations are not limited by plan, and a seat count does not block someone from accepting. A member whose only role is Academy Learner is excluded from the billable user count. See User Management. Scenario 4: Granting temporary partner access 🔗 Goal: Give an external partner secure access to specific resources only for the duration of a project. Configuration: Email: Use the partner’s domain (e.g., @partner.com). Teams: Add them only to a shared project team (e.g., Project-X-Shared). Expiration date: Set to the project’s end date to prevent new signups after the project concludes. Description: Add a note for internal reference, such as “Temporary access for Project X contractors”. Expiration does not remove existing members Setting an expiration date prevents new users from using the invitation link after that date. It does not automatically remove partners who have already joined. When the project ends, manually remove those users from the organization or team. Public invitations Public links can be forwarded broadly. Always set an expiration date and a quota to limit unintended signups. Review Access Requests 🔗 An access request is a person asking for access to a Layer5 product capability, such as Kanvas. Layer5 Cloud collects these as signup requests in a queue. A Provider Admin reviews the queue, then approves or denies each request. Approval grants the requester Kanvas access and, for someone without an account, creates one.
This is not a request for access to a specific design, workspace, or environment. A denial does not restrict any resource. To let people join your organization, use an invitation. To limit what a member can do, change their roles or remove them from the organization.
Who can review requests 🔗 Reviewing requests is a Provider Admin capability. Organization Admins cannot review or decide requests.
Task Needs Open the User Requests page View All Access Requests, held by Provider Admin Approve a request Accept Access Request, held by Provider Admin Deny a request Deny Access Request, held by Provider Admin Approve or deny from a notification link Signed in as a Provider Admin Anyone who is signed in can file a request. Filing needs no role.
How requests arrive 🔗 A signed-in person files a request from the Playground card on their dashboard. The request is stored with the person’s name and email, a form type, a status, and a task link. A request filed this way carries placeholder values that appear as-is in the queue: form type Cloud, organization Cloud org, occupation Cloud user, a placeholder task link, and a role taken from the person’s first role or cloud user.
A new account receives the Kanvas (meshmap) role at its first sign-in, so the queue matters mainly for existing accounts that do not hold it.
A request needs an email, a first name, a last name, and a valid task link. A request that omits one is refused with a message naming the missing field. Creating a request sends no email or notification.
Review the queue 🔗 The User Requests page lists ID, name, last name, email, occupation, organization, role, form type, status, task ID, task, and created time. Processed rows are shaded. The default view is pending requests only. Filter by status (Pending, Approved, or Denied) or by form type (Meshmap, Docker Extension, Playground, or Event). Requests filed from the dashboard card are stored with form type Cloud and are not reachable through the form type filter. Find them with search or by clearing the form type filter. Search is a case-insensitive substring over first name, last name, email, organization, and task link. Order by created time or updated time.
Approve a request 🔗 Approval acts only on a request whose status is pending. Layer5 Cloud then:
Looks for an existing account with the request’s email address. If an account exists, adds the meshmap role to it. Roles the account already holds stay in place. The person receives a role-change email. If no account exists, creates one with the request’s name and email, marks the email verified, and sets the account up so the person can sign in. Saves the status as approved. Sends the request to the deployment’s signup-request webhook, which notifies the requester and updates the request’s tracking task. Records an event: <admin email> approved signup request for <email>. Approval has no confirmation step. If the webhook call fails, the status stays saved and you see the failure, so the request does not return to pending. A request with form type epsma-book skips steps 1 to 3: approval only records the status and sends the notification.
Deny a request 🔗 Denial asks for confirmation. It sets the status to denied, sends the same webhook notification, and records <admin email> denied signup request for <email>. Denial removes nothing. It does not remove a role or an account, and it does not restrict any resource. It closes the request.
Approve or deny from a link 🔗 Notification links open the decision directly. The link requires a Provider Admin session. If you are signed out, you are sent to sign in and returned to the page. A person who is not a Provider Admin receives Forbidden. If the request is no longer pending, you are sent to the User Requests page with a notice that it was previously processed, and nothing changes. Opening one of these links changes the request. Treat them like a button, and do not open them to preview.
Situation Result The request is not pending signup request for <email> previously processed. Nothing changes. The request id is unknown unable to get signup request. The caller is not a Provider Admin Forbidden. Approval cannot create the account cannot create account at the moment, with the cause from the identity provider. The webhook call fails An error is shown and an alert event is recorded. The status is already saved. Statuses are pending, approved, and denied. A processed request cannot be decided again. Catalog publishing uses a separate approval queue.

User Accounts 🔗 Anyone who uses Layer5 Cloud signs into a user account. Your user account is your identity on Layer5 Cloud and has a username and profile. For example, see Five’s profile.
Five, Platform Engineer Organization: Orbital Labs
Role: User (Platform Engineer)

Curious, enthusiastic, and reliably the first to discover that a feature works differently than the docs say it does.
See full cast →
Maya Chen, Org Admin Organization: Orbital Labs
Role: Org Admin + Development Team Admin

Your user account can own resources such as designs, connections, credentials, and API tokens. Any time you take an action on Layer5 Cloud, such as creating a design or changing a member’s roles, the action is attributed to your user account and written as an audit event that names that account.
A user account carries a profile: first and last name, email address, avatar, tagline, country, region, and social links. The username shown on the profile is the account’s identifier. It cannot be edited by the person or by an administrator. A person who needs a different sign-in address changes their email address instead, and the new address must be verified before it becomes active.
Layer5 Cloud enforces no limit on the number of users, seats, or organizations when people are created, added, or invited. Seats are a billing concept: a subscription’s billable user count is derived from the organization’s active members, and the count adjusts the subscription quantity without blocking anyone from joining. Members whose only role is Academy Learner are excluded from that count. A member added with no role is not counted. The count never falls below the plan’s minimum.
Info For plan names, see Layer5 subscription plans. Teams allow you to organize users into groups and assign access to workspaces, or to assign roles with associated keychains and keys. A person added to an organization or a team without a role is a member who holds no role. Membership and roles are separate.
Info Team Admin assigns the Team Admin role inside that team. It does not create user accounts. Organization Admin and Provider Admin hold Create User by default. See Teams and Roles. Organizations may have any number of teams, and teams may have any number of users. User accounts are owned by the person, not by an organization.
Users of one organization may be granted access to resources (for example workspaces and designs) of another organization through a resource-access mapping. Roles and permissions are organization-scoped: the permissions a user has in one organization do not apply in another.
Info Creating user accounts requires Create User, which Organization Admin and Provider Admin hold by default. Team Admins manage membership of their own team. They do not create user accounts. See User Management. Account Linking 🔗 You can link your Layer5 account to supported social sign-in providers after signing up, and you can unlink previously added providers at any time. Layer5 Cloud can also link providers automatically during sign-in when the provider returns a verified email address that already belongs to your account. This is how it works:
You create an account with the email address alice@example.com and a password. When signing in later, click to sign in with a social sign-in provider such as GitHub or Google that returns the same verified email address alice@example.com. Layer5 Cloud recognizes that the verified email address already belongs to your existing account and automatically links that provider. You are not prompted to re-enter your password for this linking step. After the link is created, you can sign in with either your password or any linked social sign-in provider. If a provider that is already linked to your account later reports a different verified email address, Layer5 Cloud still signs you in to the same account. The email already stored on your Layer5 account is not silently replaced or automatically updated.
Rules and Limitations
You cannot link the same social sign-in to multiple Layer5 accounts The provider a person used to create the account cannot be unlinked If you delete your account, any linked OAuth providers (for example, GitHub) are removed with the sign-in identity Re-registering with the same email creates a new account and does not re-link the OAuth provider or restore the deleted account Automatic linking depends on the provider returning a verified email address. When GitHub or Google reports an address it has not verified, Layer5 Cloud does not record that address on the account If a linked provider later reports a different verified email address, Layer5 Cloud preserves the email already stored on your account, signs you in to the same account, and records an audit entry Each active email address belongs to one account. Layer5 Cloud refuses a second active account for an address that already belongs to one You may unlink a social sign-in provider other than the one used to create the account When a person signs in with GitHub or Google through an organization’s custom domain, Layer5 Cloud resolves the provider’s verified email address itself: it creates an account when none has that address, signs in when the provider is already attached, or attaches the provider without a prompt when an account has the same verified address but not this provider.
Account Deletion 🔗 A person deletes their own account from their profile. Only a Provider Admin deletes another person’s account. Organization Admins remove members from their organization instead. Deletion is permanent, and Layer5 Cloud offers no recovery.
What deletion removes and what it keeps 🔗 Item After deletion Organization memberships and organization roles Ended in every organization. Each membership is kept as an ended record, so organization history shows when access ended. Team memberships and team roles Ended in every team, kept as ended records Provider-wide roles Removed Sign-in identity, password, and linked GitHub and Google sign-in Removed The account record Marked deleted and set to inactive. Its public profile is no longer served. Sessions and API tokens Stop working. Every API token is revoked. The person is signed out. The account’s email address Released, so it can be used to sign up again Organizations and teams the person owns Handed on: each passes to its longest-standing Organization Admin (Team Admin for a team), or else its longest-standing member. One with nobody else in it is deleted, unless the organization is the parent of another live organization. Credentials designated to an organization Handed to the organization’s owner, or else its longest-standing Organization Admin. For an organization the person owned, that is its new owner. Designs and other resources the person authored Remain. Deployed designs are not taken down. Content published to the catalog Remains public Audit events Remain, including an entry for the deletion “Longest-standing” means the membership that was created first. Members whose own accounts are deleted, and anonymous accounts, are never chosen. The new owner keeps the roles they already had. Ownership does not change anyone’s roles. An organization that is the parent of another live organization is never deleted this way. If such an organization has nobody else in it, it keeps the deleted account as its owner of record and the audit trail records why. The account is still deleted.
When deletion is refused 🔗 Because owned organizations are handed on first, a refusal is rare. Layer5 Cloud refuses to delete an account that holds a credential designated to an organization it does not own, when that organization has no live owner or Organization Admin to receive it, because the credential would be orphaned. The refusal names the organization and changes nothing. The same rule applies when a Provider Admin deletes someone else’s account. To proceed, promote another member of that organization to Organization Admin, or release the credentials, then retry.
Registering again with the same email address 🔗 Deleting an account releases its email address. Registering again with it, by email and password or with GitHub or Google, on Layer5 Cloud or on an organization’s custom domain, creates a new, separate account with a new account ID. The new account inherits nothing from the deleted one: no profile, preferences, organization or team memberships, roles, ownership, linked sign-in providers, or access to its resources. It gets its own personal organization, or, on a custom domain whose organization offers an open invitation, the placement that invitation gives any new account. An account is identified by its account ID, not by its email address, so the deleted account stays deleted and its audit records keep naming it. To regain access to an organization, ask one of its administrators to add the new account and assign its roles again.
Account status 🔗 Every account has one status. The status decides whether the account appears in member lists, counts toward billing, and can sign in.
Status Meaning active A working account. Only active accounts appear in member lists by default, in the public user directory, and in the billable user count. pending An account that has been created or invited but has not yet signed in, or a password registration whose email address is not yet verified. Pending accounts are hidden from member lists until an administrator applies a filter. inactive A deleted account. It cannot sign in, its public profile is no longer served, and API requests made with its tokens fail. anonymous An anonymous account. It never appears in member lists, user search, or the active users list, and it sees only the public portion of other users’ profiles. What others can see 🔗 Every account has a public profile. Display name, avatar, tagline, country, region, social links, join date, badges, and public activity are visible to anyone, including people who are not signed in. Email address, role names, teams, and organizations are hidden from signed-out and anonymous viewers and visible to signed-in viewers.
The public user directory lists active accounts by display name and avatar only, and can be searched without signing in. It never shows email addresses. An account without a first or last name appears as “Meshery User” followed by the first eight characters of its identifier.
Badges are public claims about a person. No one can grant a badge to their own account, a Provider Admin included. See Recognizing User and Contributor Milestones.
Active users are accounts that signed in within the last 24 hours. The list does not reflect a live connection. The Last Active time on the Users page is the most recent sign-in.
How people join an organization 🔗 Path Starting point Result Create a user The person has no account Layer5 Cloud creates a pending account and emails a link to set a password. The new account belongs to no organization until someone adds it. See Create a user. Add an existing user The person already has an account The account becomes a member with no role. Roles and teams are separate steps. See User Management. Invite The person has an email address, a link, or an address in an allowed domain The person joins when they accept, with the roles and teams the invitation lists. See User Invitations. Removal from an organization 🔗 Removing a person from an organization ends their access to that organization only. Their membership, their organization roles, and their membership in the organization’s teams end. Their account, their memberships in other organizations, the resources they created, and the audit trail remain. An organization’s owner cannot be removed. Ownership cannot be transferred. See User Management.
Removal ends membership. Account deletion, above, ends the account itself in every organization at once.

Whiteboarding in Kanvas (3:41) follows one late-night incident from page to postmortem on a single live design. Its page has chapters and a transcript.
The whiteboarding feature introduces versatile, freestyle drawing capabilities within Kanvas. Whiteboarding is enabled by default for all users and augments your ability to diagram with a suite of predefined shapes, and pen and pencil annotation, allowing you full freedom of expression of your engineering diagrams.
Looking for a specific operation? This page introduces whiteboarding and the drawing tools. For the per-object operations - adding, copying, cloning, locking, deleting, styling, resetting styles and resizing shapes, sections and textboxes - see Working with Canvas Objects. Key Functionality 🔗 Drawing Tools Integration Incorporates a comprehensive set of drawing tools resembling popular whiteboard applications. Enables you to draw shapes, group components , annotate, and highlight specific elements within the infrastructure design canvas. Real-time Collaboration Facilitates simultaneous collaboration among multiple users within the tool. Supports live editing and instant visualization of changes made by collaborators. Non-Invasive Annotations Annotations, shapes, or drawings created within the tool remain separate visual aids, not altering the actual infrastructure components. Using the Whiteboard Tools 🔗 Whiteboarding is on by default in every design. Its tools wait in the dock at the bottom of the Designer canvas: shapes, comments, images, sections, and the pen and pencil. The pencil draws freeform notes without connecting components, and the pen - Connector mode, Command+E or Ctrl+E - draws annotation edges that explain relationships and flow. See Understanding Tool Modes for how each mode behaves.
The dock, left to right: the select and hand tools, components, Kubernetes, shapes, comments, images, text, sections, then the pen and the pencil.
Everyone working in the design sees each shape, annotation, and edit as it happens, and each collaborator is identified by their avatar.
Turning the Tools On or Off 🔗 To hide or restore the whiteboard dock, right-click an empty area of the canvas, choose Options, and toggle Enable Dock. Enable Pen and Enable Pencil in the same panel show or hide those two tools.
Feature Highlights 🔗 Diverse Drawing Capabilities
Shapes, text, and annotation tools for expressive design enhancements. Effortless Collaboration
Seamless real-time collaboration empowers teams to brainstorm and iterate designs collectively. Identification of collaborators through avatars ensures clarity in collaborative sessions. Preservation of Infrastructure Integrity
Annotations exist solely as visual overlays, leaving the underlying infrastructure unaltered. Undo/Redo functionalities allow for design exploration without permanent modifications. Customizing Annotations and Shapes 🔗 Shape Customization 🔗 Shapes within the canvas offer flexibility. Select any shape to access a tooltip with options to resize, reshape, and change colors. This allows for precise adjustments similar to popular design software.
Text Annotation Customization 🔗 Text annotations come with various options. Customize fonts, sizes, alignments, and styles easily. Text boxes resize for seamless integration with the canvas.
Interactive Tooltip Interface 🔗 The tooltip is your gateway to customization. It’s simple and intuitive, offering a range of editing options upon selection. It’s designed for easy navigation, mirroring popular design software.
Advanced Customization Features 🔗 Manage layers, group elements, for better organization. These advanced tools ensure collaborative work while preserving design integrity.
Customizing Line Styles 🔗 You have the flexibility to customize lines to fit your design needs and architectural specifications. Lines can represent various relationships, such as data flow, dependencies, or communication between components. By adjusting line properties like curve style, arrow style, and line type (e.g., solid or dashed), you can visually convey different meanings, making your design easier for others to interpret. Use the design tooltip to adjust these visual elements and create clear, meaningful connections between components in your architecture.
Adding Line Animations 🔗 Take your designs a step further by adding animations to the lines, like the marching ants effect, to emphasize flow or movement between components. This feature improves visual clarity by highlighting the direction and movement of processes or data throughout your system, making interactions more intuitive. Adding this animation is simple, just click on the line and use the design tooltip.
Consistent Functionality 🔗 The customization tools apply uniformly to all annotation types. Changes made within the tooltip reflect instantly on the canvas, facilitating real-time collaboration.
Benefits 🔗 Enhanced Communication
Facilitates clearer communication by allowing visual annotations on specific design components. Reduces ambiguity and ensures better understanding of design intentions. Efficient Collaborative Workflows
Real-time collaboration accelerates feedback loops, enhancing team productivity. Enables instant sharing of ideas and design iterations among team members. Safe Environment for Creativity
Offers a risk-free environment for drawing, experimenting, and ideation without impacting the actual infrastructure. Encourages creativity and exploration within the design canvas. Use Cases 🔗 Team Collaboration: Multiple users collaborating on infrastructure designs, adding annotations and insights simultaneously. Educational Context: Instructors and students using the tool for visualizing concepts or workflows in remote learning environments. Architecture and Healthcare Planning: Professionals in architecture or healthcare visualizing and annotating designs collaboratively. Conclusion 🔗 The whiteboarding and freestyle drawing feature enriches Kanvas’s visual infrastructure designer tool by seamlessly integrating drawing capabilities without compromising the integrity of the underlying infrastructure. Its versatility in enabling real-time collaboration, preserving data integrity, and fostering a safe creative space positions it as a powerful asset for effective communication, efficient collaboration, and innovative ideation within diverse professional settings.

Layer5 Academy is a platform that provides a comprehensive learning experience for anyone beginning their journey into cloud native infrastructure or advancing along that path.
Three types of Academy content formats 🔗 Learning Paths: Guided sequences of courses that break down complex topics into manageable modules. Challenges: Practical exercises that focus on solving specific problems, often structured in a competitive or scenario-based format. Certifications: Formal assessments that validate professional skills and provide recognized credentials. Roles Served 🔗 Learners: Engage with Learning paths, challenges, and certifications to build and validate cloud-native skills Content Creators (Instructors): Develop and publish structured materials, and manage the overall learning experience Platform Developers: Extend and maintain the Academy platform, enabling new features and integrations Academy is an Enterprise-tier capability. An organization needs an Academy configuration from Layer5 before it can publish its own content. All three content types share the same lifecycle, enrollment model, and test engine. They differ in intent and in the credential they award.
Learning path Challenge Certification Assessment Tests throughout. Final tests gate completion. Practice tests do not. Tests that verify the solution. Final tests gate completion. Exams. The final exam gates completion. Credential Completion badge Completion badge Completion badge, plus a certificate when the content defines one Every test follows the same rules for scoring, attempt limits, time limits, and prerequisites. The Learner Guide describes them.
How content flows 🔗 Academy content is written as Markdown in the organization’s own Git repository. Layer5 Cloud holds the registry of that content and every learner’s record against it.
Author. A content creator registers the content in Layer5 Cloud, choosing its type, title, level, categories, tags, workspace, team, access end date, and the badge it awards. New content starts as public, beginner, and not ready. The creator then writes the Markdown in the organization’s Git repository. Publish. An organization admin or owner publishes a version. The publish workflow sends the organization ID and version to Layer5 Cloud, which builds that version into the Academy site. Content counts as published once its status is ready. Catalog. Published content appears in the Academy catalog. The catalog is public: anyone can browse it without signing in. An organization’s own Academy domain shows only that organization’s content. Enroll. A signed-in learner enrolls, which creates a registration with status Registered. If the content carries an invitation, enrolling also accepts it and adds the learner to the invitation’s team. Learn and test. Layer5 Cloud records the current item, completed items, quiz grades, and time spent. Each test attempt is a timed session scored on the server. Credential. Passing the final test marks the registration Completed, awards the content’s badge, and issues a certificate if the content defines one. A certificate has a public verification page and arrives by email. Measure. Instructors watch registrations, completion, and test pass rates in the Instructor Console, and can withdraw learners or update the content’s team, access, expiry, workspace, and badge. Layer5 Cloud records each of these Academy events in the organization’s audit log: content created, updated, or deleted; registration and withdrawal; progress updates and completion; content marked ready; test started and evaluated; and certificate issued.
Roles and capabilities 🔗 Access follows the role a user holds in the organization that owns the content. The Learner role grants access to Academy content. The instructor console requires the View Academy Metrics permission, which Academy Admin, Organization Admin, and Provider Admin hold by default.
Capability Anonymous Learner Academy Admin Organization Admin Provider Admin Browse the catalog Yes Yes Yes Yes Yes Enroll, take tests, earn badges and certificates No (sign-in required) Yes Yes Yes Yes Withdraw your own registration No Yes Yes Yes Yes Withdraw another learner’s registration No No Yes Yes Yes Use the instructor console No No Yes Yes Yes Create, update, and delete content No No Yes Yes Yes Publish a content version No No No Yes (organization admin or owner) Yes

Benefits of Using Relationships 🔗 Improved Visibility: Clear visual representation of connections between components Enhanced Design: Make informed decisions about component selection and placement Automated Configuration: Relationship-driven actions automate configuration of components Increased Flexibility: Use of selectors and operators provides flexibility in defining relationships Better Understanding: Easily comprehend the overall structure and dependencies of your managed systems What are Relationships 🔗 Relationships in Meshery characterize how components connect and interact with each other. They define the structure and dependencies between components in your designs, providing a clear representation of your infrastructure’s architecture. Relationships are highly expressive, capturing various forms of interaction between interconnected components regardless of their genealogy.
Meshery recognizes different kinds of relationships:
Hierarchical Relationships: Parent-child relationships showing clear lineage Edge Relationships: Connections depicting how components interact with each other TagSets Relationships: Connections based on shared Labels or Annotations 👉 Learn more about relationships
Creating Relationships in Kanvas 🔗 Kanvas provides an interactive interface to create and visualize relationships in your designs. Different types of relationships can be initiated in various ways:
Creating Edge Relationships 🔗 Edge relationships represent connections between components that interact with each other. These include network connections, bindings, permissions, and firewall rules. To create an edge relationship:
Single-tap on a component to open the edge picker Select the desired relationship type from the edge picker Drag the connection line to a compatible target component Release to establish the relationship Kanvas will highlight compatible target components as you drag the connection line, making it easier to identify potential relationships.
Creating Hierarchical Parent-Child Relationships 🔗 Hierarchical relationships represent parent-child connections between components. To create a hierarchical relationship:
Simply drag a child component and drop it inside the parent component The parent-child relationship will be automatically established For example, dragging a Kubernetes Pod into a Namespace creates a hierarchical relationship where the Namespace is the parent of the Pod.
Creating Inventory Wallet Relationships 🔗 Similar to Parent-Child relationships, Inventory Wallet relationships represent a relationship where a component is directly attached to another component, such as a sidecar container or WASM filter. These are visualized as a badge at the bottom right corner of the parent component with the number of inventory items displayed as a label.
To create an Inventory Wallet relationship:
Drag the attachment component (like a sidecar) to the host component After successful creation, a green badge will appear on the host component Clicking on this badge reveals all inventory items Creating MatchLabel Relationships 🔗 MatchLabel relationships (also referred to as TagSets) are automatically created when you input matching labels in the configuration for components. These relationships represent connections between components that share the same Labels or Annotations.
For example, if you add the same label app: frontend to both a Service and a Deployment, Kanvas will automatically establish a MatchLabel relationship between them and visualize it as a tagset around the matching components.
Keeping Configuration in Sync 🔗 Kanvas leverages Meshery’s evaluation engine to maintain dependencies between related components. When components are bound by a relationship, changes in one component can automatically update the configuration of related components.
For example, if you create a network relationship between a Service and a Deployment, updating the port in the Service will automatically reflect in the container port configuration of the Deployment. This eliminates the need to manually find and update configurations across multiple components.
The direction of syncronisation depends on the kind of relationships . for parent child relationships implicated configuration of child is updated to match with parent ( eg the value of namespace will be set to name of the parent namespace) . for edge relationships the configuration of the target will be syncronised with the source component eg the port number inside the deployment will be mutated to match the port number in service and similarly for inventory relationships the configuration of parent will get mutated to syncronise with the inventory item
Deleting Relationships 🔗 Similar to creation, relationships of different kinds can be deleted in different ways:
Edge Relationships: Can be deleted by clicking the delete button on the edge menu which can be opened by tapping on the edge Hierarchical Parent-Child Relationships: Can be deleted by dragging the child component out of the parent What to Expect from Relationships 🔗 Relationships help define semantic connections and dependencies between components, showing how one component can influence or modify others. Kanvas relationship visualization makes it easy to understand complex infrastructure details, such as:
How traffic flows through services and components (using network relationships) How resources are sandboxed or provisioned (using parent-child relationships) Which components affect or enhance other components through volume mounts, permissions, etc. Managing Evaluation/Visualization for Relationships 🔗 Individual relationship kinds can be toggled on or off from the relationships section of the designs. When a relationship is toggled off:
It won’t be considered for evaluation or visualization It will no longer be identified, validated, synchronized, or visualized in your design This gives you control over which types of relationships you want to focus on in your infrastructure design.

Academy Administrator Academy Administrator 🔗 What is the purpose of this role?
Management of an organization’s academy, learner management, and access to academy instructor console. Who can assign this role?
Organization Administrators When this role first assigned?
Manually assigned by an Organization Administrator. How many instances of these roles?
Min: 0, Max: many Who can remove assignment of this role?
Organization Administrators What permissions does this role have?
Check Permissions Reference Learner Academy Learner is an organization role. It is separate from the User role. Holding it grants access to Academy content and registration. Learners and billing There is no seat cap that blocks someone from receiving Academy Learner. A member whose only role is Academy Learner is excluded from the organization’s billable user count. The count still never falls below the plan’s minimum, and it does not stop anyone from joining. Learner 🔗 What is the purpose of this role?
To enroll in academy content within the organization’s academy. Who can assign this role?
An Organization Admin of that organization, a holder of Assign User Roles there, or a Provider Admin. Academy Admin does not assign organization roles by virtue of that role. When this role first assigned?
When an authorized administrator assigns it, or when an invitation lists Academy Learner. There is no automatic learner role and no separate learner invite link. An invitation is an organization invitation that can name this role. How many instances of these roles?
Any number. The role is available on every plan. Who can remove assignment of this role?
The same people who can assign it. Removing the role does not end the membership. What permissions does this role have?
Check Permissions Reference Status as a Learner
Each individual academy content item (learning path, certification, or challenge) that a learner enrolls in tracks one of the following 4 status types:
Status What it means registered (enrolled) They signed up but haven’t started completed They finished the course failed They didn’t pass withdrawn They left the course

To deploy a design, navigate to the Actions button at the top of the Design canvas.
Click on the Deploy icon.
This opens a modal that will take you through all the steps before the final deployment.
Click on Open In Operator to see the pre-filtered view of the deployed resources in the cluster
Click Finish
Deployment Errors 🔗 Missing Namespace: This error occurs when you attempt to create a Kubernetes resource without specifying a namespace. Kubernetes requires that all resources have an associated namespace. Empty Label Selector: This error indicates an empty label selector. Troubleshooting Errors 🔗 When reviewing validation, dry run, or deployment issues, you’ll notice specific error codes denoted from time to time.
As a system, Meshery itemizes different errors that occur and assigns a unique error code to each along with details on how to remediate the issue at hand.
For the comprehensive list of error codes refer to Error Code Reference in the Meshery documentation.
If you encounter persistent issues consider consulting the Meshery Community forum
Using the Notification Center for Troubleshooting 🔗 The Notification Center in Meshery helps manage events during the deployment process. It provides real-time updates and alerts on the status of the deployment. This feature can be particularly useful for troubleshooting, as it:
Displays immediate feedback on the success or failure of each deployment step. Highlights specific error messages and codes, helping you quickly identify and understand issues. Offers links to detailed documentation and guides for resolving common problems. Keeps a log of past notifications, allowing you to track and review previous errors and their resolutions. By actively monitoring the Notification Center, you can promptly address issues as they arise, ensuring a smoother deployment process. Learn more about Managing Events with the Notification Center.
Current behavior 🔗 Deploy needs Deploy Design, a non-empty design, and a Meshery you run. kanvas.new shows a prompt titled SELF-HOSTED FEATURE. If you select no Kubernetes context, Kanvas deploys to all connected clusters. The dialog title is Deploy design "<name>". Deploying does not need Meshery Operator. The same design applied again updates objects in place.
Every created resource is labeled design.meshery.io/id and annotated design.meshery.io/version and component.meshery.io/id. meshery-server-1096 means no selected context resolved to a connected cluster. meshery-server-1073 means the connection is not in the environment or cannot reach the cluster. meshery-server-1095 means the kubeconfig is invalid. No environments found means the organization has no environment (Create Environment and Edit Environment). If the Finish step spins and never reports, the request failed before an event, often an expired session.
