body:
In Kanvas, the Instance Details tab provides a detailed view of Kubernetes resources such as Nodes, Pods, Deployments, and more. This tab is essential for understanding the configuration and status of individual resources within your Kubernetes cluster. The Instance Details tab is accessible when you select a specific Kubernetes resource from the Resources tab. It allows you to view and manage the details of that resource, including its configuration, status, and associated events.
Depending on the type of resource selected, the Instance Details tab will display relevant information. For example, if you select a Node, it will show details about the node’s status, capacity, and conditions. If you select a Pod, it will display information about the pod’s containers, their statuses, and any associated labels.
Node Details Example: Kubernetes Node details.
Container Details Example: Kubernetes Pod Container details.
What the Details panel shows 🔗 Select any component on the Operator canvas and the Details panel reports that resource’s live state, as discovered by MeshSync. The panel is assembled per resource kind, so you only ever see fields that apply to the resource in front of you:
Identity and lifecycle - name, namespace, kind, API version and age. Status and conditions - the resource’s current status, with its Kubernetes conditions collapsed into an expandable list. Labels and annotations - shown as chips. Clicking a label adds it to the active view filter, so you can pivot straight from one resource to everything that shares that label. Workload shape - ready and available replica counts, update or deployment strategy, node selectors, tolerations, and the container images in the pod template. Networking - cluster IP, external IPs, service type, load balancer ingress addresses and Ingress rule hosts. Storage - access modes, storage class, requested size, bound claim, and the volumes mounted into the pod. Containers - each container and init container with its spec alongside its runtime status. Deep links - the Node, Namespace and ServiceAccount a resource is attached to. Clicking one re-filters the canvas onto that resource, which is the quickest way to walk from a failing pod to the node it landed on. Because MeshSync streams changes from your cluster continuously, the panel reflects the current state of the resource rather than a snapshot taken when you opened it.
Actions available from the Details panel 🔗 The header of the Details panel carries the actions that apply to the selected resource:
Action Available on What it does Initiate Terminal Session Pods and Containers Opens a shell into the container. See Interactive Terminal. Initiate Log Session Pods and Containers Live-tails the container’s logs. See Log Streaming. Initiate Performance Test Services and Ingresses Generates load against the resource’s endpoint. See Performance Testing in Operator. Open In Design Resources deployed by Meshery Opens the design that produced this resource in Designer mode, with this component selected for configuration. Open Source Design Resources deployed by Meshery Opens the source design itself in Designer mode. Download All resources Downloads the resource’s full JSON representation to your machine. The same actions are available by right-clicking the component on the canvas.
Resource metrics and events 🔗 Operator mode surfaces the standard Kubernetes signals you would otherwise gather with kubectl describe and kubectl get events, without leaving the canvas.
Node capacity metrics 🔗 Select a Node and the Details panel renders three gauges - CPU, memory and ephemeral storage - derived from the two figures Kubernetes reports in the node’s status:
capacity - the total resources the node has. allocatable - the portion of that capacity available to ordinary Pods, after Kubernetes holds back what it reserves for the kubelet, the container runtime, the operating system and the eviction threshold. Each gauge shows the difference between the two as a percentage of capacity - in other words, the share of the node that is not available to your workloads. The gauges are color-banded, shifting from green through amber to red as that share climbs past 30%, 60% and 90%, so a node with unusually little left for Pods stands out. Full Capacity and Allocatable tables sit alongside the gauges for the exact numbers.
System reserve, not utilization These gauges describe how the node’s capacity is divided between Kubernetes itself and the Pods it can schedule. They say nothing about what the Pods currently running on the node are requesting or consuming - Operator mode does not render live utilization figures or time series. For those, pair Kanvas with your metrics stack. Workload state 🔗 For Pods, Deployments, StatefulSets and DaemonSets the panel reports ready and available replica counts, per-container restart counts and states, and the QoS class assigned to the pod - the numbers you need to tell a slow rollout from a stuck one.
Kubernetes events 🔗 MeshSync discovers Kubernetes Event objects like any other resource, so events can be drawn on the Operator canvas alongside the resources they describe. Open the Layers panel, expand Monitoring, and enable Events. Selecting an event component shows its full detail - reason, message, involved object, count and timestamps - in the Details panel.
Because events are namespaced and short-lived, they are most useful narrowed down: filter to the namespace you are investigating before enabling the Events layer.

In Layer5 Cloud, a collection of permissions is represented as a keychain. One or more keychains are grouped together and assigned to a role. Later, a role can be assigned to a user. This is the general flow of how keychains reach a user.
A key allows one action, such as Create Token. A keychain groups related keys, such as everything needed to manage teams. A role groups keychains, and users hold roles in an organization or team. A user’s effective keys in an organization are the union of the keys in every keychain of every role the user holds there. A keychain grants nothing by itself. It takes effect only through a role that includes it.
Keychains make permissions reusable. Many roles need the same set of keys. Instead of attaching those keys to each role one by one, Layer5 Cloud puts them in one keychain and includes that keychain in each role. The same keychain can belong to many roles, and a role can include many keychains. Adding a key to a keychain grants it to every role that includes the keychain, and removing a key withdraws it from all of them at once.
Keys, keychains, and roles are records of the whole Layer5 Cloud deployment, not copies inside each organization. What is scoped to an organization is the role assignment. A change to a keychain, or to the keychains a role includes, applies to every user who holds an affected role in every organization.
For instance, the system-shipped Team Management keychain groups the keys for managing teams and team membership, including View Team, View Teams, Add User to Team, Invite User to Team, Remove User from Team, Create Team, Delete Team, Edit Team, Assign Roles to Team members, and Remove Roles from Team members. You can perform those operations when your user account holds a role that includes Team Management in the organization the request runs in. View All Teams is part of Organization Management, not Team Management.
Note The same keychain can be assigned to multiple roles. One or more keychains can be assigned to a role. Keychains are deployment-wide. They are not assigned inside one organization. The organization context decides which roles, and therefore which keychains, apply. Keychains Types 🔗 Layer5 Cloud ships 30 default keychains, each grouping the keys for one area. The system account owns them. Representative examples:
Keychain What it groups User View Viewing keys every user needs, including View Tokens, View Sessions, View Keys, and View Keychains User Management Managing users and their roles Team View Viewing teams and their members Team Management Managing teams and team membership Organization Management Managing organizations, their teams, and their users Security Management Token administration, including Create Token, Delete Token, and Download Token Provider Management Deployment administration, including Edit Key, Delete Key, Create Keychain, Edit Keychain, Delete Keychain, and Assign Keychains to Roles Environment Management Managing environments assigned to a workspace Workspace Management Managing workspaces of your organization Events Management Event statistics, audit, and summaries The remaining default keychains cover the catalog, lifecycle actions, extensions, settings, performance, views, collaboration, infrastructure, curation, the Academy, and the Kanvas action sets (Designer Actions and Operator Actions). Default Permissions lists the permission rows the docs matrix is built from and shows which roles hold which of those keys. Catalog approval keys such as Approve Catalog Request are grouped in the Chargeback keychain in the permission list, not in Provider Management.
Only a Provider Admin can change a default keychain, as with every other keychain. See Who can change a keychain.
Keychains Management 🔗 Create Keychains 🔗 Only a Provider Admin can create a keychain. The interface also requires the Create Keychain key, which only Provider Admin holds by default. This is the rule as of Layer5 Cloud v1.0.280.
Open the Keychains tab and create a keychain. Give it a name and choose the keys it bundles. Layer5 Cloud creates the keychain and adds each key to it. If adding a key fails, the interface reports it as “Failed to add key to keychain”. Open the keychain and confirm every key you chose is present.
You are recorded as the keychain’s owner. A custom keychain appears only in its owner’s keychain list, together with the system-owned keychains. Other administrators, including other Provider Admins, do not see it in their list, although any Provider Admin can still change or delete it on the server. Ownership only decides that list. It grants no right to change the keychain. A custom keychain does not belong to an organization.
A keychain does nothing until a role includes it. Creating and editing roles is a Provider Admin action. On hosted Layer5 Cloud, an organization cannot complete this path alone. On a self-hosted deployment, your Provider Admins can. Keychains are not organization-scoped. A role that includes your keychain grants its keys to every user who holds that role, in every organization.
Note If you do not hold View Keychains in the selected organization, the Keychains tab shows a permission error. Every default user role holds View Keychains through User View. Create Keychain stays disabled until you use a Provider Admin account. View Keychains 🔗 Review keychains by navigating to the Keychains page. Anyone holding View Keychains can open the tab. The list shows system-owned keychains and the viewer’s own.
Note If you do not hold View Keychains for your selected organization, you will see a disabled Keychains tab. Switch to an organization where your role includes View Keychains, or ask an Organization Admin to check your role. Assign Keychains 🔗 Including a keychain in a role, or removing it, is a Provider Admin action. The server requires the Provider Admin role for the whole deployment. Organization Admin does not hold Assign Keychains to Roles.
Open the Roles page as a Provider Admin. Add the keychain to a role, or remove it. See Roles. The change applies to that role in every organization, because roles are global. Assign the role to the users who need it, in the organization where they need it. See Users. Test with a user who holds the role. Sign in as that user in a specific organization and confirm the controls the keys govern are enabled.
Permission Assignment at Teams, Organization and Provider Levels Team Admin can assign roles to users in a team. Team Admin cannot create, edit, or assign keychains. Organization Admin can assign roles to users in an organization. Organization Admin cannot create, edit, or assign keychains. Only Provider Admin can create, edit, or delete a keychain, add or remove its keys, or include it in a role. The server checks that role across the whole deployment. Keychains Lifecycle 🔗 Layer5 Cloud ships with 30 default keychains. The system account owns them. Only a Provider Admin can add or remove keys on a default keychain, or on any other keychain.
Deleting a keychain removes its key mappings, so the keychain stops granting anything immediately, in every role that included it. Deleting is a soft delete. Removing a key from a keychain stops that key flowing to every role that includes the keychain. Adding a key to a keychain grants it to every holder of every role that includes the keychain. Authorization is evaluated on every request, so users gain or lose access on their next action, without signing in again.
Best Practice Default roles carry the default keychains, and every new user receives a default role. A change to a default keychain therefore changes permissions for users across the deployment, regardless of organization. Leave default keychains as shipped unless that is the intended outcome.
On a self-hosted deployment, to grant a different combination of keys, a Provider Admin creates a new keychain and includes it in a new role, and then the role is assigned to the users who need it. Keychains and roles are shared by every organization, so per-organization differences come from which roles a user holds in that organization.
Who can change a keychain 🔗 Keychains and their assignment to roles apply across the whole provider, not to one organization. Only a Provider Admin can create, edit, or delete a keychain, add or remove its keys, or include it in a role or remove it from one. This is the rule as of Layer5 Cloud v1.0.280.
Layer5 Cloud enforces keychain operations in two places. The interface enables or disables each control based on the keys you hold. The server checks the matching key and then confirms that the caller holds the Provider Admin role for the whole deployment. Holding the Provider Admin role inside one organization does not satisfy that check.
Operation Who can do it Where it is enforced View the keychain list and a keychain’s keys Anyone holding View Keychains, which every default user role holds through User View. The list shows system-owned keychains and the viewer’s own. Interface: the Keychains tab requires View Keychains. Server: returns only system-owned keychains and the caller’s own. Create a keychain Provider Admin. The interface also requires Create Keychain. Server and interface Rename a keychain, add keys, remove keys Provider Admin. The interface also requires Edit Keychain. Server and interface Delete a keychain Provider Admin. The interface also requires Delete Keychain. Server and interface Include a keychain in a role, or remove it Provider Admin Server When the server refuses a change to a keychain, it answers HTTP 403 with a JSON error. A caller who lacks the route’s key receives code meshery_cloud-1108. A caller who holds the key without being a Provider Admin for the whole deployment receives code meshery_cloud-3336, “Only a Provider Admin can change roles, keychains or permission keys”.
Note Create Keychain, Edit Keychain, Delete Keychain, and Assign Keychains to Roles belong to the Provider Management keychain, so by default only Provider Admins see these controls enabled. Everyone else can still view keychains. Change the keys in a keychain 🔗 Needs: the Provider Admin role. The interface also requires Edit Keychain.
Open the keychain’s update dialog, rename it, or change the selected keys. The interface adds and removes only the difference. Removing a key stops that key flowing to every role that includes the keychain, immediately.
Delete a keychain 🔗 Needs: the Provider Admin role. The interface also requires Delete Keychain.
Delete the keychain from its row and confirm in the “Delete Keychain” dialog. Deleting removes the keychain’s key mappings. The keychain stops granting anything at once, for every role that included it.
As with every keychain, only a Provider Admin can edit or delete a default keychain.
Troubleshooting 🔗 Symptom Cause Fix The Keychains tab shows a permission error You lack View Keychains in the selected organization. Ask an Organization Admin to check your role. Create Keychain is disabled You lack the Create Keychain key. Use a Provider Admin account. 403 with code meshery_cloud-1108 or meshery_cloud-3336 You are not a Provider Admin for the whole deployment. Keychains and their assignment to roles apply across the whole provider. Ask a Provider Admin to make the change. A user still lacks a capability The keychain is not on the user’s role, or the user holds the role in a different organization. Add the keychain to the role, and check the role is held in the organization in use. Keychain endpoints 🔗 Success responses are JSON unless stated. Errors from these handlers return a plain-text message. Refusals from the authorization layer return JSON. Paths sit under /api. Owning a keychain does not authorize a change to it. For a Provider Admin, a malformed keychain id on these routes returns 400 with a plain-text message.
Method and path Who may call Behavior GET /auth/keychains Signed-in user Lists keychains you can see. Parameters: page, pageSize, order, search (matches the keychain name). GET /auth/keychains/{keychainId} Signed-in user Returns one keychain. GET /auth/keychains/{keychainId}/keys Signed-in user Lists the keys in a keychain. search matches the key description. POST /auth/keychains Provider Admin holding Create Keychain Creates a keychain owned by the caller. Only the name in the body is used. PUT /auth/keychains/{keychainId} Provider Admin holding Edit Keychain Updates the keychain name. POST /auth/keychains/{keychainId}/{keyId} Provider Admin holding Edit Keychain Adds a key. DELETE /auth/keychains/{keychainId}/{keyId} Provider Admin holding Edit Keychain Removes a key. DELETE /auth/keychains/{keychainId} Provider Admin holding Delete Keychain Soft-deletes the keychain and its key mappings. POST and DELETE /identity/orgs/{orgId}/roles/{roleId}/keychains/{keychainId} Provider Admin holding Assign Keychains to Roles Adds or removes a keychain on a role. Roles are global, so the change applies in every organization. See Keys for the individual permissions, and Cloud API for authentication and the organization header.

This guide walks you through the Layer5 Academy platform’s multi-repository architecture. You will learn the role of each core component and master the practical workflows for theme development, local testing, and end-to-end validation with Layer5 Cloud.
The Multi-Repository Model 🔗 The Layer5 Academy platform is built on a “separation of concerns” architecture. Instead of a single monolithic repository, we use a multi-repository model where content, style, and build configurations are managed independently. This approach keeps the system modular, simplifies maintenance, and allows teams to work on different parts of the platform concurrently.
At a high level, the academy-theme provides the visual style for content from repositories like academy-example, and the academy-build repository acts as the central factory, assembling everything into the final website.
Core Repositories 🔗 The Layer5 Academy platform is composed of several core repositories.
academy-theme 🔗 This repository is the “skin” for the entire Academy. It controls the website’s design, including all the layouts, colors, and fonts.
Content repositories automatically import this theme as a Go Module. As a content creator, you do not need to fork or clone this repository; your academy will use these styles by default.
Currently, we only support customizing shortcodes in your content repository, not full theme customization. For requests regarding new archetypes, layouts, or theme enhancements, please open an issue in the academy-theme repository.
academy-example 🔗 This is the “starter kit” for anyone new to creating Academy content. It provides a pre-configured site that new organizations can fork to get started quickly.
Learn How to create your own learning path
This content repository doesn’t build the final website itself. Instead, it uses an automated workflow to act as a “gatekeeper” for new content. When you create a new GitHub Release, it triggers the following process:
Sanity Check: It first runs a local build to ensure the new content has no fundamental errors that would break the site.
Publishing Notification: If the check passes, it calls a reusable action from the academy-build repository. This action securely sends a request to the Layer5 Cloud API, using your configured ACADEMY_ORG_ID and ACADEMY_TOKEN secrets.
Publishing Trigger This request effectively says: “A new version of content is ready for this organization. Please update it.” This workflow does not build the final site; it only validates the content and notifies the build system. academy-build 🔗 This is the central hub of the entire system. It contains the main Hugo configuration for the production build and uses Go Modules to manage the versions of all content modules and the academy-theme.
When its workflow is triggered, an automated process acts like a master assembly line:
Collects Parts: It begins by gathering all the necessary components—academy-theme and all the course content from the various content repositories.
Assembles the Website: Next, it combines everything. It applies the theme’s design to all the course content, building a single, complete website.
Deploys Online: Finally, it takes the newly built website and automatically pushes it to the cloud platform, making the updates live for everyone to see.
If the build fails, the previous version of your Academy stays live. The content repository’s own workflow validates and notifies. It does not build the site learners see. Publishing a release is accepted only from an organization admin or owner.
Developer Workflows 🔗 How to Develop and Preview Locally 🔗 Use this workflow for rapid local development and iteration. If you’re only changing Markdown files and want a fast preview loop, run these commands within a content repository (such as layer5-academy):
layer5-academy as an Example We’ll use layer5-academy for these examples because it hosts all official Layer5 learning paths. It serves as a feature-complete reference, allowing you to see how a complex, real-world content repository is structured. go mod tidy: Cleans up and verifies Go module dependencies. make setup: Installs necessary tools and modules. make site: Starts the local Hugo development server. You can then view your content by navigating to http://localhost:1313/academy.
Local preview shows structure, content, and links. It does not show your organization’s branding, and it cannot score assessments, count attempts, or record progress, because those run on the Layer5 Cloud server.
How to Develop the Academy Theme 🔗 If you need to modify the academy-theme and see its effect on real content, you’ll use the go mod replace directive:
Modify the Theme: Make your code changes in your local clone of the academy-theme repository. Redirect the Dependency: In the go.mod file of the content repository you’re using for previewing (e.g., layer5-academy), add a replace directive to point Hugo to your local theme directory: replace github.com/layer5io/academy-theme => ../academy-theme Apply Changes and Relaunch: Run go mod tidy to apply the replace directive you just added. Then, restart the server with make site. The local server will now use your local theme code, allowing you to see your changes instantly. How to Use End-to-End Testing with Layer5 Cloud 🔗 Use this workflow for end-to-end testing that mirrors the production environment. This is the ultimate way to verify your changes work correctly within the Layer5 Cloud UI before they go live:
All steps in this section should be performed from the root of your local academy-build repository.
Install Dependencies: Run this command once to install necessary dependencies.
make setup Prepare Local Dependencies: If you’re testing local changes from other repositories (like a theme or content module), edit the go.mod file in academy-build to point to your local versions using a replace directive:
replace github.com/layer5io/academy-theme => ../academy-theme replace github.com/layer5io/layer5-academy => ../layer5-academy Build for Staging: Run the command to build the entire Academy site specifically for the staging environment.
make stg-build Sync with Cloud: After the build completes, run the following command to sync the generated static files with the Layer5 Cloud staging environment:
make sync-with-cloud Preview on Staging: Your changes will be available on the staging environment within approximately 10 minutes.
Local vs. Cloud Discrepancies The local preview (make site) is excellent for rapid development, but it is not a 100% accurate representation of the final product. The Cloud UI acts as a wrapper around the Academy content, which can introduce subtle differences. These are often caused by CSS class conflicts or variations in JavaScript execution within the larger application.
Always verify your changes in the staging environment before considering them complete.
When to Use a Holistic Build Test 🔗 If you need a faster way to check the final output without syncing to the cloud, you can run a production-like build locally from the academy-build repo:
make prod-build This command generates the final static files in the public/ directory. You can inspect the generated HTML and JSON files here to diagnose build-time issues before deploying.
Best Practices 🔗 Keep Dependencies Clean: After testing with local replace directives in your go.mod file, always remember to remove them and run go mod tidy before committing your changes. This prevents accidental check-ins of local paths. Test Incrementally: Start with local development for rapid iteration, then progress to holistic builds, and finally test in the staging environment. Version Control: Always commit your changes to version control before testing in staging to ensure you can track and revert changes if needed.

In Kanvas, you can share a design with specific people and set its visibility. A grant is for one person and has no access level: there is no view-only or comment-only option. A person who can open a private design through a grant can edit it, comment on it, clone it, and download it, and can change its visibility between private and public.
Sharing requires an account Anonymous visitors to kanvas.new can create and edit designs without signing in, but sharing a design requires a signed-in account. Choosing Share as an anonymous visitor prompts you to sign in; once you do, share as described below. Sharing Views You can share and control access to Views in the same fashion as you do for Designs. Verify People with Access after sharing In some earlier cases, the Share modal could report success while the grant or revoke was not applied. If you shared a design or view and collaborators still cannot open it—or someone you removed still has access—open Share on that resource and re-check the People with Access list. Re-add anyone who is missing, remove anyone who should not retain access, and confirm that collaborators can open the resource. Always treat People with Access as the source of truth after every share. Understanding visibility levels 🔗 Designs have visibility statuses that defines who can access your designs. These options offer different levels of exposure for content within your workspaces:
Private: Designs with visibility status private define only you, the creator, and the user or team that have access based on granted access permission can view and edit the design. Other users cannot access it unless you explicitly share it with them.1
Public: Making a design “Public” makes it accessible to anyone with the link or the design id, including anonymous visitors. Any signed-in user can edit a public design. A newly saved design is public, whatever visibility the client requests. Make a design private before you put sensitive architecture in it. A design cannot change visibility while it is published.
Why use public Public status is useful for sharing designs broadly, for example, as open-source templates, public demonstrations, or for soliciting feedback from a wider community. If your goal is to share broadly only within your organization, consider using a combination of private designs shared with specific organization-wide teams or workspaces. Published: The published visibility setting is designed for sharing designs with a wider audience. Published designs become discoverable to other users and allow them to view, download, and clone the design. Users can find published designs through Cloud Catalog (open catalog). Granting access to individual users 🔗 When you share a design, those users or teams become collaborators. You can share your designs with other users by using the “Share” modal. This modal allows you to grant access to individual users or teams. The following steps show how you can grant access to individual users:
Accessing the “Share” Modal:
There are two primary ways to open the “Share” modal for a design:
From an Open design:
First, open your Design or View in Kanvas. Click the main “Share” button, which is typically located in the top right corner of the editor interface. From the Recent Designs list:
Click the more options icon (often represented by three vertical dots ⋮) associated with that design. Select “Share” from the context menu that appears. Once the “Share” modal is open, search for the person and add them. The search covers every user on Layer5 Cloud your role may search, not only your organization. It returns ten matches at a time and nothing for an empty search. The people picker uses the View All Users permission. Without it the search is rejected and the dialog does not find anyone. The dialog finds individual users only. From the “Share” modal, you can also change the overall visibility status of the design (switching between Private and Public).
Share is hidden while the design is empty or published, and while it is still loading. Kanvas checks the Share Design permission before it offers Share. Under the local provider, sharing returns HTTP 501 Not Implemented.
Updated Share modal (Sep 2026): add users, People with Access, Private/Public visibility, and Copy Link. Owner vs. Collaborator 🔗 When you share a design, or when a design is shared with you, what you can do with it depends on whether you are the Owner or a Collaborator.
Owner: You are the Owner if you created the design. As the Owner, you have complete control over your design. This includes: Viewing, editing, and modifying all aspects of the design. Deploying the design. Sharing the design with other users or teams (making them Collaborators) and revoking their access. Changing the design’s overall visibility (e.g., from Private to Public). Deleting the design. Limitation: Ownership Transfer transferring ownership of a design to another user is not currently supported in Kanvas. Collaborator (Shared User/Team): When an Owner shares a design with you or your team, you become a Collaborator. As a Collaborator, you can actively work on the design. This typically means you can: View the design details. Modify configurations, add or remove components, and essentially edit the design’s content. Deploy the design. A collaborator cannot delete the design. Only the owner, or a provider administrator, can delete it. Ownership never transfers. Sharing the design onward, and revoking access, depend on the collaborator’s own Share Design permission, not on the grant. Most default organization admin roles include Share Design, so expect a collaborator to be able to share the design onward unless your organization has changed its roles. Layer5 Cloud does not restrict visibility changes to the owner. A person with a grant can switch the design between private and public. How You Get Collaborator Access:
When an Owner shares a design, they add users or teams as Collaborators. Whether you are added individually or are part of a team that gains access, you receive the standard Collaborator permissions described above.
Managing Access: Revoking and Inviting
As the Owner of a design, you can manage who has access to it at any time using the “Share” modal. This allows you to:
Grant access to new users or teams: Add them as Collaborators on your design. Revoke access from existing Collaborators: If someone no longer needs access, you can remove them. For example, if Sarah is added as a Collaborator to a design, she can edit it. If the design is shared with the “Engineering Team” and Sarah is a member, she also gains the same Collaborator access to edit the design through her team membership.
Workspaces and teams do not open a private design Adding a design to a workspace, and assigning teams to that workspace, does not open a private design to those teams. Layer5 Cloud checks the owner, provider administrators, and the design’s own grants. The Share dialog finds individual users only. Layer5 Cloud accepts a grant for a team through its API, but no access check honors it, so team members gain nothing from it. To give several people access, grant each person. Organization membership alone does not open a private design. Sharing Your Design with a Link 🔗 You can easily share a direct link to your design:
Open the “Share” modal for your design. Click the “Copy Link” button. This button is always available, whether your design is Private or Public. How the link works:
For Private Designs: If your design is Private, copying and sending the link acts as a convenient pointer. However, the recipient must also be explicitly added as a Collaborator in the “Share” modal to be able to open and access the design. The link alone does not grant them access if they haven’t been given permission. For Public Designs: If your design’s visibility is set to Public, anyone with the link can typically access it according to the permissions defined for Public designs (as discussed in “Understanding visibility levels” – for example, they might be able to view, comment, and edit). Link Sharing vs. Permissions Using “Copy Link” is a quick way to direct people to your design, but remember that actual access is always controlled by the design’s visibility status (Private/Public) and the explicit permissions you’ve granted. Sharing with Multiple Users via Teams 🔗 You cannot give a whole team access with one grant. The Share dialog finds individual users only, and a team grant is not honored by the access check. Grant each member.
There are two primary ways to share designs with teams:
Direct Sharing via the “Share” Modal:
You can add a team as a Collaborator directly through the design’s “Share” modal, similar to how you add individual users. This gives the team explicit access to that specific design.2 Indirect Sharing via Workspace Association (Intended Mechanism):
Another way access is intended to be managed for teams is through Workspaces. The general idea is: Place your design (e.g., a Private Design) into a Workspace. Assign one or more Teams to that same Workspace. By this association, members of the assigned Team(s) should then inherit access to the designs within that Workspace, including Private designs. Learn more about auditing the access permission within workspace
Share and visibility notifications 🔗 Kanvas surfaces explicit notifications when a share or visibility action cannot complete. These messages replace earlier silent failures so you can tell success apart from an incomplete request.
Situation What you see What to do You change visibility on a resource kind that does not support a visibility mutation A notification that the visibility change is unsupported for that resource (not a success message) Keep the resource’s current visibility, or use a resource kind that supports Private / Public / Published transitions. You click Share while the design or view body is still loading, or after the body failed to load A notification that sharing is unavailable Wait until the resource finishes loading, then open Share again. If the body failed to load, refresh or reopen the resource and retry once it loads successfully. The Share modal cannot load the access list A notification that the access list failed to load, instead of an empty collaborator list Close and reopen Share, or refresh the page. Do not assume that an empty list means nobody has access—until the list loads, the owner row and existing grants may be hidden, which also blocks revoke actions. People with Access is authoritative After any grant or revoke, confirm the result in People with Access before you rely on the change. A success path updates that list; if the list did not load or the expected user is missing, treat the share as incomplete and retry. This functionality is not fully implemented yet. Users might occasionally observe that even when a team is assigned to a workspace, members of that team may not be able to access private designs within that workspace without explicit individual or team-level sharing for the design itself. ↩︎
This feature (direct sharing with teams via the “Share” modal) is not yet fully implemented and is planned for a future update. ↩︎

The Views tab is located on the right side of the screen just beside the Details tab in Kanvas Operator. It lists every view you can reach in the current workspace - the ones you created and the ones teammates have made public - so that you can move between saved perspectives of your clusters without rebuilding the filters each time. Think of views for Operator mode as you would designs for Designer mode.
A view is a named, saved set of filters over the resources that MeshSync has discovered in your connected clusters: the namespaces, kinds, labels and search terms that decide which resources are drawn on the Operator canvas. Saving those filters as a view means the same slice of your infrastructure comes back on demand, for you and for your team.
Managing Views 🔗 Here’s what you can do with views in Operator:
1. Save a view 🔗 To save a view, simply give your view a title in the Name field at the top of the canvas. Any changes made to the view will be automatically saved. Alternatively, click on the “Save as” button at the top of the canvas. A modal will pop up for you to give your view a name and save it.
2. Set view visibility 🔗 You can choose to set your views to be either public or private. When views are set as public, everyone within your workspace can access these views. Views set as private are visible only to the person who created the view, ie the owner.
3. Share a view 🔗 Sharing a view lets you collaborate with team members. In the share modal, you can add the user you want to share the view with. You can also set your view access as either public or private. When it’s set to public, anyone with the link to the view can edit the view. When it’s set to private, others can view but only the owner can edit.
Views use the same Share modal and access list as designs. After you grant or revoke access, confirm the result under People with Access. For guidance on verifying access and for the notifications Kanvas shows when share or visibility actions cannot complete, see Sharing Designs.
To share a view,
Click on the actions icon to the right of the view you want to share.
You’ll find a list of actions. Share is the third icon from the left
Click on the share icon to open up the share modal.
Enter the name of the user you want to share a view with and set the view access.
4. Delete a view 🔗 You can delete a view when you no longer have use of it. You can only delete a view that you created. Views created by others and made public cannot be deleted, except by the owner of that view.
5. Export a view 🔗 To export a view, click on the export icon in the actions list. The view will be downloaded to your device in json format.
6. View info 🔗 View info shows you the owner of the design, the view visibility (whether it’s set to public or private), the date the design was created and the date it was last modified. If you’re the owner of the view, you’ll also see an input field where you can add notes about the design.
7. Open a view 🔗 Open a saved view to return to the slice of infrastructure it describes. Kanvas re-applies the view’s filters and redraws the canvas against the current state of your clusters, so an opened view always shows live resources rather than a snapshot.
From the Views tab, click the view you want to open. From the file menu at the top left of Kanvas, choose Open… and pick the view from your workspace. From Layer5 Cloud, open the workspace that the view is assigned to and select it there. 8. Edit a view 🔗 A view is edited by changing what it shows. With the view open, adjust the filters in the Layers panel - namespaces, kinds, labels - or type into the search bar, and rename the view in the Name field at the top of the canvas. Kanvas saves those changes back to the view automatically; the cloud icon beside the name reports whether the current state has been persisted.
Who may edit a view follows its visibility, and the two behave very differently:
Public views are editable by anyone in your organization. Changes are saved to the view itself, so everyone who opens it afterwards sees them. If you only wanted your own variation, take a copy with Save as… instead - see Duplicate a view. Private views are editable by their owner, by anyone the owner has granted access to through the share modal, and by organization administrators. Everyone else is refused. Deleting is stricter than editing: only the owner, or an organization administrator, can delete a view, whatever its visibility.
9. Duplicate a view 🔗 To work from an existing view without altering it, open the view and choose Save as… from the file menu. Give the copy a name and Kanvas stores it as a new, independent view owned by you. The original is left untouched, and the copy starts out private until you change its visibility.
10. View component details 🔗 A view is a window onto real resources, so every component drawn on the Operator canvas can be inspected in place. Click a component and the Details panel on the right shows that resource’s live state as MeshSync reports it - status and conditions, labels and annotations, containers, and the relationships that connect it to the rest of the cluster.
For a full description of what the panel shows for each kind of resource, and of the actions available from it, see Instance Details.

body:
Account consolidation merges every duplicate Layer5 Cloud account that belongs to one person into a single canonical account. The canonical account takes ownership of the duplicates’ designs, connections, memberships, roles, and other data, keeps their email addresses so old sign-ins still land in the right place, and retires the duplicates.
Operator-only Consolidation is a command-line tool, consolidate-users, that a deployment operator runs with direct database access. It is not an API, not a UI feature, and not automatic. Customers of the Layer5-hosted service cannot trigger it and have no control over it. Operators of a self-hosted Layer5 Cloud run it themselves. What changed 🔗 The identity provider behind Layer5 Cloud could create a separate account for each sign-in method one person used. A person who registered with a password and later signed in with GitHub or Google could end up with two or three accounts, even when they shared the same email address. Designs, organizations, and workspaces created under one sign-in method appeared to disappear when the person signed in with another.
Consolidation treats each group of accounts that belong to one person as a cluster and collapses the cluster into one account. For each affected person, resources move to a single retained account, including:
Designs and views Workspaces and environments Connections and credentials Performance profiles and results Schedules API tokens Organization and team memberships and roles Keychains and keys Teams the duplicate owns Invitations the duplicate created Academy registrations and test submissions Event trackers Resource access grants Revoked tokens stay on the retired account on purpose and still read as revoked.
Organizations are handled separately from that transfer. An organization owned by a duplicate account with no other active members outside the cluster, typically the organization Layer5 Cloud creates for every new account, is deleted. Before it is deleted, an empty workspace (no designs, environments, or views) is soft-deleted, and a non-empty workspace moves, with its ownership, to the canonical account’s earliest-created organization. An organization that does have other active members is preserved, and its ownership transfers to the retained account. Related organizations are deleted leaves first, children before parents.
If a connection name collides during the merge, the duplicate is renamed with a (merged) suffix, and (merged, 2), (merged, 3), and so on for any further collisions on the same name, so both remain identifiable.
People whose accounts are merged receive no notification.
Nothing for you to do Customers do not run consolidation. If you sign in with a different method and resources appear to be missing, contact support with the email addresses you have used to sign in. Signing in with multiple methods 🔗 Signing in with email and password, GitHub, or Google using the same verified email address always resolves to the same account:
You create an account with alice@example.com, whether by setting a password or signing in with GitHub or Google. Later, you sign in with a different method (for example, Google instead of GitHub) using a provider that returns the same verified email address. Layer5 Cloud recognizes the verified email address and signs you into your existing account rather than creating a new one. Your designs, organizations, and workspaces are available regardless of which sign-in method you used to create them. Each email address belongs to a single active account, so a second account can no longer be created for an address that already belongs to one. For how sign-in methods attach to one account, see Account Linking.
Your email addresses 🔗 Your account has exactly one primary email address at a time. That is the address shown on your profile and the one used to identify you.
If your account absorbed a duplicate during consolidation, Layer5 Cloud also keeps a record of the addresses that duplicate used. Each of those addresses continues to work for:
Accepting invitations sent to that address Role assignments made against that address These additional addresses are not displayed in the Layer5 Cloud interface. The account holder, or a Provider Admin, can list them through the API at GET /api/identity/users/{userId}/emails.
Wanting separate accounts 🔗 Each email address maps to exactly one active account. If you deliberately want separate accounts, for example to keep a testing environment separate from production, use a distinct email address for each account.
For organization admins: billing impact 🔗 The billable user count follows organization membership and counts distinct people, so a person who had several accounts in one organization counts once after the merge. The count is recalculated on its regular schedule and never falls below the plan’s minimum number of users. There is nothing to adjust manually.
Minimum-seat plans Billable seats never drop below your plan’s minimum. If your plan was already at its minimum-seat floor, consolidation has no effect on your seat count or billing. Why consolidation is required 🔗 A Layer5 Cloud database migration enforces one active account per email address. That migration refuses to apply while duplicate accounts remain, and reports:
Refusing to enforce email uniqueness: N live duplicate-email cluster(s) remain in users. Run the consolidate-users command (default mode, then –by-email) to clear them first
A second variant of the check refuses when two active entries in the email-address records share one address. Self-hosted operators who upgrade across this migration must run consolidation first. Once the migration applies, Layer5 Cloud cannot create a second active account for an address that already belongs to one.
How consolidation works 🔗 Consolidation runs in four phases: discovery, planning, merging, and linking the identity. Discovery and planning only read data. Merging and linking write only in a live run.
Discovery groups live, non-anonymous accounts that have not already been merged by the identity-provider identity they share. Accounts with no email address are ignored. An account in Pending status joins a cluster only when its email exactly matches an active account already in that cluster. A cluster needs two or more accounts. An active account whose email resolves to no identity, and an email address that maps to more than one identity, are never merged. They are reported for review.
Each cluster keeps one canonical account, in this order: an Active account wins over one that is not, then the earliest-created account, then the account with the lowest id. Every other account in the cluster is retired.
Each cluster merges inside one database transaction:
Every duplicate must still be live and unmerged. If any changed since planning, the cluster is skipped with “skipped (already merged / changed since planning)”. A skip does not stop the run. Duplicate role assignments the canonical account already holds are soft-deleted. The rest move. Colliding connection names are renamed as described above. Every live record a duplicate owns moves to the canonical account. Organization and team memberships are recomputed inside the transaction. Two memberships duplicate when they share the same organization or team and the same role. A different role in the same scope is kept. When two memberships duplicate, the higher-privilege role wins, ranked from highest: Provider Admin, Organization Admin, Team Admin, Workspace Admin, Workspace Manager, Academy Admin, User, Academy Learner. Unknown role names tie, and the older membership wins. Organizations a duplicate owns are deleted or transferred as described in What changed. Each duplicate’s live email-address records are retired, and each distinct address the duplicates used is added to the canonical account as a non-primary address with source consolidation. Each duplicate account is soft-deleted, and one audit record is written per duplicate. After the transaction commits, consolidation records the canonical account on the person’s identity-provider identity, so later sign-ins resolve to it. The link is written only when the identity has no linked account yet or is linked to an account in the same cluster. A failed identity link does not undo the merge. Re-running the tool retries the link. A failed merge step rolls back that cluster only and stops the run. Re-running is safe: a finished cluster is a no-op.
Running it (self-hosted operators) 🔗 Prerequisites: the identity-anchor backfill tool has been run, ambiguities from a dry run have been reviewed, a full database backup has been taken, and a separate identity-provider database URL is configured. Without a separate identity-provider URL, the tool falls back to the main database connection, which is valid only in local development where both databases share one instance.
Flag Default Behavior --dry-run true Prints the plan and writes nothing. --yes false Confirms writes. A live run needs both --dry-run=false and --yes. --yes alone is still a dry run. --dry-run=false without --yes aborts with “refusing to run live without –yes; pass –yes to confirm writes, or keep –dry-run”. --limit N 0 (all) Caps the number of clusters processed per run. Ignored with --cluster. --cluster <email or identity id> none Processes one cluster, matched by the canonical account’s email, a duplicate’s email, or the identity id. --by-email false Residual mode, run after the default mode. Merges duplicate-email clusters that have no identity, or a single identity with no active link, keyed on the shared email. An email shared by more than one identity is skipped and reported. Ignores --cluster. Run the default mode first, then --by-email. Run each as a dry run before running it live.
Each run prints whether it is a dry run or live, the number of clusters and ambiguities, then a plan per cluster or one merge line per cluster. On error, the tool prints consolidate-users: <error> and exits with status 1. Apart from a failed identity link, a merge-time error means that cluster’s transaction rolled back and the run is safe to repeat. One refusal to know: “Canonical user has no live organization to re-home a non-empty workspace into” means a non-empty workspace needs a destination and the canonical account owns no live organization. “Failed to apply an organization consolidation decision” includes the case where an organization being deleted has a live child organization outside the delete set.
Related reading For how sign-in providers link to your account, see Account Linking.

body:
Zara Osei is the Team Admin for Orbital Labs’ Infrastructure Team. Her mandate: model the team’s GCP-native data pipeline in Kanvas so that the architecture lives alongside the infrastructure it describes — versioned, shareable, and auditable. The pipeline ingests events via Cloud Pub/Sub, processes them with Dataflow, stores analytical results in BigQuery, and archives raw payloads to Cloud Storage — all orchestrated on a GKE cluster. This tutorial walks through how Zara builds that design, data-pipeline-gcp, in the orbital-production workspace.
Prerequisites 🔗 A Kanvas account and access to the orbital-production workspace in Orbital Labs No cluster and no GCP account. This tutorial only draws and shares a design. Kanvas stores no environment on a design. Zara does not attach prod-gcp, and the canvas does not overlay connection status or a live cluster version onto components. Environments are chosen when someone deploys: the Deploy stepper asks which environments to target and deploys to the Kubernetes connections assigned to them. This tutorial does not deploy.
Tutorial 🔗 Step 1: Create the design 🔗 Zara opens Kanvas and navigates to the Designer view. From the workspace selector she picks orbital-production — the workspace where Orbital Labs’ production infrastructure designs live.
She selects New Design, enters data-pipeline-gcp as the design name, and confirms. Kanvas creates the design and opens a blank canvas. From this point everything she does is auto-saved and tracked in design history.
Step 2: Add GCP components 🔗 With the canvas open, Zara opens the Component Library panel and filters by provider: GCP. She drags the following components onto the canvas, giving each a descriptive display name as she goes:
GKE Cluster — named pipeline-cluster; this is the compute backbone that will host Dataflow workers and any auxiliary services Cloud Pub/Sub Topic — named events-ingest; the entry point for incoming event streams Dataflow Job — named stream-processor; the managed pipeline that reads from Pub/Sub and writes downstream BigQuery Dataset — named analytics-store; the long-term destination for processed records Cloud Storage Bucket — named raw-archive; stores unprocessed event payloads for replay and compliance She arranges them left-to-right to mirror the data flow direction, which makes the diagram readable at a glance.
Step 3: Draw data-flow edges 🔗 Zara switches to edge mode and draws the connections that define how data moves:
An edge from events-ingest (Pub/Sub) to stream-processor (Dataflow), representing the subscription pull An edge from stream-processor to analytics-store (BigQuery), the primary write path for processed records A second edge from stream-processor to raw-archive (Cloud Storage), the archive branch for raw payloads An edge from pipeline-cluster (GKE) to stream-processor, indicating that the Dataflow worker pool runs inside the GKE cluster She labels the Pub/Sub to Dataflow edge subscription-pull so reviewers immediately understand the consumption pattern.
A line is a registry relationship only when the edge menu offers one between those two components. A registry relationship is part of the model: Kanvas can write values from one component’s configuration into the other’s. If the menu offers nothing that connects the pair, document the flow with the Pen tool. An annotation line is saved with the design and seen by collaborators, but it changes no configuration and is never deployed.
Step 4: Leave the design unbound from an environment 🔗 With the topology drawn, Zara does not open Design Settings to attach prod-gcp. Kanvas has no environment stored on the design, so there is no connection-status overlay and pipeline-cluster does not show a live cluster version. The design can later be deployed to more than one environment without changing the drawing.
Step 5: Add labels 🔗 Zara adds labels so teammates can see which architectural layer each component belongs to:
She selects events-ingest and sets the label ingestion-layer She selects stream-processor and sets processing-layer She selects analytics-store and raw-archive and sets storage-layer on both She selects pipeline-cluster and sets compute-layer A label is data on the component. It is not a TagSet, and Designer does not filter the canvas by label. A TagSet is a shaded region Kanvas draws on its own when a registry relationship defines a label match for those components. Zara cannot draw a TagSet, and many models define none. Labels stay visible in the component configurator.
Step 6: Validate the design 🔗 Before sharing, Zara runs Validate from the toolbar. Validate runs in the browser against each component’s schema. It checks configuration only. It skips annotation objects such as Pen lines, and it does not check relationships, edges, namespaces, or any environment binding.
The report lists each component that has errors. With no errors it reads “No validation errors.” A missing required field is a warning. Warnings never block saving or sharing. A clean report means every component’s configuration matches its schema. It does not mean the pipeline would deploy.
Step 7: Share with Five 🔗 With validation passing, Zara opens Share. Share is available once the design has components. She searches for Five by name or email and adds him. A share is a grant to one named user. It carries no permission level: there is no view-and-comment option, and the canvas is not read-only for him. Share only with people who should be able to edit. Five can open the design, change it, and leave comments. Comments are Comment components stored in the design, so the thread is saved with the design.
The data-pipeline-gcp design is now in orbital-production and ready for collaborative review. It is not connected to live infrastructure.
Info Meet Zara and the rest of the team at Meet Five and the Cast.

body:
Deleting a design removes it permanently. There is no trash, no recycle bin, and no undo: the design record is destroyed, and every workspace it was assigned to loses it at the same time. Before you delete, check that what you actually want is not one of the two softer actions described under Related actions that are not deletion.
Who Can Delete a Design 🔗 Deleting a design requires the Delete a design permission, and beyond that you must own the design. A user who holds the permission but is not the owner is refused - only the design’s owner, or a provider administrator, can delete it.
If the Delete action is grayed out for you, your role does not carry the permission. See Default Permissions for which roles hold it by default, and Keychains for how an organization administrator can grant it.
Deleting a Single Design 🔗 Go to My Designs in Layer5 Cloud, or open the design’s detail page. Choose Delete from the design’s actions. A confirmation dialog opens, naming the design. Click Delete to confirm, or dismiss the dialog to cancel. Once the deletion succeeds you are returned to My Designs and the design is gone from the list.
Deleting Several Designs at Once 🔗 The table view of My Designs supports bulk deletion.
Switch to table view. Select the rows you want to delete using the checkboxes. Choose Delete from the bulk actions. Confirm in the dialog, which names how many designs will be deleted. Each design in the selection is deleted independently. If one of them fails - for example because you do not own it - the rest still go through, so check the list afterwards rather than assuming the whole batch succeeded.
What Deletion Removes 🔗 The design itself, including its design file, name, and metadata. Its assignment to every workspace it belonged to. Collaborators who reached the design through a shared workspace lose access to it, because there is nothing left to reach. Deleting a design does not affect infrastructure. If the design was deployed, the deployed resources stay running in your clusters. Undeploy the design first if you want its resources removed as well - once the design is deleted, you no longer have the definition Meshery would need in order to undeploy it.
Related Actions That Are Not Deletion 🔗 Two nearby actions are frequently mistaken for deletion. Neither destroys the design.
Action What it does When to use it Unpublish Removes a design from the public catalog. The design remains in your account as a private design. You want to withdraw a design from public view but keep it. Remove from workspace Unassigns the design from one workspace. The design and its other workspace assignments are untouched. You want to tidy a workspace, not lose the design. Removing a design from a workspace is labelled Delete in the workspace’s design table, and its confirmation dialog says “from workspace name”. That phrase is the thing to check: if the dialog names a workspace, you are unassigning; if it does not, you are deleting the design outright.
Deletion is permanent There is no recovery path for a deleted design. If you may want the design later, export it as a Design (YAML) or Design (OCI image) file before deleting - both formats are lossless and can be imported back into Kanvas.

Design Embedding enables you to export a design in a format that can be seamlessly integrated into websites, blogs, or platforms supporting HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. This embedded version provides an interactive representation of the design, making it easier to share with infrastructure stakeholders. Embedding Your Design 🔗 To embed your Kanvas design, follow these steps: Access Embed Option: Within the Kanvas Designer, select the design you wish to embed. Click on the export icon in the menu for the selected design. The export modal will appear, click on the “Embed” option. Download the Embedding Script: Click on the download icon presented in the same modal to download the embedding script. Embedding in Static Sites 🔗 The embed code for static site:
Make sure the src attribute in the script tag points to the location of the downloaded embedding script on your local filesystem or server. Customization 🔗 You can customize the styles for the embedded design in two ways: globally via CSS classes, or for a single instance via an inline style parameter. Global Styling (via CSS Classes) 🔗 For advanced global styling, you can override the default CSS rules in your site’s stylesheet. This will affect all embedded designs on your site. The main classes are: .meshery-embed-container: The main container for the embedded design. You can target its .full or .half variants for specific sizing adjustments. .cy-container: The canvas element within the container where the design itself is rendered. Here is an example of how you could override these classes: Instance-specific Styling (via style Parameter) 🔗 For styling a single instance, the recommended method is to use the style parameter directly in the shortcode. This provides maximum control and will override any default styles or global CSS. {{< meshery-design-embed src="..." id="..." style="width: 60%; height: 28rem; border-radius: 1.5rem;" >}} Embedding in React Projects 🔗 Install the Package: To integrate the Design into your React project, start by installing the package via npm: npm i meshery-design-embed Incorporate the Component: Use the component to seamlessly embed designs within React and its associated frameworks. import MesheryDesignEmbed from '@layer5/meshery-design-embed' function Design() { return ( <>
); } Make sure the embedScriptSrc attribute in the component points to the location of the downloaded embedding script on your react filesystem. Usually the script is located “static” folder Embedding with Hugo 🔗 To prepare your Hugo site to support design embedding, perform the one-time task of adding the following shortcode definition to your site’s set of supported shortcodes. Shortcode Definition 🔗 Click to expand the full Shortcode Definition {{ $script := .Get "src" }} {{ $id := .Get "id" }} {{ $size := .Get "size" | default "full" }} {{ $style := .Get "style" }}
Shortcode Explanation 🔗 src (Required): The path to the exported JavaScript file for your design. id (Required): A unique ID for the embedded design container. size (Optional): A preset for simple sizing. Accepts "full" (default) or "half". This parameter is ignored if style is used. style (Optional): For advanced customization. Allows you to provide any custom CSS inline styles. This parameter has higher priority and will override the size parameter. Now that your site has shortcode support for embedding Kanvas designs, you can use the meshery-design-embed shortcode in any Hugo markdown file where you want to display embedded designs to your site visitors. Using the Shortcode 🔗 To embed a Design in your Hugo pages, use the meshery-design-embed shortcode. You will need the design’s exported JavaScript file and its unique ID. Usage Examples 🔗 Place the exported .js file in an appropriate folder (e.g., a nearby images folder) and reference it in the shortcode. Default (full-width) display: {{< meshery-design-embed src="../path/to/your-design.js" id="your-unique-design-id-full" >}} Half-width display: {{< meshery-design-embed src="../path/to/your-design.js" id="your-unique-design-id-half" size="half" >}} Custom styling: {{< meshery-design-embed src="../path/to/your-design.js" id="your-unique-design-id-custom" style="width: 60%; height: 28rem; border-radius: 1.5rem;" >}} Embedded Design Example 🔗 When Hugo builds your website, it will process the shortcode and generate the necessary HTML and JavaScript to embed the interactive Kanvas design. Here’s an example of how an embedded design appears: {{< meshery-design-embed src="../export-designs/embedded-design-dapr.js" id="embedded-design-7d183e77-09e1-4b69-a5ee-3e3870e9c5f4" >}} Open Design

In Layer5 Cloud, permissions are represented as keys, each serving as a unique identifier for a specific permission. One or more keys can be grouped together and assigned to a keychain. Then this keychain can be assigned to a role and that role can be assigned to a user. A user never receives a key directly. This is the general flow of how keys reach a user.
Keys, keychains, and roles are defined once for the whole Layer5 Cloud deployment. They are not copied or customized per organization. What varies per organization is which roles a user holds there. A user’s effective keys in an organization are the union of the keys from every role they hold in that organization, so the same person can hold a key in one organization and lack it in another. Holding an additional role only adds keys. It never removes any. Provider Admin holds every key and passes every check in every organization. For how this fits with authentication and cross-organization resource sharing, see Security Boundaries.
For instance, consider the system-shipped default key Create Organization, which corresponds to the permission to create an organization in the Cloud. To create an organization, you need the Create Organization key in a keychain that is assigned to a role associated with your user account in that organization.
Note The same key can be assigned to multiple keychains. One or more keys can be assigned to a keychain. Keys are deployment-wide. The organization context decides which of your roles, and therefore which keys, apply to a request. A default installation ships more than 240 keys grouped into 30 default keychains. The system account owns every default key and keychain.
Keys Types 🔗 Keys follow one of four shapes. A few grant an action that is not a simple change to a resource.
Create - Create keys permit you to create resources. For example, the Create Organization key allows you to create an organization. View - View keys permit you to access and retrieve resources. For example, the View All Teams key lets you see all the teams within a selected organization. Edit - Edit keys permit you to change resources. For instance, the Edit Organization key allows you to update an organization’s details. Delete - Delete keys permit you to remove resources. For instance, the Delete Token key allows you to revoke a token. Action - Action keys grant a workflow step. For example, the Approve Catalog Request key allows you to approve a catalog request to publish a cloud-native design to Cloud Catalog, and the Connect GitHub Account to Workspace key enables you to connect your GitHub account to your workspace. Keys Enforcement 🔗 A key has an effect only where something checks it. Two places do.
The server. On a guarded action, the server resolves the organization of the request and tests whether the user holds the required key there. A missing key returns HTTP 403 with a JSON body. This check is what actually protects the action. The interface. The Layer5 Cloud UI reads your effective keys for the organization in context and disables or hides controls for actions you cannot perform. For more on the organization context switcher, see Organizations. Not every key is checked in both places. Some security keys are enforced only by the interface: the server does not test Delete Token, and tests Create Token only when you approve a desktop app or CLI sign-in. For that approval, Create Token must be held in at least one organization you belong to. The organization you have selected, or the one a custom domain belongs to, does not matter. Changes to keys, keychains, and roles are checked on the server, which also requires the Provider Admin role for the whole deployment. The security permission keys table lists which security keys the server enforces.
Because a key grants nothing unless a check names it, a custom key is only a record. Adding one to a keychain and a role changes no behavior anywhere.
Each key that the interface does check is enforced at specific UI elements. For instance, the Create Organization key is enforced at the Create Organization button on the Organizations page. The button is disabled if you do not hold Create Organization through a role in the selected organization.
Keys Management 🔗 View Keys 🔗 Review keys by navigating to the Keys page. Every signed-in user can open the Keys tab. It lists the system’s keys plus any keys you created, and searches by key name. Viewing keys requires no key on the server.
Review Key Usage 🔗 Keys themselves do not carry a usage counter. There is no “last used” column on the Keys page. What a key’s use leaves behind is the event that the action itself produced, and those events are what you audit.
Every action a user takes is recorded on the Audit Logs page, which answers who did what, and when:
User ID - the account that performed the action, which is the account whose key was exercised. Category and Action - what was done, for example a workspace being created or a team being deleted. These correspond to the capability the key grants. Acted Upon - the resource the action was performed on. Description and Created At - the detail of the event and the time it occurred. Filter by Actor ID to follow one user’s activity, or by Category and Action to see everyone who exercised a particular capability over a period. Because keys are evaluated in the context of an organization, the log you are reading is the log for the organization you currently have selected.
Workspaces additionally keep their own activity log, scoped to that one workspace. See View Recent Activity.
Key and keychain changes do not write audit events. Creating, downloading, and deleting a token do. See Tokens.
Assign Keys 🔗 Changing which keys a keychain carries, or which keychains a role includes, is a Provider Admin action for the whole deployment. Holding Provider Admin inside one organization does not satisfy that check. On hosted Layer5 Cloud, Layer5 operates the Provider Admin role, so organizations cannot change keys. On a self-hosted deployment, the operator’s Provider Admins can.
To grant an existing key to a user, assign a role that already carries it. Do not add the keychain to a shared role unless every holder of that role in every organization should gain it.
Select the organization in the organization context switcher in the top navigation bar. Confirm which role already carries the key. The Default Permissions matrix lists the default roles. Keychains explains how keys are grouped. Open the Users page and assign that role to the user in this organization. You can also invite a user and assign the role separately. See Users and Roles. A Provider Admin who needs a new combination of keys creates a keychain, includes it in a role, and then assigns that role. See Keychains.
Permission Assignment at Teams, Organization and Provider Levels Team Admin can assign roles to users in a team. Team Admin cannot edit keys or keychains. Organization Admin can assign roles to users in an organization. Organization Admin cannot edit keys or keychains. Only Provider Admin can create, edit, or delete keys, change which keys a keychain carries, or change which keychains a role includes. The server checks that role across the whole deployment. Keys Lifecycle 🔗 Layer5 Cloud ships with more than 240 default keys. Default keys are owned by the system. Each key is uniquely identified by a UUID, which is how the system references the key.
Creating or editing a key, including changing which keychains carry it, requires the Edit Key key. Deleting a key requires the Delete Key key. Both belong to the Provider Management keychain, which only Provider Admin holds by default, and the server also requires the caller to hold the Provider Admin role for the whole deployment. As of Layer5 Cloud v1.0.280, only a Provider Admin can change keys.
Deleting a key is a soft delete. The key stops granting access immediately and disappears from every keychain that contained it. Because keys are deployment-wide, editing or deleting one changes access for every organization at once.
Anatomy of a key 🔗 The Keys tab lists each key with these fields:
Field Meaning Key ID A UUID that identifies the key. Name The action the key grants, for example Create Token. Description What the action does. Category The resource the key acts on, for example Token or Keychains. Subcategory The default keychain family the key belongs to, for example Security Management. Owner The account that owns the key. Default keys are owned by the system. Created At, Deleted At When the key was created and, if deleted, when. Who can see and change keys 🔗 Key Governs Default holders besides Provider Admin Enforced by View Keys Seeded for the Keys tab User, Team Admin, Workspace Admin, Organization Admin Not checked. Every signed-in user sees the Keys tab. Edit Key Creating and changing a key None Interface and server. The server also requires the Provider Admin role. Delete Key Deleting a key None Interface and server. The server also requires the Provider Admin role. The list shows system-owned default keys, plus keys you created. Keys are deployment-wide, not per organization.
When the server refuses a change to a key, it answers HTTP 403 with a JSON error. A caller who lacks the route’s key receives code meshery_cloud-1108. A caller who holds the key but is not a Provider Admin for the whole deployment receives code meshery_cloud-3336, “Only a Provider Admin can change roles, keychains or permission keys”.
Tracing a missing permission 🔗 When a user cannot perform an action, work from the key outward:
Identify the key the action requires. A 403 response or a disabled control both point to a missing key. Find the roles that carry that key in Default Permissions. Security keys are listed above and on Keychains, Sessions, and Tokens. Check which roles the user holds in the organization the request ran in, not in the organization they usually work in. Grant a role that carries the key in that organization. Limits 🔗 Keys do not rotate or expire. A key grants its action until it is deleted or removed from the user’s roles. Keys have no per-key usage counter. Use the Audit Logs page instead. On hosted Layer5 Cloud, only Provider Admins edit or delete keys. A key and its keychains are deployment-wide. Organizations tailor access by assigning roles, not by changing keys. Key endpoints 🔗 Success responses are JSON unless stated. Errors from these handlers return a plain-text message. Refusals from the authorization layer return JSON. Paths sit under /api.
Method and path Who may call Behavior GET /auth/keys Signed-in user Lists keys you can see. Parameters: page, pageSize, order, search (matches the key name). Default order: most recently updated first. GET /auth/keys/{keyId} Signed-in user Returns one key. A malformed id returns 400. POST /auth/keys Provider Admin holding Edit Key Creates or updates a key. DELETE /auth/keys/{keyId} Provider Admin holding Delete Key Soft-deletes the key. Returns 204. GET /identity/orgs/{orgId}/users/keys Signed-in user Returns your effective keys in the organization. The interface uses it to enable controls. For a Provider Admin, a malformed id on a write returns 400 with a plain-text message. See Cloud API for authentication and the organization header.
