body:
Operator mode gives you continuous visibility across all of your clusters and workloads: MeshSync discovers every resource in every connected cluster and streams changes back to Kanvas, so the canvas is a live picture rather than a periodic snapshot. Performance testing closes the loop on that picture. Having found the service you are interested in, you can generate load against it in place and keep the result as a reusable performance profile.
Continuous visibility across clusters and workloads 🔗 The Operator canvas draws every resource MeshSync has discovered across the Kubernetes clusters connected to your Meshery deployment. Filters in the Layers panel narrow that down to the clusters, namespaces and kinds you care about, and a saved view makes a given slice repeatable. Because discovery is continuous, resources appear, change status and disappear on the canvas as they do in the cluster - you are never looking at a stale export.
From there, the Details panel gives you the state of any single resource, log streaming and the interactive terminal give you its behavior, and performance testing gives you its response under load.
Initiating a performance test 🔗 Performance tests are run against the resources that expose an endpoint, so the action is available on Service and Ingress components. It is not offered on Pods, Deployments or other kinds.
Switch Kanvas to Operator mode and locate the Service or Ingress you want to test. Either right-click the component and choose Initiate Performance Test, or select the component and click the performance action in the header of the Details panel. The Performance panel opens on the right of the canvas, pre-filled from the resource you selected. Where the target URL comes from 🔗 For a Service, Kanvas derives the target URL from the resource itself rather than asking you to type it. It reads the service’s type and its declared ports, and builds an endpoint accordingly:
Service type Endpoint ClusterIP http://<clusterIP>:<port> NodePort http://<nodeIP>:<nodePort> LoadBalancer http://<ingress IP or hostname>:<port> ExternalName http://<externalName>:<port> A service that declares several ports yields several endpoints, and the first of them is the one seeded into the form. If you want to test a different port, pick it from the URL field before running.
For an Ingress, the action is offered but no URL is derived - an Ingress has no type, clusterIP or ports for Kanvas to read, so the URL field arrives empty and you supply the host and path you want to test. The same is true of a ClusterIP service that has not been assigned a cluster IP.
Reaching the endpoint The load is generated by Meshery, so the endpoint has to be reachable from wherever your Meshery Server runs. A ClusterIP address is reachable from inside the cluster but not from outside it. Selecting a performance profile 🔗 The Performance panel is Meshery’s performance test form, loaded in performance-profile mode: the settings you run with are saved as a named profile, and existing profiles can be selected and re-run instead of being retyped. That is what makes a test repeatable - the same load, against the same endpoint, before and after a change.
Kanvas seeds a new profile from the selected component, so a straightforward HTTP endpoint can be tested on the seeded values alone:
Setting Seeded value Profile name <Kind> - <component name>, for example Service - checkout URL to test The first endpoint derived from the service; empty for an Ingress Concurrent requests 10 Queries per second 20 Duration 30s Load generator fortio Every one of these can be changed before you run. Endpoints that need more than a plain GET will need more than the defaults, and the form exposes what they require: request headers, cookies, content type and body, a CA certificate upload for TLS endpoints, and additional load-generator options. Nothing runs until you start the test explicitly - opening the panel does not generate load.
Saved profiles, historical results and comparisons between runs live in Meshery’s performance management screens. For the full description of profiles, load generators and how results are interpreted, see Performance Management in the Meshery documentation.
See Also 🔗 Instance Details: Inspect the live state of the resource you are testing. Performance Limits and Tuning: Understand the limits of Kanvas itself when working with large designs. Current behavior 🔗 The action is Initiate Performance Test, offered on Service and Ingress only. The panel is 400 px wide and only one panel exists. Opening it generates no load. Seeded values are 10 concurrent requests, 20 queries per second, 30s duration, and load generator fortio. The profile name is <Kind> - <component name>. The form needs View performance profiles to appear, and Run Test needs Run test. The Kanvas interface does not check a permission before it opens the panel. Layer5 Cloud defines Perform performance test in Operator and Select performance profile in Operator, held by default only by Organization Admin and Provider Admin. Meshery Server generates the load, not the browser. A ClusterIP address is reachable from inside the cluster only.

On-premises Deployment of Layer5 Cloud 🔗 A self-hosted deployment runs the same Layer5 Cloud that Layer5 operates, on infrastructure you control. Your users sign in against your identity services, your organizations and designs live in your database, and Meshery Servers in your network connect to your deployment as their remote provider.
One Helm chart, layer5-cloud, installs the application and its two identity services. You supply the database, the ingress, and the TLS certificate.
Component Provided by What it does Layer5 Cloud server layer5-cloud chart Serves the web UI and the API, enforces organizations, teams, roles, and keys, and runs the signaling endpoint for real-time co-editing. Listens on port 9876. Kratos Subchart Owns accounts: password sign-in, social sign-in, email verification, and account recovery. Hydra Subchart Issues OAuth2 tokens to the UI, to Meshery Servers, and to API clients. PostgreSQL You Holds three databases on one server: meshery, kratos, and hydra. Ingress controller and TLS You Publishes one hostname. Routes / to the server, /kratos to Kratos, /hydra to Hydra, and passes WebSocket upgrades on /collaboration. SMTP relay You Sends invitations, notifications, and identity mail (verification and recovery). Webhook receivers You Optional endpoints that receive support requests, signup decisions, and Kanvas entitlement events. Meshery Server is deployed separately and is not part of this chart. See Meshery Server registration.
Area On your deployment Provider administration Your operators hold the Provider Admin role. They create the first organization, assign custom roles, and approve signup requests. See Default Permissions. Default sign-in providers You register the Google and GitHub OAuth applications that every organization without its own credentials uses. See Identity Services. Mail The shared relay is yours. Organizations can still register their own. See Email / SMTP Troubleshooting. Branding and domains Organizations apply their own theme and domain; you set the provider-level defaults. See White-labeling. Upgrades You choose when to upgrade. The server applies database migrations at startup. GitHub You register your own GitHub App. See Self-hosted GitHub App requirements. Considerations of Self-Hosted Deployments 🔗 Planning. Decide on the database, hostname, identity providers, mail relay, provider administrator, and network paths. Deploying Layer5 Cloud. Install with Helm, create the Hydra client, and confirm the deployment is ready. Configure. Set chart values, provider initialization, and webhooks. Operate. Watch health and logs and diagnose mail delivery. Real-time co-editing has one network dependency outside your cluster: browsers must reach public STUN and TURN hosts to connect to each other. See Networking before you deploy into a restricted network. A self-hosted provider is its own signaling host. Users connected to your deployment never signal through Layer5’s hosted service.
For help with a deployment, see Support.

Spaces is where an organization keeps its workspaces, environments, and the connections those environments hold. A workspace groups teams, environments, designs, and views. An environment groups connections into a deploy target. For the model, read Workspaces and Environments. For the tasks, use the workspace guides. For every endpoint’s schema, see the REST API Reference, and for base URL and authentication see the Cloud API. All paths below sit under /api.
Workspace and environment reference 🔗 Fields, defaults, and limits 🔗 Property Workspace Environment Name Up to 255 characters. Not required or unique on the API. Up to 255 characters. Not required or unique on the API. Description Up to 255 characters. May be empty. Up to 255 characters. May be empty. Organization Required on create. Fixed for the life of the workspace. Required on create (organizationId is required). Fixed for the life of the environment. Owner The user who created it. Not recorded on create. Starting state No teams, environments, designs, or views. No connections, in no workspace. Kind Single kind. Ordinary when created through the API. Platform-provisioned environments exist and are protected. Update Only the fields sent change. Name and description are both replaced; an omitted field becomes empty. Plan check None. None. The feature matrix lists environments under Enterprise. Count limits None. An organization must keep at least one workspace. None. Layer5 Cloud creates My Workspace in any organization that has no workspace.
Scope and visibility 🔗 Question Answer Who sees a workspace or environment in a list? Every member of its organization. Team membership does not narrow the list. How is the organization chosen? A list request carries one organization identifier. The all-organizations value needs View All Organizations and otherwise returns HTTP 403. What does a missing or foreign identifier return? HTTP 404, workspace not found or environment not found. Can a workspace or environment move to another organization? No. Which relationships can cross organizations? None for teams and environments: both must share the workspace’s organization (HTTP 403 otherwise). A design assigned to a workspace takes on that workspace’s organization. Permissions by operation 🔗 Layer5 Cloud checks each key in the organization that owns the workspace or environment. Operations marked UI only are hidden in the interface but not checked by the server. Default holders are listed in Default Permissions.
Operation Permission POST /workspaces Create Workspace (organization from the request body) GET /workspaces, GET /workspaces/{id} UI only (View Workspace); organization scoping applies PUT /workspaces/{id} Edit Workspace DELETE /workspaces/{id} Delete Workspace POST, DELETE /workspaces/{id}/teams/{teamId} Assign team to workspace, Remove team from workspace POST, DELETE /workspaces/{id}/environments/{environmentId} Assign environment to workspace, Remove environment from workspace POST, DELETE /workspaces/{id}/designs/{designId} Assign Designs to Workspaces, Remove Designs from Workspaces POST, DELETE /workspaces/{id}/views/{viewId} Assign Views to Workspace, Unassign Views from Workspace GET /workspaces/{id}/views, GET /workspaces/{id}/events View Workspace GET /workspaces/{id}/teams, /environments, /designs None POST /environments Create Environment (organization from the request body) GET /environments, GET /environments/{id} UI only (View Environment); organization scoping applies PUT /environments/{id} Edit Environment DELETE /environments/{id} Delete Environment POST, DELETE /environments/{id}/connections/{connectionId} Assign connections to environment, Remove connections from environment GET /environments/{id}/connections View Environment List parameters 🔗 Parameter Applies to Meaning orgId Workspace and environment lists The organization to list. Required. search All lists Case-insensitive match on name or description. order All lists Order by created_at or updated_at. Environment connection lists also accept name. Default is newest first. page, pageSize All lists Zero-based page and page size. filter Lists of a workspace’s teams, environments, designs, views, and an environment’s connections {"assigned": true} (default) lists what is in; {"assigned": false} lists what is not yet in. For designs, the not-yet-in list holds only designs the caller owns. visibility Lists of a workspace’s designs and views Repeatable. Keeps only designs or views with that visibility. Responses 🔗 Operation Condition Response Create workspace Organization missing or malformed HTTP 400, organizationId is required or invalid organizationId format Create workspace Name or description over 255 characters HTTP 500, Unable to create workspace Update workspace Empty or null body HTTP 400, Unable to update workspace Update or delete workspace Not in the caller’s organizations HTTP 404, workspace not found Delete workspace Last live workspace in the organization HTTP 500, cannot delete workspace: at least one workspace must exist for the organization Assign team or environment Team or environment in another organization HTTP 403, unable to add team to workspace or unable to add environment to workspace Assign environment Platform-provisioned environment HTTP 403, this environment is provisioned by the platform and cannot be added to a workspace Remove environment from workspace Never attached HTTP 404, no such environment assignment Create environment Organization missing HTTP 400, organizationId is required Delete environment Platform-provisioned HTTP 403, this environment is provisioned by the platform and cannot be deleted here Delete environment No live environment HTTP 404, no environment with the requested id Assign connection Platform-provisioned environment HTTP 403, this connection cannot be assigned to this environment Remove connection Platform-provisioned environment HTTP 403, this connection cannot be detached from this environment Remove connection Never assigned HTTP 404, no such connection assignment Assigning a team or environment that is already assigned succeeds and returns the existing assignment. Every workspace create, update, delete, assign, and unassign writes an event to the workspace’s activity log, and a failure writes an error event.
What deletion ends 🔗 Deleting a Ends Leaves in place Workspace Team, environment, design, and view assignments Teams, environments, connections, designs, views, and their owners Environment Connection assignments and workspace attachments Connections, credentials, workspaces, and the connections’ other environments Access that flowed through a deleted or detached link ends at once. See Access Control for Connections and Credentials.

The Academy Content Template Creator is a step-by-step wizard that helps you create structured templates for your Academy content. This generator streamlines the process of creating learning paths, challenges, and certifications by collecting all necessary metadata and generating a ready-to-use template.
Getting Started 🔗 Access the Creator: Click on the “Create New Content” card in your Academy dashboard Create Your Content: The wizard will guide you through 5 essential steps to create your content template Since it’s straightforward, let’s walk through a practical example to demonstrate the process.
Example: Creating “Meshery Contributors Certification” 🔗 This example demonstrates how to use the Academy Content Template Creator to build a certification program for Meshery contributors. Each step shows what information to enter, followed by specific example values.
Step 1: Basic Information 🔗 Type: Choose “Certification” from Learning Path, Challenge, or Certification Title: “Meshery Contributors Certification” Description: “A comprehensive certification program for developers looking to become active contributors to Meshery” Step 2: Content Details 🔗 Categories: “open-source, cloud-native” Add Tags: “meshery”, “kubernetes”, “golang”, “contribution”, “open-source” Banner Image: “images/meshery-contributors-banner.svg” Step 3: Content Access 🔗 Workspace: “Meshery Academy” Team: “Contributors Program” Access Status: Enabled Content Access End Date: Leave blank for permanent access (Meshery always welcomes contributors) Understanding Access Status: Enabled vs Disabled
Access status sets the invitation to enabled or disabled. It defaults to enabled. It does not by itself hide the catalog card. New content starts public, not ready, and beginner. Catalog visibility is that public flag. Access status only governs enrollment.
Enabled: a signed-in learner can enroll. Enrolling accepts the invitation.
Disabled: the invitation blocks enrollment. Learners who already enrolled keep their role and team membership. Their progress is not paused.
Content Access End Date is the invitation’s expiry. Leave it empty for no expiry. Expiry is checked at enrollment. After it passes, new learners cannot enroll. Learners who already enrolled keep their role and team membership.
The team field accepts one existing team. That team is added to the invitation, and learners join it when they enroll. You can type a new workspace name. The team must already exist.
Step 4: Recognition 🔗 The Recognition step defines the badge or certificate awarded upon completion. You have two options:
Use Existing Recognition: Choose from the Layer5 collection Create New Recognition: Design a custom badge with an image URL For our example:
Create a “Meshery Contributor” badge with the Meshery logo Step 5: Generate Template 🔗 After clicking “Continue” in Step 4, a success notification appears in the bottom-right corner confirming your template has been created successfully.
Navigation Between Steps You can navigate back to any previous step to make modifications. When you return to earlier steps and make changes, your entries in the subsequent steps will remain intact. Generated Template Output for Meshery Contributors Certification:
This template provides the YAML front matter metadata for static site generators (like Hugo/Jekyll). After copying it, we can directly create new content files in our Academy repository.
--- type: "certification" title: "Meshery Contributors Certification" description: "A comprehensive certification program for developers looking to become active contributors to Meshery" weight: 1 banner: "images/meshery-contributors-banner.svg" id: "unique-content-id" level: "beginner" --- Provide a brief summary of what learners will gain. <!-- Add your Academy content here --> Important Reference IDs Make note of two key identifiers for your content files:
Content ID: Unique identifier for this specific content Organization ID: Your organization’s identifier (remains constant) The level key in this output always reads beginner, whatever difficulty you picked on Content Details. Set it to beginner, intermediate, or advanced yourself. The creator also includes tags and categories when you entered them, and commented competencies and prerequisite_knowledge samples you can uncomment. weight is fixed at 1 until you change it.
Content ID Updates The creator writes the record when you advance from Recognition to Generate Template. You can go back and your entries stay, but advancing to the last step again creates another record with a new content ID and a new invitation. Use the ID on the final screen of your last run, and treat any earlier record as unused. Next Steps 🔗 After generating our template:
Copy the Template: Use the provided copy button to get your front matter Create Your Content File: Paste the template into a new .md file in your academy repository Add Your Content: Replace the placeholder comment with your actual learning material Manage Invitation 🔗 Auto-Generated Invitations 🔗 Navigate to Identity → Invitations to find your automatically created invitation. The first column labeled “INVITATION” contains a shareable link that you can copy.
What Can the Invitation Link Do for You? 🔗 The auto-generated invitation link is a powerful tool that helps instructors efficiently manage learner access and streamline the enrollment process.
1. What accepting the invitation does 🔗 Enrolling accepts the invitation. Acceptance is where access is decided.
Team: The learner is added to the one team you picked, if they are not already a member. The creator does not assign several teams. Role: Academy Learner is assigned in the organization if the learner does not already hold it. Who can accept: The email list starts empty, so anyone who is signed in can accept. The invitation is not limited to people already in your organization, and it does not email the team for you. Add exact addresses or @domain entries on the invitation to restrict who can accept. See User Invitations. 2. Sharing the link 🔗 Copy the invitation link from the invitation list and send it yourself. The link registers a learner for the content by accepting that invitation. It does not send mail on its own.
Customize Invitation Properties 🔗 Click the pencil icon to access the invitation customization form. The invitation form contains eight properties. Three are automatically generated by the system for convenience, which you can modify according to your needs:
Auto-Generated Properties:
Name: Academy Invitation for <slug>, using the generated slug, not the title you typed. Description: Identifies the organization and the curricula the invitation is for. Roles: Defaults to Academy Learner. Academy roles lists what that role can do. Empty quota means unlimited acceptances, and the invitation counts each person once. Admin Role Invitations Academy admins can invite other instructors to become co-admins by changing the Roles property from “Academy Learner” to “Academy Admin” during invitation customization. Customizable Properties:
1. Emails - Invitation Email List 🔗 The email list restricts who may accept. It starts empty, and an empty list lets any signed-in user accept. It does not send the invitation for you.
Supported Formats: Individual emails: test@domain.com Domain entries: @domain.com (only addresses at that domain may accept) Duplicate Handling: The system automatically merges duplicate entries Quantity Recommendations: Small team invitations: 10-50 email addresses Department-level invitations: 100-200 email addresses Large organizations: Use domain wildcards like @company.com instead of listing individual emails 2. Expires At - Expiration Settings 🔗 Control when the invitation expires:
Flexibility: Supports any time setting, extension, and recovery. Leave blank for permanent access What happens at expiration? Expiration is only checked when users attempt to accept the invitation If the expiration time has passed, users cannot proceed with the invitation Expiration check compares server current time vs. set expiration time Can I modify expired invitations? Yes, you can recover and extend expiration times by entering edit mode 3. Quota - Usage Limits 🔗 Set limits on how many users can accept the invitation:
When quota is exceeded: Operates on a first-accept, first-in basis Users beyond the quota cannot join, even with a valid invitation link Recovery options: If quota is reached, you can increase the quota to restore access Admin console provides real-time usage monitoring 4. Teams - Team Assignment List 🔗 Specify which teams invited users will join:
Team Selection: Choose one existing team. The creator accepts a single team, and learners join that team when they enroll. No Teams Available: If your organization has no teams, create one first. Team Structure Changes During Organization Restructuring:
If team structure changes after invitations are sent Some teams may be merged or deleted New users can still join remaining valid teams Permission Management Updates:
Team permission policies may change Some teams might close to new users Other teams continue accepting new members normally 5. Status - Enabled/Disabled 🔗 Control invitation accessibility:
Enabled: Enrollment can accept the invitation. Disabled: Enrollment fails. Learners who already enrolled are not removed. Invitation Idempotency Acceptance is idempotent. A learner who accepts twice gains no duplicate membership or role, and the invitation counts them once. When an enrollment hits a disabled, expired, full, or email-restricted invitation, the request fails with a server error. The registration is recorded before the invitation is evaluated, so the learner can appear in the Learners view without having joined the organization or the team. Fix the invitation, then have the learner enroll again.
Content created while the console is scoped to all organizations belongs to the provider organization. It has no attached invitation, so enrollment accepts nothing and grants no team or role.
You can change the team, access status, and end date later from the Curricula view of the Instructor Console. To bring in a co-instructor, create an invitation with the Academy Admin role instead of Academy Learner.

You can group components using tags. Tags are key-value pairs that help you organize and categorize components within your design. Tags can be used to visually group components. Designer has no filter that shows only components with a given tag. Operator mode filters live resources by namespace, kind, model, label, and free-text search. Palette search matches model and component names, not labels.
Related Concept Kubernetes resources are capable of being assigned Label and Annotation key/value pairs. When pairs of Labels or Annotations match, a relationship is formed and visualized as shown below. Grouping Components with Tags 🔗 To group components using tags, follow these steps.
Labels and Annotations 🔗 Designs support two different types of tags: Labels and Annotations. Labels are often used to identify components and are visible on the design canvas. Annotations are often used to provide additional information about components.
Performance Consideration Tags are indexed and searchable. However, the performance of design operations may degrade as the number of tags increases. To ensure an optimal user experience, we recommend using tags judiciously and limiting the number of tags used in a design.
TagSets draw only in Full render mode, and only while at most 30 are drawn. Past 30, Kanvas skips the rest and shows “Skipped rendering of N matchlabels relationships due to limit of 30”. Grouping does not turn itself off at 10 tags, and there is no Group Components control that re-enables it after that limit. The TagSets layer must also be visible.

A workspace is a named grouping inside an organization. It brings together the teams who do a piece of work, the environments they deploy to, and the designs and views they work on. A workspace does two separate jobs:
It organizes resources. Designs and views live in a workspace, and the workspace decides which organization they are listed under. It grants connection access. Assigning a team to a workspace gives that team’s members read-only access to the connections in the workspace’s environments. That is the only access a team assignment grants. You can create Workspaces to group related Designs and Environments and to decide which teams can read which connections.
Key Features 🔗 Connection access: Assigning a team grants read-only access to the connections, and their credentials, in the workspace’s environments. Logical Grouping: Within Workspaces, you can group related environments, designs, and views. Organization-wide visibility: Every member of an organization can list and open every workspace in that organization. Team assignment does not narrow what you see. One design, one workspace: A design or view belongs to at most one workspace. Assigning it moves it. The last workspace stays: An organization always keeps at least one workspace. Workspace Relationships and Restrictions 🔗 Every member of the organization can list and open every workspace. Team membership does not hide workspaces. A workspace may have zero or more environments. Creating a workspace assigns no team and no environment. A team assignment grants read-only access to connections in those environments. It does not grant access to designs or views. One or more teams can be assigned to a workspace, and the same team can be assigned to more than one workspace. The team must belong to the workspace’s organization. After creating a Workspace, assign teams, move designs into the Workspace, and associate one or more Environments so those Environments’ connections become readable by the workspace’s teams.
Like a shared drive (or shared collection of files), Workspaces are your Google Drive, while Designs are your Google Docs.
Key Workspace Components 🔗 Environments 🔗 Environments are a central part of a workspace. They serve as a logical grouping for managing connections. A connection, in this context, can be either managed or discovered. Examples of connections include Kubernetes clusters, Prometheus instances, Jaeger traces, Nginx servers, and more. One or more environments can be assigned to a workspace. Same environment can be assigned to multiple workspaces. Assigning Environments to Workspaces Assign any number of Environments to one or more Workspaces. See Environments section for more information. Profiles 🔗 A profile represents a person or persona in the organization and groups the connections it publishes through. Assigning a profile to a workspace makes it visible to the members of the workspace’s teams. The same profile can be assigned to multiple workspaces. See Profiles. Designs 🔗 A design or view belongs to at most one workspace. Assigning it to a workspace is a move, not a copy: Layer5 Cloud removes every earlier workspace assignment, then adds the new one. The workspace a design sits in decides the organization under which the design is listed, and the organization in which the Share Design permission is checked. Placing a private design in a workspace does not open it to the workspace’s teams. Share the design to give someone access. See Sharing Designs. When you list the designs you can add to a workspace, the list shows only designs you own that are not already in it. Moving a design requires the Assign Designs to Workspaces permission in the destination workspace’s organization. Layer5 Cloud does not also require access to the workspace the design leaves. Design Ownership in Workspaces Designs belong to only one Workspace at any given time. Ownership does not change when a design moves. See Designs section for more information. Teams 🔗 A Workspace is closely associated with Teams. Teams are groups of users with varying permissions, and they are at the center of resource access and management within a Workspace. One or more teams can be assigned to a workspace. Same team can be assigned to multiple workspaces. Team Access Control in Workspaces Team assignment grants read-only access to the connections in the workspace’s environments. It does not grant access to designs, and it does not decide who can see the workspace. See Teams. Connections 🔗 Connections refer to various resources that can be either managed or unmanaged, but are discovered and made accessible for use. Examples of Connections include Kubernetes clusters, Prometheus instances, Jaeger services, Nginx deployments, and more. These Connections serve as a fundamental part of Workspaces, as users can deploy infrastructure designs within the context of these Connections. Connections can be assigned to one or more environments. Same connection can be assigned to multiple environments. Learn More About Connections See Connections section for more information. Best Practices 🔗 To make the most of Workspaces, here are some best practices:
Clearly define permissions in the form of team assignment to ensure proper access control. Use Infrastructure Designs to standardize resource deployments. Regularly review and update your Workspace’s resources and configurations. Workspaces enhance collaboration within your teams, providing a structured environment for sharing and managing resources. By following best practices and understanding the core components of Workspaces, you can maximize the benefits of this feature.
Looking for Practical Workspace Management? For a step-by-step guide on how to create, edit, and manage your workspaces, see the Managing Workspaces documentation. Example: Orbital Labs Workspace Setup 🔗 The following illustrates how Five and Maya set up workspaces at Orbital Labs to segment access across infrastructure and development workflows. See Meet Five and the Cast for the full seed inventory.
Workspace Inventory 🔗 Workspace Owner Org Teams with Access Environments orbital-production Orbital Labs Infrastructure only prod-aws (EKS + RDS + S3 + CloudFront + SQS), prod-gcp (GKE + Cloud SQL + Cloud Storage + Pub/Sub) orbital-staging Orbital Labs Infrastructure + Development staging-aws (EKS + S3 + ElastiCache), staging-azure (AKS + Azure Blob + Azure Service Bus) orbital-dev Orbital Labs Development only dev-local (kind + LocalStack) Creating orbital-staging 🔗 Five creates the orbital-staging workspace to give the Development team a shared environment for feature-branch testing - without handing them the keys to production.
Steps Five follows:
Navigate to Workspaces and click Create Workspace Name the workspace orbital-staging Save - the workspace is created with no team access and no environments assigned Maya then assigns team access:
Open the orbital-staging workspace settings Add the Infrastructure team so its members can read the connections in the workspace’s environments Add the Development team so its members can read those same connections Why both teams? Assigning a team grants read-only connection access, not design access. Infrastructure and Development can both read the staging connections. Development still cannot read production connections, because it is not assigned to orbital-production. To let Rex or Jordan open a private design, share that design with them. Organization-wide visibility 🔗 Workspace visibility is organization-wide. Every member of an organization can list and open every workspace in that organization, whether or not one of their teams is assigned to it. The Workspaces, Environments, and connection areas of the Cloud UI appear only to people who hold the matching View Workspace, View Environment, and View Connections permissions.
A workspace belongs to exactly one organization for its whole life. Editing a workspace changes its name, description, or metadata, never its organization.
What a team assignment grants 🔗 A member of a team reaches a connection through four live links. Breaking any one of them ends the access.
Link Created by Broken by 1. User is a member of a team Adding the user to the team Removing the user from the team 2. Team is assigned to a workspace Assign team to workspace Removing the team from the workspace, or deleting the workspace 3. Environment is assigned to the workspace Assign environment to workspace Removing the environment from the workspace, or deleting either one 4. Connection is assigned to the environment Assign connections to environment Removing the connection from the environment, or deleting the environment The result is read-only. Modifying or deleting a connection still requires owning it. Two other routes reach a connection independently of this chain: owning it, and holding the View All Organizations key. See Environments.
One workspace per design 🔗 Because a design sits in at most one workspace, promotion from one workspace to another is a move. There is no approval step and no copy. The same rule applies to views. Removing a design from its workspace leaves it with no workspace. The design and its owner are unaffected.
The last workspace 🔗 Every organization receives a workspace when it is created, so designs always have somewhere to live. Layer5 Cloud creates My Workspace in any organization that has no workspace.
An organization always keeps at least one workspace. Deleting the last one is refused with cannot delete workspace: at least one workspace must exist for the organization. Two simultaneous deletes cannot both succeed and leave the organization empty.
Deleting a workspace ends every team, environment, design, and view assignment it holds, in one step. The teams, environments, designs, views, and connections themselves remain. Designs and views that were in the workspace are left in no workspace until you assign them to another one. Team members lose any connection access that flowed through the deleted workspace.
Names, edits, and activity 🔗 A name and description are each limited to 255 characters. Names are not unique: two workspaces in one organization can share a name. An edit changes only the fields you send.
Each workspace records an activity log: creating, editing, and deleting the workspace, and assigning or removing teams, environments, designs, and views. Every entry carries the email address of the person who acted. Reading the log requires the View Workspace permission.
Permissions 🔗 Every workspace action is checked in the organization that owns the workspace. Creating a workspace is checked in the organization you create it in. The keys are View Workspace, Create Workspace, Edit Workspace, Delete Workspace, Assign team to workspace, Remove team from workspace, Assign environment to workspace, Remove environment from workspace, Assign Designs to Workspaces, Remove Designs from Workspaces, Assign Views to Workspace, and Unassign Views from Workspace. Default holders are in Default Permissions.
Layer5 Cloud enforces no plan check on workspace actions. Creating, editing, deleting, and assigning work the same on every plan, governed only by those permissions.
Related 🔗 Managing Workspaces covers creating, editing, and deleting workspaces and assigning their members. Environments explains the deploy targets a workspace exposes. Promote a Design moves a design from a staging workspace to a production workspace.

body:
Stellar Dynamics is Orbital Labs’ biggest enterprise client — and its most exacting one. Marcus Webb, Org Admin for Stellar Dynamics, needs to build stellar-saas-platform in Kanvas: a full Azure-native SaaS architecture that his engineering team will own and operate, but that Orbital Labs’ Infrastructure Team needs to review for architectural alignment. The twist is that Marcus and Five work for different organizations. This tutorial demonstrates how Kanvas cross-organization design access makes that collaboration possible without collapsing the permission boundary between the two orgs.
Architecture overview 🔗 The stellar-saas-platform design models Stellar Dynamics’ production SaaS stack. It spans five Azure services:
Component Role AKS (Azure Kubernetes Service) Compute backbone — application workloads Azure SQL Relational data layer Azure API Management API gateway — external and internal traffic Azure AD Identity and access management Event Hub Event streaming and async messaging Marcus owns the design in the stellar-main workspace under the Stellar Dynamics org. The stellar-enterprise environment holds active connections for AKS, Azure SQL, Azure API Management, and Azure AD — making it the natural binding target.
Tutorial 🔗 Step 1: Marcus opens Kanvas as Stellar Dynamics Org Admin 🔗 Marcus logs into Layer5 Cloud using his Stellar Dynamics credentials. His account carries the Org Admin role for Stellar Dynamics, which gives him full design and workspace management permissions within that org.
He navigates to Kanvas → Designer and confirms that the workspace selector shows stellar-main — the workspace designated for Stellar Dynamics’ primary architecture work.
Step 2: Create the stellar-saas-platform design 🔗 Marcus selects New Design from the Designer toolbar. He names the design stellar-saas-platform and, because stellar-main is already selected as his active workspace, the design is created there automatically.
He adds a short description — “Azure SaaS platform: AKS, SQL, APIM, AAD, Event Hub” — so the design is identifiable in the workspace list without opening it.
Step 3: Add Azure components and draw connections 🔗 Marcus opens the Component Library and filters by provider: Azure. He places five components on the canvas:
AKS Cluster — named saas-aks; the compute layer running all application microservices Azure SQL — named saas-sql; relational persistence for the SaaS data model Azure API Management — named saas-apim; the API gateway handling all inbound traffic from external clients Azure AD — named saas-aad; identity provider and RBAC authority for both the platform and its tenants Event Hub — named saas-events; the event streaming backbone for async workloads and audit logging With all five components on the canvas, Marcus draws the connection edges:
saas-apim → saas-aks — API Management routes validated requests to AKS workloads saas-aks → saas-sql — application microservices read and write to Azure SQL saas-aks → saas-events — microservices publish domain events to Event Hub saas-aad → saas-apim — API Management delegates authentication to Azure AD (OAuth 2.0 / OIDC) saas-aad → saas-aks — workload identity is managed through Azure AD for pod-level auth He annotates the saas-aad → saas-apim edge with oauth2/oidc to make the authentication protocol explicit for reviewers.
Step 4: Leave the design unbound 🔗 Kanvas does not store an environment on a design, and the canvas does not overlay connection status or a live cluster version. stellar-enterprise stays a deploy-time choice: the Deploy stepper asks which environments to target. This tutorial does not deploy.
Step 5: Cross-org sharing with Orbital Labs 🔗 This is the step that makes the tutorial interesting. Marcus wants Five — a Platform Engineer at Orbital Labs — to review the design. But Five is not a member of Stellar Dynamics; he belongs to a completely separate organization.
Cross-org sharing is possible here because both Stellar Dynamics and Orbital Labs are managed under Constellation Cloud, a shared MSP provider. Dr. Aiko Sato, Constellation Cloud’s Provider Admin, has already configured cross-org access permissions that allow design sharing across the two orgs. Without that provider-level configuration, the Share dialog would not surface users from the other organization at all.
Marcus opens the Share panel on stellar-saas-platform. He types Five’s name in the user search field. Because Dr. Aiko Sato has established the cross-org trust relationship, Five appears as a valid share target even though he belongs to Orbital Labs. A share has no permission level. Five can edit the design and leave comments.
Marcus clicks Share. Five receives an in-app notification in his Orbital Labs account.
Cross-Org Access Cross-organization design sharing requires that both organizations exist under a shared Provider (Constellation Cloud in this scenario). The Provider Admin (Dr. Aiko Sato) must have configured cross-org permissions before sharing can occur. See Roles and Keychains for the permission model. Step 6: Five reviews the design from Orbital Labs 🔗 Five opens the shared design notification from his Orbital Labs account. The stellar-saas-platform design loads in Kanvas. He can inspect all five Azure components, explore their configuration panels, and view the connection annotations. The canvas is not read-only: a share does not disable drag, connect, or delete.
After a few minutes of review, Five leaves a comment pinned to the saas-apim component:
“You’re missing a WAF in front of API Management — Zara is going to notice.”
He also adds a general design comment noting that the Event Hub retention period should be explicitly configured if the audit logging use case requires replay beyond the default 24-hour window.
Marcus receives a notification that Five has left comments and opens the comment thread.
Step 7: Marcus acts on the review 🔗 Marcus reads Five’s comments. The WAF observation is valid — Stellar Dynamics’ security baseline requires a Web Application Firewall in front of any public API endpoint. He adds an Azure Application Gateway component (with WAF tier selected in the configuration panel) to the canvas:
He names it saas-waf-gateway He draws an edge from saas-waf-gateway → saas-apim, replacing the implicit external-client entry point with an explicit WAF-gated path He annotates the new edge with waf-v2 to indicate the WAF policy tier Marcus resolves Five’s WAF comment and replies: “Added Application Gateway (WAF v2) in front of APIM. Retention on Event Hub is set to 7 days in the environment config — will surface that in the design next pass.”
The stellar-saas-platform design now reflects the correct architecture, the review loop is documented in the comment history, and the cross-org collaboration happened entirely within Kanvas — no design files exported, no screenshots emailed.
Info Meet Marcus, Five, Dr. Aiko, and the rest of the cast at Meet Five and the Cast.

What sessions are 🔗 A session is the credential Layer5 Cloud issues each time someone signs in. It is what keeps a browser tab, a second device, or a connected Meshery Server signed in, and it is what you end when you want one of those sign-ins to stop working. Sessions expire on their own. API tokens do not.
Layer5 Cloud sessions use OAuth 2.0 for authentication. OAuth 2.0 is a standard protocol for authorization and focuses on client developer simplicity while providing specific authorization flows for web applications, desktop applications, mobile phones, and so on.
These are the Layer5 Cloud deployment defaults. Operators of a self-hosted deployment can change them.
Credential Default lifetime Behavior Access token 24 hours The browser session ends when it lapses. Activity in the interface does not extend it, so a browser user signs in again after 24 hours. Refresh token 1000 hours (about 41 days) Clients such as Meshery Server use it to obtain a new access token. Each refresh token works once. Every refresh issues a new one. A failed refresh returns an error. Sign-in flow 12 hours Time allowed to complete a sign-in. Privileged-action window Set by the deployment; 15 minutes in the packaged default Sensitive actions, such as profile changes, ask you to authenticate again once this window has passed since sign-in. Anonymous Kanvas session 24 hours For use without signing in. It does not appear on the Sessions tab. The browser keeps the session in the provider_token cookie. Page scripts cannot read it (HttpOnly), it is sent only over HTTPS, and it uses SameSite Lax, so other sites cannot send it along with their own requests except on ordinary top-level navigation. A second cookie, has_session, tells the interface that a session exists. It carries no secret, page scripts can read it, and it lapses with the session.
Creating and using sessions 🔗 Every sign-in creates its own session. Each browser, device, and Meshery Server that signs in through Layer5 Cloud holds a separate session with its own expiry, and any number of them can be active at once. Ending one session leaves the others untouched.
A session acts as the user who signed in. What it can do in an organization is whatever the roles that user holds there allow, checked on every request. See Keys for how roles grant permissions.
To use a session, sign in to your Layer5 Cloud user account. The session cookie is stored in that browser. Use the same browser until the session expires. You can have multiple sessions active concurrently, on the same device or on different devices. Each session receives its own authentication token and expiry time.
It is possible to use the same account from two sessions at once. For example, you may open the same Kanvas design in two sessions and see your avatar twice in the design, along with your mouse cursor. You can use this to collaborate with yourself or with others.
Users see their own sessions on the Sessions tab of the Security page. Each row shows the session’s ID, name, purpose, and creation date. The tab requires the View Sessions key, which every default user role holds. The list shows no device, browser, or location for a session. Search filters by name or purpose, and the newest sessions appear first.
Revoking sessions 🔗 A session ends in one of three ways:
Expiry. The access token lapses at its lifetime. Activity does not extend it. Logout from the Sessions tab. The session’s token is revoked immediately. The next request that presents it fails. The action records the same audit event as deleting a token: <email> revoked token <name> (category token, action delete). The confirmation reads Token "<name>" deleted, because a session is stored as a token. Signing out of the app. Signing out ends the browser’s identity session and revokes its stored grant. Changing your password does not end your other sessions. Layer5 Cloud has no sign-out-everywhere action and no idle timeout setting. To end your other sessions, log each one out from the Sessions tab.
The deleted session cannot be restored. Whoever used it must sign in again.
Who can use Logout The Logout action on the Sessions tab requires the Delete Token key, which only Organization Admins and Provider Admins hold by default. Users, Team Admins, and Workspace Admins see Logout disabled, even though their roles hold the Logout from a Session key. Layer5 Cloud lets each user log out only their own sessions. No role can end another user’s session from this tab. The server deletes only your own tokens. Delete Token is enforced by the interface for this control. The server does not test the Delete Token key on the delete request. See Sessions in Layer5 Cloud.
If you suspect your account is compromised 🔗 End every session you do not recognize. A creation date you cannot account for means someone else signed in with your credentials. Change your password. Changing the password does not end other sessions, so complete step 1 first and check the list again afterward. Review your API tokens and revoke any you did not create. Tokens never expire and are not sessions, so signing out does not revoke them. If you cannot sign in, ask an Organization Admin or Provider Admin to help recover the account. Layer5 Cloud has no “sign out everywhere” action. End each session from the list.
How the browser stores a session 🔗 Cookie Purpose Attributes provider_token The browser session credential HttpOnly, Secure over HTTPS, SameSite Lax has_session Tells the interface a session exists. Carries no secret and cannot authenticate a request. Readable by page scripts, SameSite Lax, expires with the session The cookie’s scope depends on how the organization signs users in:
Platform sign-in provider. The cookie is shared across the platform’s hosts, so one sign-in covers them. Organization’s own identity provider, or a custom domain outside the platform’s domain. The cookie is host-only and is never sent to any other host. See Organizations for how custom domains and identity providers decide where a user signs in.
Sessions and API tokens 🔗 Sessions and API tokens both authenticate as you, and Layer5 Cloud revokes them through the same mechanism. They differ in how they start and how long they live. Tokens and sessions share one store. isOauth=false selects API tokens and isOauth=true selects sessions.
Session API token Created by Signing in from a browser, device, or Meshery Server Creating it on the Tokens tab with a name and purpose Lifetime 24-hour access token, renewable by clients for up to about 41 days No expiry Ended by Expiry, Logout on the Sessions tab, or signing out Deleting it on the Tokens tab Used for Interactive use and connected Meshery Servers Scripts and API clients sending a Bearer token The Tokens tab never lists sessions, and the Sessions tab never lists API tokens.
You see only your own sessions. Sessions are scoped to your user account, not to one organization.
What Layer5 Cloud does not offer 🔗 No organization-level session policy. Lifetimes are set for the whole deployment. No idle timeout setting in the product interface. No device, browser, or location detail on a session. No action that ends every session at once. Session endpoints 🔗 Paths sit under /api unless noted. A missing or revoked credential returns 401 with {"message": "user must be logged in to perform this operation"}. When Layer5 Cloud cannot read the revocation record, it refuses the request rather than accept a token it cannot check.
Method and path Who may call Behavior GET /identity/tokens?isOauth=true Signed-in user Lists your sessions. Default order: newest first. search matches name and purpose. The response never contains token values. DELETE /identity/tokens?tokenId= Token owner Revokes the session. A malformed id returns 400 with invalid token id. An unknown or already-deleted id returns 400 with tokens does not exist. Writes a delete event. POST /refresh (outside /api) Holder of a refresh token Exchanges a refresh token for a new session credential. Returns 400 with a JSON error if the token is missing, malformed, or already used. GET /logout (outside /api) Signed-in browser Ends the browser’s identity session. Key Governs Default holders besides Provider Admin Enforced by View Sessions The Sessions tab User, Team Admin, Workspace Admin, Organization Admin Interface Logout from a Session Seeded for ending a session User, Team Admin, Workspace Admin, Organization Admin Not checked. The interface uses Delete Token for Logout. Delete Token The Logout control on the Sessions tab, and revoking a token Organization Admin Interface only. The server deletes only your own tokens.

body:
Everything you place on a Kanvas Designer canvas is an object, and every object answers to the same small set of gestures. You add it, you style it, you copy or clone it, you lock it so nobody nudges it, you resize it, and eventually you delete it. That is true whether the object is an Amazon EKS cluster, a dashed section drawn around a group of services, a textbox holding a caption, or a plain shape used as a legend key.
This page documents those gestures once and calls out the places where a particular kind of object behaves differently. If you are looking for the freestyle pen and pencil tools instead, see Whiteboarding.
The four kinds of canvas object 🔗 Object What it is Where it comes from Component A real piece of infrastructure under management - a Deployment, an S3 bucket, a Lambda function. Components carry configuration and can be deployed. The components and Kubernetes tools in the dock, or an import. Shape A purely visual primitive - circle, hexagon, arrow, flowchart symbol, cloud-provider glyph. Shapes carry no configuration and are never deployed. The shapes tool in the dock. Section A labeled, dashed rectangle used to fence off a region of the canvas. Other objects dropped inside a section become its children and move with it. The section tool in the dock, or S. Textbox A resizable box whose content is text. Used for titles, callouts and annotations that are not tied to a single component. The textbox tool in the dock, or T. Shapes, sections and textboxes are annotations, and Kanvas keeps them distinct from the infrastructure in a design. They carry no configuration to deploy, they are left out of the design’s component count, and the Layers panel can hide or reveal all of them as one group. Annotating a design therefore carries no risk to the infrastructure that design describes.
Adding objects to the canvas 🔗 Adding shapes 🔗 Open the shapes tool in the dock. Kanvas presents its shape libraries: Amazon Web Services, Azure Architecture, Dev Icons, Google Cloud Platform, Arrows, Flowchart, Shapes and Simple Line Icons. Search across all of them from the box at the top, or drill into one library at a time.
The shapes tool lists every shape library available to your design Drill into a library to browse its contents. The built-in Shapes library alone carries 66 primitives - Actor, Barrel, Bevel, Card, Circle, Cloud, Cone, Corner, Crescent, Cross, Cube, Diamond, Explosion, Flash, HalfFrame, Heptagon, Hexagon and more.
The built-in Shapes library, expanded Drag a shape from the picker onto the canvas to place it where you want it. If you find yourself reaching for the same library repeatedly, pin it to the dock - see Pinning a Model to the Dock.
Adding sections 🔗 Drag the section tool from the dock onto the canvas, or press S to drop a section near the center of the canvas.
A new section arrives as an 80-pixel-tall rectangle with a dashed border, a transparent fill and a label rendered along its top edge rather than through its middle - so the region it encloses stays readable. Drag other objects into it and they become children of the section: move the section and they move with it.
Adding textboxes 🔗 Drag the textbox tool from the dock onto the canvas, or press T. The keyboard route places the textbox near the center of the canvas and puts the cursor straight into it, so you can start typing immediately.
A new textbox arrives 60 pixels tall with a dashed gray border and a transparent fill, and its text sits at the top left of the box. To edit the text of an existing textbox - or of any shape, since shapes accept body text too - double-click it.
A textbox carrying a caption, with its dashed border and transparent fill Selecting and acting on objects 🔗 Context-click (right-click) any object to open its menu. The menu is the same for shapes, sections, textboxes and components; entries that do not apply to the object under the cursor are simply not shown.
Action Keyboard What it does Copy Ctrl/⌘ + C Puts the object on your system clipboard Duplicate Ctrl/⌘ + D Clones the object into the same design Lock / Unlock - Pins the object’s position, or releases it Delete Delete or Backspace Removes the object from the design Reset styles - Restores the object’s styling to its model’s defaults The circular context menu, open on a selected object Every one of these acts on your whole selection, not just the object under the cursor. To build a selection first, hold Shift or Ctrl/⌘ and drag a selection box across the canvas; Ctrl/⌘ + A selects everything. All of these actions are undoable with Ctrl/⌘ + Z.
Copying 🔗 Copy writes the selected objects to your system clipboard, so you can paste them with Ctrl/⌘ + V into the same design, into a different design, or into a different browser tab running Kanvas. Pasted objects land at your cursor.
Copy carries the object’s styling with it. A shape you have recolored, re-bordered and captioned arrives in the target design looking exactly as it did in the source.
Cloning 🔗 Duplicate - “clone” in the permission model - skips the clipboard and drops a copy straight into the current design, offset 50 pixels right and 50 pixels down from the original so the two do not sit on top of each other. The clone gets fresh identifiers; relationships drawn between members of the cloned selection are cloned along with it, so duplicating a section and its children reproduces the whole arrangement intact.
Use Duplicate when you want another one here, and Copy when you want one somewhere else.
Locking and unlocking 🔗 Locking an object fixes its position on the canvas. A locked object can still be selected, inspected, styled and deleted - what it cannot do is move, whether you drag it directly or drag a selection box across it. Unlock it from the same menu to release it.
Lock state is stored on the object and saved with the design, so it survives a reload and is visible to your collaborators. It is the cheapest way to protect a finished layout from an accidental nudge during a review.
Tip: Lock the frame, not the contents Locking a section fixes the section itself; the objects inside it stay free to move. Lock a section once your regions are settled and you can rearrange components inside them without ever knocking a boundary out of alignment. Deleting 🔗 Delete removes the selected objects from the design. Pressing Delete or Backspace does the same thing to whatever is currently selected.
Deleting a section deletes the section itself, not the objects inside it. If you want the contents gone too, select them along with the section before you delete.
Configuring styles 🔗 Select any object and Kanvas floats a style toolbar above it. The toolbar is where every visual property of the object lives:
Shape - swap the object’s outline for any of the primitives in the shape switcher. Background - fill color from the editor palette, plus an opacity slider from 0 to 1. Border - color, thickness (0-25) and style: solid, dotted, dashed or double. Layer order - push the object forward or back through the stack. Name - the label drawn with the object. Link - an external URL the object points at. Image - a background image, supplied by URL. Text - font size, weight, color, decoration, and horizontal and vertical alignment for the object’s body text. Animation - none, blink, ripple, bounce or pulse. With more than one object selected, a change made in the toolbar applies to every object in the selection. That is the fastest way to bring a whole region of a design onto one palette.
Per-object differences 🔗 The toolbar adapts to what the object can actually do, so the controls you see depend on what you have selected.
Shapes Sections Textboxes Shape, background, border, layer order, name, link, image, animation Yes Yes Yes Text styling Yes No Yes Accepts other objects as children Yes Yes Yes Default appearance Solid 1px border, 10% fill opacity Dashed 1px border, transparent fill, label on the top edge Dashed 1px gray border, transparent fill Sections deliberately carry no body text: a section is a frame, and its identity is the label along its top edge. If you want prose inside a region, put a textbox in it.
Note: styling never changes configuration Restyling an object changes only how it is drawn. It does not touch a component’s configuration and it does not change what gets deployed. To edit a component’s configuration, use the configuration panel - see Working with Components. Resetting styles 🔗 Reset styles, in the object’s context menu, re-applies the styling recorded in the object’s model definition - shape, colors, border, dimensions, background image and text styling - throwing away every change you made in the style toolbar.
Reset works from the definition, not from an edit history, so it is not an undo: it returns the object to the way that kind of object looks when it is first placed, no matter how many rounds of styling it has been through. The object’s position, its lock state, its configuration and its relationships are untouched.
This is the fast way out of a styling experiment that went wrong, and the fast way to bring one object back into line with the rest of a design.
Resizing 🔗 Select a single object and Kanvas draws a bounding box with eight handles around it - one at each corner and one at the midpoint of each edge.
Drag a corner handle to resize in both axes at once. Drag an edge handle to resize in one axis only. Hold Shift while dragging to preserve the object’s aspect ratio. The new dimensions are stored on the object and saved with the design. Empty sections and textboxes are resized exactly the same way - grow a textbox to fit a longer caption, or a section before you start filling it.
Note: containers do not show resize handles The handles appear on objects that do not contain other objects. Once a section - or any shape - has objects nested inside it, Kanvas treats it as a container and stops offering the handles; size it before you fill it, or move the contents out, resize, and move them back. Permission reference 🔗 Kanvas gates canvas actions by mode and by object capability, not by role. The permission catalog in Layer5 Cloud lists a key for each shape, section, textbox, and component-styling action in the table below (add, copy, clone, lock, delete, configure styles, reset styles, and resize), and a Provider Admin can include them in keychains and roles. Kanvas does not check those keys on the canvas today, so withholding one does not hide a control.
The permissions Kanvas does enforce on the toolbar are Validate Design, Deploy Design, Undeploy Design, and Share Design. See Reference.
Permission What it grants Documented in Add shapes Place shapes from any shape library onto the canvas Adding shapes Copy shapes Copy a shape to the clipboard for pasting elsewhere Copying Clone shapes Duplicate a shape into the same design Cloning Lock shapes Fix and release a shape’s position Locking and unlocking Delete shapes Remove a shape from the design Deleting Configure shape styles Change a shape’s outline, colors, border, layers, image, text and animation Configuring styles Reset shape styles Restore a shape to its model’s default styling Resetting styles Add sections Place sections onto the canvas Adding sections Copy sections Copy a section to the clipboard for pasting elsewhere Copying Clone sections Duplicate a section into the same design Cloning Lock sections Fix and release a section’s position Locking and unlocking Delete sections Remove a section from the design (its contents are kept) Deleting Configure section styles Change a section’s outline, colors, border, layers, image and animation Configuring styles Reset section styles Restore a section to its model’s default styling Resetting styles Add textboxes Place textboxes onto the canvas Adding textboxes Copy textboxes Copy a textbox to the clipboard for pasting elsewhere Copying Clone textboxes Duplicate a textbox into the same design Cloning Lock textboxes Fix and release a textbox’s position Locking and unlocking Delete textboxes Remove a textbox from the design Deleting Configure textbox styles Change a textbox’s outline, colors, border, layers, image, text and animation Configuring styles Reset textbox styles Restore a textbox to its model’s default styling Resetting styles Reset component styles Restore a component to its model’s default styling Resetting styles Resize components Change a component’s width and height with the resize handles Resizing Related reading 🔗 Whiteboarding - the pen and pencil tools, and line styling. Understanding Tool Modes - selection, pan and connector modes. Keyboard Shortcuts - the full shortcut reference. Working with Components - configuring the components you place. Reviewing Designs - comments, which are annotations with their own lifecycle.

Kanvas tutorials walk through real-world design scenarios using two fictional organizations — Orbital Labs, a cloud-native startup on the Team plan, and Stellar Dynamics, their enterprise client on the Enterprise plan — both managed under the Constellation Cloud provider. Each tutorial follows a cast of named characters as they build, share, and collaborate on infrastructure designs, so you can see how Kanvas permissions, workspaces, environments, and cross-org access work together in practice.
Info Meet Five, Maya, Zara, Marcus, Dr. Aiko, and the full cast at Meet Five and the Cast. Collaboration and Catalog 🔗 Collaborative Editing Collaborative Editing — share a design, set Private or Public visibility, invite collaborators, and review with comments.
Publishing to Catalog Publishing to Catalog — publish from Details → Publish to Catalog, then follow review and Catalog visibility.
Featured tutorials 🔗 Kubernetes Hands-on Playground tutorials for pods, deployments, services, and more — plus a visual request-flow walkthrough. Start at the Kubernetes tutorials hub.
GCP Data Pipeline Building a GCP Data Pipeline Design — model Pub/Sub, Dataflow, BigQuery, and GKE in Designer.
Cross-Org Access stellar-saas-platform — share and review designs across organizations.
AWS Deploy AWS EC2 Instances with Meshery using AWS Controllers for Kubernetes (ACK). See also the AWS tutorials hub.
Azure Deploy Azure resources and an Azure Storage Account with ASO. See the Azure tutorials hub.
Artifact Hub Publishing Meshery Designs to Artifact Hub — export and publish designs to a repository.
WordPress Embedding a Meshery Design in a WordPress Post — publish interactive designs on your site.

Kanvas lets you export a design in several formats, so you can:
keep versioned backups collaborate offline push artifacts to OCI-compatible registries or Helm repositories integrate designs into CI/CD or GitOps pipelines embed interactive diagrams in documentation and blogs Export in Two Steps 🔗 Open the export menu Within the Kanvas Designer, select the design you wish to export in the design drawer. Click on the export icon in the menu for the selected design. Pick an export format Choose the option that matches your workflow (see table below). Quick Reference: Export Formats 🔗 Format Keeps full design metadata? Typical uses Design (YAML) ✔ Backups, sharing, re-import into Kanvas Design (OCI image) ✔ Store in Docker Hub/GHCR; registry-based versioning Kubernetes Manifest (YAML) ✖ (lossy) kubectl apply; raw K8s deployment Helm Chart (.tar.gz) ✖ (lossy) Helm repos, GitOps (Argo CD/Flux), Artifact Hub Embed Design (JS snippet) - Interactive diagrams in docs or dashboards Detailed Format Guide 🔗 Design (YAML) 🔗 Exports a complete, lossless copy of your design.
This format preserves all Meshery-specific metadata, including:
Visual layout Annotations and comments Component grouping and configuration Use it to back up or move designs between Meshery instances. The file is saved as <design-name>.yml.
Design (OCI Image) 🔗 Exports your design as an OCI-compliant container image.
This format preserves all design metadata, just like the Design (YAML), but in a form suitable for container registries.
When to use:
Version and distribute your design via Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry, AWS ECR, etc. Integrate with registry-based workflows or team collaboration tools Store designs alongside application artifacts The exported file is named <design-name>.tar, and can be pushed using tools like docker push or oras push.
Source-Type Formats 🔗 A design can also be exported back out as the kind of source it was built from. Two source types are supported: Kubernetes Manifest and Helm Chart. Both are lossy - the Kanvas-specific layout, annotations, and comments are dropped, because neither format has anywhere to carry them.
Docker Compose is an import source only. There is no Docker Compose export; converting a design to Compose is not supported.
Kubernetes Manifest (YAML) Lossy Export 🔗 Exports your design as raw Kubernetes YAML files, ready to apply with kubectl.
Best used when:
You want to deploy directly to a cluster You’re integrating with CI/CD tools that expect plain manifests You no longer need visual layout, annotations, or design metadata This format strips out Meshery-specific context and includes only standard Kubernetes resource definitions.
If you want to preserve the full editable design, use Design (YAML) instead.
Helm Chart (.tar.gz) Lossy Export 🔗 Packages your design as a standard Helm chart archive (.tar.gz).
Best used when:
You want to deploy via Helm (helm install) You’re working with GitOps tools like Argo CD or Flux You plan to publish to a Helm repository or Artifact Hub This format includes only Kubernetes resource definitions. Design layout, annotations, and other Meshery-specific metadata will not be included.
If you want to keep your design fully editable in Meshery, use Design (YAML) instead.
Embed Design (JavaScript Snippet) 🔗 Exporting your design as an embedding allows you to integrate it into websites, blogs, or other platforms that support HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
The embedded design version offers a visually interactive representation of your design, making it easy to share with infrastructure stakeholders.
Learn more about Embedding Designs.
Best Practices and Tips 🔗 Need Recommended format Preserve every design detail Design (YAML) or OCI image One-off deployment Kubernetes Manifest Share a reusable package Helm Chart Show an interactive diagram Embed Design Publish to Helm repo Helm Chart (.tar.gz) Store in container registry Design (OCI image) Note:
If you plan to keep editing in Meshery, avoid lossy formats. A Helm .tar.gz can be placed in any Helm repo and installed with helm install. An OCI image can be versioned and pulled just like an application image. Frequently Asked Questions 🔗 Can I re-import a Helm Chart or Kubernetes manifest into Meshery for editing? You can import the resources, but design-time metadata (layout, annotations) is lost, so the graph will not reappear as originally designed.
What gets removed in a lossy export? Layout coordinates, visual grouping, comments, and any Meshery-only metadata.
Is the Helm `.tar.gz` ready for `helm install`? Yes. After export, run helm install <release> <chart.tgz> or add it to a Helm repo.
Should I use Helm Chart or OCI image for sharing? Use Helm if your consumers deploy via Helm; use OCI if you rely on container registries for versioning.
Do I need to be logged in to export a design? No, login is not required. You can export as a guest user.
Can I export someone else's published design? Yes. Any published design can be exported, not just your own.
Can I export an earlier version of a design? No. Every export - in any format - is generated from the current state of the design. A design carries a single version number, which increments as the design is updated, and neither exporting nor downloading offers a way to ask for an earlier one.
The View Save History button in Kanvas (on the save-status indicator) shows the design’s save history as a list of events. It is an audit trail of who changed the design and when; it is not a set of restorable snapshots, and you cannot export from it.
If you need a version you can come back to, export a copy at the point you care about - Design (YAML) or Design (OCI image) are the two lossless formats - and keep it, or push the OCI image to a registry under a tag.
Where does the exported file go? After export, your browser will either prompt you to choose a save location or automatically download the file to your default downloads folder.
What each export keeps 🔗 Design file YAML downloads as <design name>.yml and re-imports losslessly, including layout, annotations, and metadata. The OCI image export is an archive you push with a registry tool. Kubernetes manifest and Helm chart exports keep resources only, not layout. The embeddable JavaScript module is a static canvas snapshot and is not re-imported as a design. In Operator mode, a view downloads as <view name>.json. Docker Compose export, SVG export, export of an earlier version, and per-format export options are not available. The catalog’s light and dark snapshot images are produced after publishing and are not a user export.
