body:
What tokens are 🔗 An API token lets software act as you. Scripts, CI/CD pipelines, mesheryctl, and other Meshery clients present it to Layer5 Cloud instead of signing in through a browser. Because a token carries your full authority and never expires, deciding how many tokens to create, who holds them, and when to delete them is a security decision.
A token is a credential bound to your user account. A client sends it as a bearer token in the Authorization header of each request. The Cloud API reference shows the exact form.
A token is not scoped to an organization. One token reaches every organization you belong to. Each request chooses the organization it runs in, so a single pipeline token can act in several organizations if you are a member of each. See Specifying Organization Context.
Layer5 Cloud does not record permissions inside the token. It evaluates your roles at the moment of each call, in the organization of that request. There are no token scopes. You cannot limit a token to read-only access, to one organization, or to a subset of your permissions. To give automation narrower authority, give it a token from an account whose roles are narrower.
API Tokens are User-Scoped, Not Organization-Scoped Layer5 Cloud API tokens are scoped to your user account, not to a specific organization. This means a single API token provides access to all organizations you are a member of, similar to how GitHub Personal Access Tokens work. For users who belong to multiple organizations, see Specifying Organization Context in the REST API documentation to learn how to control which organization your API requests operate on. Access tokens 🔗 Layer5 Cloud REST API uses OAuth 2.0 access tokens for authentication and authorization. Access tokens are opaque tokens that conform to the OAuth 2.0 framework. They are used to authenticate requests to Layer5 APIs and are associated with a user account.
Tokens never expire. Layer5 Cloud offers no expiry setting, and a token remains valid until it is deleted. This differs from sessions, which Layer5 Cloud creates at each sign-in and which lapse on their own. A token is the right credential for unattended automation. A session is the right one for a person at a browser.
Role changes apply at once. When an administrator grants or removes a role, the next request made with your token reflects the change. Removing the user ends the token. If your account is disabled or deleted, Layer5 Cloud refuses every request that presents your tokens. Creating tokens 🔗 You can create a token for your user account at any time. Tokens never expire, but can be revoked. Every token has a name, which is required. The Tokens tab also asks for a purpose. Both are labels. They appear in your token list and help you recognize each token later, and they have no effect on what the token can do. Name the consumer (for example, ci-snapshots) and state what it does in the purpose.
Layer5 Cloud creates the token for your user account. It has no expiry and no scope settings. The list shows the ID, name, purpose, and creation date. It never shows the token value. The list is searchable and sortable, and shows the newest tokens first by default.
See Tokens in Layer5 Cloud.
Before you start 🔗 You need the Create Token permission to create a token in the interface. User, Team Admin, Workspace Admin, Organization Admin, and Provider Admin hold it by default. A user without it sees the create control disabled. You need View Tokens to open the Tokens tab. Every default user role holds it. Decide which consumer gets this token. Create one token per consumer so you can revoke one without breaking the others. Open the Tokens tab under Security and start a new token. Enter a name and a purpose.
Using tokens 🔗 To use a token to authenticate to Layer5 Cloud’s REST API, pass the token as a Bearer token in the Authorization header of your HTTP request:
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \ -H "X-Current-Orgid: <organization-id>" \ https://cloud.layer5.io/api/environments The token authenticates you, not an organization. It reaches every organization you belong to. Name the organization for each request with the X-Current-Orgid header. Layer5 Cloud reads that header name only. See Specifying Organization Context.
What the token can do equals what you can do in that organization. If your role changes, the token’s reach changes on the next request.
For GitHub Actions, store the token as a repository secret. See Use GitHub Actions.
Deleting tokens 🔗 Deleting a token is how you revoke it. Revocation takes effect immediately and cannot be undone. A deleted token cannot be downloaded again, and every request that presents it fails. There is no way to restore a deleted token. Anything still authenticating with it will start failing, so replace it with a newly created token first if it is in use.
Layer5 Cloud checks revocation on every request. If it cannot complete that check, it refuses the request rather than accept a token that might be revoked.
To delete a token:
Go to the Tokens page in Layer5 Cloud. Each row shows the token’s ID, Name, Purpose, and Creation Date. Find the token you want to remove. The list is searchable and sortable, and shows the newest tokens first by default. Click the trash can icon in that row’s Actions column. Confirm in the Delete Token dialog, which names the token it is about to delete. Click Proceed. A confirmation notification reports the deleted token by name. The deletion appears as an event in your audit log.
You can delete only your own tokens. The server does not let another user, including a Provider Admin, delete a token for its owner. The owner of a leaked token must revoke it.
Permissions Required Deleting a token in the interface requires the Delete Token key, which Organization Admin and Provider Admin hold by default. Without it the trash can icon is disabled. See Keys. Sessions Are Deleted the Same Way Your browser sign-ins are represented by their own tokens and are listed on the Sessions page rather than here. There the same action is presented as Logout instead of Delete, and it ends that session. See Sessions. Permissions are enforced by the interface The interface requires Create Token, Delete Token, and Download Token. The Layer5 Cloud server accepts requests to create and delete your own tokens without checking those keys. The restriction is current behavior, not a security boundary. See security permission keys. Get the token value 🔗 Download the token from its row in the list. This needs the Download Token permission, which User, Team Admin, Workspace Admin, Organization Admin, and Provider Admin hold by default.
The download is a JSON file named token_<id>.json in the format Meshery clients read:
{ "meshery-provider": "Layer5", "token": "<token>" } You can download a live token again at any time. A revoked token cannot be downloaded. Treat the file like a password: put the token value in your CI secret store and delete the file. Anyone who obtains the file can act as you.
The token list never shows a token’s value. Creating, downloading, and deleting a token each write an audit event, so your organization’s audit trail records who generated a token, who retrieved it, and who revoked it.
List your tokens over the API 🔗 A script can list the tokens your account holds, for example to find old ones before rotating:
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \ "https://cloud.layer5.io/api/identity/tokens?purpose=ci-snapshots" The answer lists each token’s ID, name, purpose, and creation date, never its value. purpose keeps only tokens created with exactly that purpose, matched case-sensitively. Leave it out to list every token. search matches part of a name or purpose. The list holds API tokens unless you send isOauth=true, which lists sign-in sessions instead.
Desktop clients that sign in through Layer5 Cloud create their token with the client’s name as its purpose, so the same filter lists the tokens a client created for itself.
Rotate a token 🔗 To rotate a token without downtime, create the replacement first, switch each consumer to it, then delete the old token.
Rotate on a schedule you set, and whenever a person with access to the secret leaves. Layer5 Cloud has no built-in rotation, so rotate in three steps:
Create a new token for the same consumer. Update the consumer to use the new token and confirm it works. Revoke the old token. Revoking last keeps the consumer running the whole time. Revoke at once if a token value leaked.
Who can manage tokens by default 🔗 Each action on the Tokens tab is governed by a key. Provider Admin holds every key. With the default roles:
View Tokens, which opens the Tokens tab, is held by every default user role. Download Token is held by User, Team Admin, Workspace Admin, and Organization Admin. Create Token is held by User, Team Admin, Workspace Admin, Organization Admin, and Provider Admin. Delete Token is held by Organization Admin and Provider Admin only. For every other role, the interface disables the delete control. Every token action applies only to your own tokens. You cannot list, download, or delete another user’s token. The list shows your own tokens and never the token value.
Roles that hold the keys come from the default keychains: View Tokens sits in User View, Delete Token in Security Management, and Create Token and Download Token in Security Management and User Edit.
Current behavior: token create and delete requests are not checked against the keys The Layer5 Cloud server allows any signed-in user to create and delete their own tokens through the API. It does not check the Create Token or Delete Token keys on those requests. Withholding those keys hides the controls in the interface. It does not prevent a user from minting a token. Approving a desktop app or CLI sign-in is different: the server requires Create Token in at least one organization you belong to. The organization you have selected, or the one a custom domain belongs to, does not matter, so a member of a child organization can approve a sign-in on its parent’s custom domain. A Provider Admin can mint a token on behalf of another account. That token appears in the account holder’s token list, and the account holder can revoke it.
Troubleshooting 🔗 Symptom Cause Fix The create control is disabled You lack Create Token in the selected organization. Ask an Organization Admin to create the token or to grant the key through a role. 401 with “user must be logged in to perform this operation” The token was revoked, is malformed, or the header is wrong. Check the header reads Authorization: Bearer <token>. If it does, create a new token. 403 on a specific action You lack the permission for that action in the organization named by X-Current-Orgid. Check your role in that organization. See Default Permissions. A token worked before and now fails The token was revoked, or its owner account was removed. Create a new token from an active account and replace it in the consumer. Practices that limit risk 🔗 Create one token per consumer. A separate token for each pipeline, script, or Meshery Server lets you revoke one without breaking the others. Name each token after its consumer. The name is the only way to tell tokens apart in the list. Delete a token when its consumer is retired. A token never expires, so an unused token remains a live credential until you delete it. Manage your tokens at cloud.layer5.io/security/tokens.
Token endpoints 🔗 Paths sit under /api unless noted. Success responses are JSON unless stated. A missing or revoked credential returns 401 with {"message": "user must be logged in to perform this operation"}. When Layer5 Cloud cannot read the revocation record, it refuses the request rather than accept a token it cannot check.
Method and path Who may call Behavior POST /identity/tokens?name=&purpose= Signed-in user Creates a token for the caller. name is required: an empty name returns 400 with Token name missing. purpose is optional. Writes a create event. GET /identity/tokens?isOauth= Signed-in user Lists your tokens or sessions. Default order: newest first. search matches name and purpose. purpose matches exactly, case-sensitively. The response never contains token values. isOauth=false selects API tokens. isOauth=true selects sessions. GET /identity/tokens/{id} Token owner Returns the token for download. Returns 404 for an unknown or revoked token and 400 for a malformed id. Writes a download event. DELETE /identity/tokens?tokenId= Token owner Revokes the token or session. A malformed id returns 400 with invalid token id. An unknown or already-deleted id returns 400 with tokens does not exist. Writes a delete event. GET /identity/tokens/infinite?userId=&provider= Provider Admin Issues a non-expiring token for another account. The token is listed under that account. Others receive 403. Audit events 🔗 Action Event Create a token <email> generated token <name> (category token, action create) Download a token Token <name> downloaded (category token, action download). A failed download is also recorded, with an error severity. Delete a token or log out a session <email> revoked token <name> (category token, action delete)

body:
Publishing a design makes it visible to all Meshery Cloud users and anonymous visitors. This guide explains the publishing workflow, state management, permissions, and operational constraints.
Publishing Workflow 🔗 Step 1: Access Extensions UI 🔗 Navigate to Meshery Kanvas Designer from the main dashboard.
Step 2: Select Design in Sidebar 🔗 Publish designs through two methods. Click the info (“i”) button for details.
Option 1: View designs in the sidebar Option 2: Go to Configuration → Designs You can also open Details from the File menu on an open design:
Design Details (anonymous capture, Sep 2026): metadata, visibility, and Publish To Catalog. Publish is disabled while signed out. Step 3: Submit Design Metadata 🔗 Fill out the publication form:
Type: Select design category Technology: Specify related technology Description: Explain purpose and usage Caveats: Add important considerations Step 4: Review Process 🔗 Approval workflow based on user role:
Admin submissions: Published immediately User submissions: Enter “Pending Review” Submissions in the “Pending Review” state will remain unpublished until they are manually reviewed and either approved or rejected by an Organization Admin or Provider Admin. This review process may take some time depending on the availability of reviewers. Regardless of approval or rejection, submitters will receive an email notification with the decision.
Step 5: Post-Approval Status 🔗 Once the review process is complete, you will receive an email notification informing you of the decision.
If your design is approved:
It will no longer appear in “My Designs.” Instead, it will be listed in the Catalog as a publicly available entry. This ensures that published designs remain accessible to all users while keeping personal design spaces uncluttered. If your design is rejected:
You will receive an email notification with a rejection reason. Rejected designs cannot be resubmitted directly. If you want to revise and submit it again, you must clone the design, make changes, and submit it as a new entry. Cloning a Design 🔗 To modify published designs:
Select design from Catalog Click Clone to create editable copy Make changes and submit as new version State Management 🔗 1. Design State Lifecycle 🔗 A design transitions through multiple states from creation to publication. The diagram below visually represents this process.
Phases of Publishing Process 🔗 Pre-Publish: Users freely create and edit designs. Pending Review: Submitted designs undergo an approval process. Published: Approved designs are locked and listed publicly. Withdrawn: Unpublished designs return to private storage. 2. Design State Characteristics 🔗 State Stage Visibility Operability Key Restrictions Pre-Publish Sidebar Design List & Configuration → Designs Free edit/delete/rename (editable by anyone) No restrictions Pending Review Sidebar Design List & Configuration → Designs Editable by all users (including guests) Deleting during this stage creates dead entries in the approval list Published Category List (hidden in sidebar) View-only copies (auto-appended “_copy”) Original design permanently locked (edit in category only updates metadata) Withdrawn Returns to sidebar as private Free edit/delete/rename Original cannot be republished; must create a new canvas with identical content Critical Rules:
Withdrawn designs require re-submission as new entries. Published designs are immutable. 3. Publishing Permissions 🔗 Operation Guest Regular User Owner Organization Admin Provider Admin Edit Pending Design ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔ Submit for Review ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔ ✔ Unpublish ✘ ✘ ✔ ✔ ✔ For more about roles and permissions, refer to Role Descriptions and Default Permissions.
Key Notes:
Provider Admins have root-level visibility and can see private designs from all organizations. Catalog approval queues are org-specific—only members of an organization can see its pending approvals, unless the user is a Provider Admin. FAQ 🔗 1. When my design is in “Pending Review,” can I still edit it? Will the changes take effect? 🔗 Yes, you can edit your design while it is in the “Pending Review” state, and any modifications will be automatically reflected in the submitted design. No need to resubmit the request.
2. After my design is approved and published, can I modify it? Will the category be updated? 🔗 No, once a design is published, it becomes immutable. You cannot directly edit or modify the contents. The category and metadata remain locked to ensure version consistency. However, you can create a new version by cloning the design and making modifications.
3. After my design is published, can I modify the category field? 🔗 No, the category field cannot be changed after the design is published. If a category update is required, you must clone the design, update the category, and submit it as a new entry.
4. If my design is denied (rejected), can I submit it again? 🔗 No, once a design is denied, it cannot be resubmitted. However, you can clone the design, make adjustments, and submit it as a new entry for review.
5. Can I unpublish a design after it has been published? 🔗 Only Admins and Owner can unpublish designs. Regular users and guests cannot perform this action.
6. What is the difference between Public, Private, and Published? 🔗 State Visibility Editability Notes Public Visible to all Meshery Cloud users Fully editable Available for all users to access Private Only visible to the owner and organization members Fully editable Used for drafts and internal work Published Approved and locked for public access Cannot be modified Ensures design consistency and prevents unauthorized edits

The Kanvas Designer dock allows you to keep your most-used models and tools within easy reach. You can pin any model to the dock for quick access, and unpin it just as easily.
Overview 🔗 Pinning a model adds it to the dock at the bottom of the Designer interface. This helps you:
Quickly access frequently used models Customize your workspace Streamline your design workflow How to Pin a Model 🔗 Hover over the model you want to pin in the component list on the left side of the Designer. Click the pin icon that appears next to the model name. A tooltip will show “Pin To Dock”. The model will now appear in the dock at the bottom of the Designer. Pinned Model in the Dock 🔗 After you pin a model, it appears as an icon in the dock at the bottom of the Designer and remains there for quick access throughout your workflow. This makes it easy to find and reuse your favorite models at any time.
How to Use a Pinned Model 🔗 Clicking a pinned model in the dock gives you quick access to all its components. You can use these components in your design by either clicking to add them or dragging them onto the canvas for easy placement and configuration.
Note Only models can be pinned to the dock. Individual components within a model cannot be pinned directly. How to Remove a Model from the Dock 🔗 You can remove a model from the dock in two ways:
Method 1: Using the Pin Icon 🔗 Hover over the pinned model in the dock or in the component list. Click the pin icon again (the tooltip will show “Remove From Dock”). Method 2: Using the Close Button 🔗 Click the X (close) button on the pinned model icon in the dock to remove it instantly. Good to Know You can pin as many models as your workflow needs and swap them out anytime as your project evolves. Using a pinned model 🔗 Select a pinned model to open a picker with its components. Click a component to add it near the center of the canvas, or drag it to a specific spot. The picker has its own search box and a version selector with an “All Versions” choice. A pinned model whose lookup returns nothing is not drawn.

As you build a design, Kanvas continuously evaluates the relationships between your components — to identify connections, validate them, and keep related configuration in sync. This page explains how you can choose which engine performs that evaluation, how to read the relationship indicator, and how to diagnose results that look wrong.
How Relationships Are Evaluated 🔗 Kanvas can run relationship evaluation using one of two interchangeable engines:
Server-side – the policy engine running inside your Meshery server. It is always available. Client-side – the same policy engine, compiled to WebAssembly and run inside a background worker in your browser. Because it runs locally, there are no round-trips to the server, so evaluation is typically faster. A WASM evaluation times out after 10 seconds. The default preference is Automatic, not the server. At load, Kanvas tries to start the WASM engine and waits up to 30 seconds for it to report ready. If it starts, WASM is used. If not, the Meshery server is used. Kanvas waits until changes stop for about one second, then evaluates. Another change during evaluation restarts the cycle. Evaluation runs after a configuration value or display name changes, a relationship is added or removed, a component is added, removed, duplicated, or merged, or a design loads or an import or merge completes.
Both engines produce the same relationship results. The choice affects performance, and where toil (evaluation) is done, not correctness.
Editing is never blocked Relationship evaluation runs alongside your work — it never blocks editing or saving a design. If evaluation fails for any reason, you can keep designing and saving normally; only the relationship results are affected. Changing the Evaluation Engine Preference 🔗 The engine is controlled by the Relationship Evaluation Engine preference.
In Kanvas Designer, open Settings. Find the Relationship Evaluation Engine preference. Choose one of the following values: Value What it does Automatic (recommended) Runs a one-time health check at the start of the session. If the client-side (WASM) engine passes a self-test, it is used for the rest of the session; otherwise the Meshery server is used. Meshery server Always uses the Meshery server’s policy engine. Client-side (WASM) Always uses WASM. There is no fallback. If the engine fails to start, evaluations fail silently and relationships stop updating. Switch to Automatic or Meshery server and reload. Automatic checks only that the engine initializes. It does not fall back to the server later if WASM fails after a successful start. The engine is selected once per session. Changing the preference takes full effect on the next session (for example, after reloading Kanvas).
When to prefer the server engine Leave the preference on Automatic unless you have a specific reason to change it. If client-side results ever look wrong, switching to Meshery server is the most reliable way to rule out the engine as the cause — see Diagnosing failing or unexpected results. Reading the Relationship Indicator 🔗 The relationship indicator tells you the state of the most recent evaluation:
Evaluating — evaluation is in progress. This is normal after you add, remove, or reconfigure components. Evaluated — evaluation completed successfully and the relationships shown on the canvas are up to date. There is no error state on the indicator. A failed evaluation clears the last-evaluation details, so the tooltip returns to “No relationships evaluated yet”, and the failure is logged to the browser console only. Tooltips you will see: “Evaluating relationships…” while running, “Relationships evaluated” with the elapsed time when done, and “No relationships evaluated yet” when nothing has been evaluated. When Kanvas skips applying a result it shows “Skipping evaluation application”. A successful evaluation shows no message. WASM does not fall back to the server on its own after a fault. What the one-time notifications mean 🔗 A failed evaluation does not raise an error state or a fallback notification. The failure is logged to the browser console only. If relationships stop updating, switch the engine to Meshery server and reload.
Diagnosing Failing or Unexpected Relationship Results 🔗 If relationships are missing or look wrong, turn on Enable Debugger in the Options dialog (it is off by default) and open the Evaluation Engine tab. Status reads Initialized, Not Initialized, or Not Available, plus the engine type WASM or SERVER. The tab refreshes every second. If WASM is not initialized, set the engine to Meshery server, reload, and compare.
Step 1 — Enable the debugger preference 🔗 The Diagnostics view is exposed under the Designer debugger preference.
In Kanvas Designer, open Settings. Enable the debugger preference. Open the Relationship Evaluation Diagnostics view. Step 2 — Read the Diagnostics view 🔗 The Diagnostics view reports the current state of relationship evaluation:
Status – Initialized, Not Initialized, or Not Available. Engine type – WASM or SERVER, plus any initialization error. The tab refreshes every second. There is no fallback counter. A runtime fault does not switch engines by itself. Step 3 — Force the server engine if client results look wrong 🔗 If you suspect the client-side engine is producing incorrect results:
Open Settings. Set Relationship Evaluation Engine to Meshery server. Reload Kanvas so the new engine is used for the session. Re-check the design’s relationships. If the relationships are correct with the server engine but wrong with the client-side engine, that points to a client engine issue worth reporting (see below).
Step 4 — Re-trigger evaluation 🔗 Evaluation re-runs automatically whenever you change the design — for example, by adding, removing, or reconfiguring a component, or by toggling a relationship kind on or off from the Relationships section of the Designer. Making any such change re-triggers evaluation with the active engine. There is no error state for a successful re-evaluation to clear.
Step 5 — When and how to file a bug 🔗 If relationship results are still wrong or evaluation keeps failing after the steps above — especially if the Meshery server engine also produces incorrect or failing results — file a bug. Include the following from the Relationship Evaluation Diagnostics view so the issue can be reproduced:
The engine type, WASM or SERVER, and any initialization error. The relationships you expected versus what Kanvas showed, and the design or a minimal version of it. Related reading For an overview of what relationships are and the kinds Kanvas supports, see Understanding Relationships. For creating and managing relationships in a design, see Creating Relationships.

body:
Right-clicking an empty part of the canvas - anywhere no component sits - opens the Canvas Actions menu. Where the component context menu acts on one component, this menu acts on the canvas as a whole: undoing and redoing, pasting, selecting everything, capturing the canvas as an image, and reaching help.
The menu adapts to the mode you are in. Commenting and pasting, for example, are offered in Designer mode but not in Operator mode, where the canvas reflects discovered infrastructure rather than a design you are authoring.
Editing actions 🔗 Action Shortcut Behavior Add Comment M Drops a comment at the point you right-clicked. Designer mode only. See Reviewing Designs. Undo Cmd/Ctrl + Z Reverses the last change. Redo Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + Z Re-applies the last undone change. Paste Cmd/Ctrl + V Pastes the clipboard contents at the cursor position. Designer mode only. Select All Cmd/Ctrl + A Selects every component on the canvas. Reset Design Clears every component from the canvas. Designer mode only, and destructive - see below. Reset Design 🔗 Reset Design removes everything currently on the canvas. Kanvas asks you to confirm before it does, and the confirmation reminds you that undo is usually the better tool if you only want to step back a few changes. The confirmation dialog carries a “don’t show this again” checkbox; ticking it stores that preference against your user settings, and the reset then happens immediately on every subsequent use.
Screenshot Canvas 🔗 Take Screenshot captures the canvas exactly as it is drawn - components, relationships, annotations and all - and downloads it to your machine as a PNG. The file is named Kanvas-<timestamp>.png, so repeated captures of the same design do not overwrite one another.
The capture is of the canvas rather than of your browser window: panels, the dock and the toolbar are not included, and the image is rendered from the design itself rather than screen-grabbed, so it is not limited to the part of the design currently scrolled into view.
This is the quickest way to put a design into a pull request, an incident write-up or a slide. When you need the design as data rather than as a picture - to hand to another tool, or to re-import later - use Exporting Designs instead.
Options 🔗 Options opens the canvas settings drawer, where preferences that affect how the canvas behaves and renders are gathered.
Shortcuts 🔗 Shortcuts (Cmd/Ctrl + /) opens the keyboard shortcut reference in the help drawer, listing the shortcuts available in both Designer and Operator modes.
View help center 🔗 Help Center (Cmd/Ctrl + Shift + /) opens the in-app help modal. It gathers, in one place, every route by which you can learn more about Kanvas or reach someone who can help:
Card What it opens Documentation Guides, references and how-tos for Kanvas and Meshery. Video Tutorials Walkthroughs and demos in the Layer5 video library. Quick Tips An in-app tour of core Kanvas features, shown in a drawer beside the canvas. Academy Structured learning paths in Layer5 Cloud. Discussion Forum The Layer5 discussion forum, for questions and shared knowledge. Slack The Layer5 community Slack, for real-time conversation. Keyboard Shortcuts The same shortcut reference the Shortcuts action opens. Support A form for contacting the Kanvas team with a problem or a piece of feedback. Quick Tips and Keyboard Shortcuts open in a drawer alongside the canvas, so you can keep working while you read them. Support opens its form in a modal over the canvas. The remaining five cards open in a new tab. The Help Center is also reachable from the help button at the right-hand end of the dock.

body:
Two controls decide how a design reads on screen. Layout arranges the components - where they sit relative to one another. Layers decide which of them are drawn at all.
Both are recorded in the design rather than in your browser, so they travel with it: a layout writes the components’ positions, and the Layers panel writes their visibility into the design’s preferences. Anyone else opening the design sees the same arrangement and the same components hidden. What neither touches is configuration - a hidden component is still part of the design and is still deployed, and re-running a layout changes only where components sit.
Change design layout 🔗 The layout control sits in the bottom-left corner of the canvas, showing the icon of the layout currently in use. Clicking it fans out the available layouts; picking one re-arranges every component on the canvas with an animated transition, so you can see where things moved to. The zoom controls sit at the opposite corner, bottom-right.
Layout Shape it produces Suits Constrained A force-directed arrangement that respects grouping and containment The default, and the best general-purpose choice Grid Even rows and columns Inventories and flat sets of similar components Hierarchical A layered, top-down tree following the direction of relationships Designs with a clear flow, such as ingress to service to workload Star Concentric rings around the most connected components Finding the hubs in a design Bus A breadth-first arrangement fanning out from a root Tracing what a component reaches, level by level Ring A single circle Small designs, and comparing components at a glance A design opened for the first time uses the Constrained layout. Once you drag components by hand, those positions are what the design stores; re-running a layout overwrites them for everyone, so use undo if an automatic arrangement was not what you wanted.
Layout control callout on a new design (anonymous capture, Sep 2026). Open the control near the bottom-left of the canvas to pick Grid, Constrained, Hierarchical, and related layouts. Layouts on large designs Re-running a layout across a very large design is the most expensive operation on the canvas. If a design is slow to arrange, see Performance Limits and Tuning. Configure visible layers 🔗 The Layers panel controls what the canvas draws. Open it from the Layers button in the toolbar above the canvas, beside Comments, Actions and Share. Every entry has an eye toggle: switch it off and that entity disappears from the canvas until you switch it back on.
Layers panel (anonymous capture, Sep 2026): By Type, Component Badges, and Components. Filename in the audit set is historical — this shot is the Layers drawer, not the per-component configurator. In Designer mode the panel is organized into four sections:
By type - a single toggle each for Annotations (comments, shapes, text and other non-semantic components) and Configurable Components (the semantic components that actually get deployed). Turning annotations off is the fastest way to see the deployable shape of a design on its own. The count beside each is the number of components of that type in the design. Component Badges - Validation Warnings, Deployment Errors and Inventory badges. These are the small markers Kanvas draws on components; hiding them declutters a design that is mid-review. See Interpreting Component Badges. Components - every kind present in the design, grouped by model. Expanding a group lists the individual components, each with its own visibility toggle, so you can hide one Deployment without hiding the rest. Clicking a component’s name selects it on the canvas and zooms the view to it. Relationships - each relationship kind, type and subtype found in the design, with its own toggle and a count. TagSet relationships appear here under that name. The header of the panel expands or collapses every section at once.
Because visibility travels with the design, the Layers panel is a way of presenting a design as much as a way of reading one - hide the noise before you hand a design to someone else and they will open it the way you left it.
Layers in Operator mode The Layers panel is present in Operator mode too, but it filters rather than hides: instead of design components it lists the Kubernetes resource kinds MeshSync has discovered - Cluster, Workloads, Configurations, Networking, Storage, Monitoring and Custom Resources - and choosing among them changes which resources are fetched and drawn. Those choices are what a saved view records. Render mode 🔗 Layout and layers decide what is drawn and where. Render mode, in the Options drawer, decides how much detail each component is drawn with - from full fidelity down to a wireframe - and can be set to adapt automatically as a design grows. Reach for it when a design has become large enough that panning and zooming feel heavy.

body:
Designs are rarely built from nothing. A platform design usually starts from an existing one - a team’s base cluster layout, a reference architecture from the catalog, a design a colleague already published - which you then extend. Kanvas supports that by letting you drag a design straight onto the canvas and decide, at that moment, whether it should join what is already there or replace it.
Dragging a design onto the canvas 🔗 Drag a design from the design list, the catalog or your workspace and drop it onto the canvas.
What happens next depends on what is already on the canvas:
The canvas is empty. The dropped design is simply loaded. There is nothing to lose, so Kanvas does not ask. The canvas already has components. Kanvas opens the Merge Design dialog, telling you which design you are about to bring in, how many components it contains, and which design it would be merged into. Choosing what happens 🔗 The Merge Design dialog offers three choices:
Choice Result Merge into current The dropped design’s components are added to the canvas alongside the existing ones, positioned where you dropped them. Open as new The dropped design is opened on its own, displacing what is currently on the canvas. Cancel Nothing changes. Merge with existing nodes on the canvas 🔗 Merge into current combines the two designs. Every component and relationship from the dropped design is added to the design you already have open. The block’s top-left corner moves to the drop position when you dropped a file. Otherwise it lands 50 pixels right and 50 pixels down from its original coordinates, and it can overlap existing components. Every component and relationship in the incoming design receives a new identifier. Kanvas does not match or de-duplicate against existing components, so merging the same design twice doubles its components. Names, kinds, configuration, styles, and the internal layout of the incoming block are preserved. The incoming design’s name, id, version, visibility, catalog data, layer preferences, and workspace are not carried over. Relationship evaluation runs as for any edit, and autosave persists the result after three seconds. If the merged design exceeds your plan’s component limit, the save fails and the merged components remain unsaved on the canvas. Merging needs no permission key, but the incoming design must be one you can read: your own, public, published, or shared with you. Cancel on a merge prompt does not delete a design the import already saved. A failed merge shows Failed to merge design: <reason>.
Merging does not consume the design you dragged. It remains in your design list, unchanged and independently owned - what you have merged is a copy of its contents into the design in front of you.
Displace the current nodes on the canvas 🔗 Open as new does the opposite: the dropped design becomes the design you are working on, and whatever was on the canvas is replaced by it. Use it when the drag was really a “let me look at that one instead” rather than a merge.
Because this discards what is on the canvas, Kanvas will not do it silently if you have unsaved changes - you are asked to confirm first. Saved designs are safe either way: the design being displaced is not deleted, only closed, and you can open it again from your design list.
Importing rather than dragging 🔗 The same merge decision appears when you import a design from a file, a Helm chart, a Kubernetes manifest or a Docker Compose file while a design is already open. If the canvas is empty the import is loaded directly; if it is not, you are asked whether to merge or to open the import as a new design. See Importing Designs.
See Also 🔗 Saving Designs: How Kanvas persists the result. Starting from scratch: The end-to-end walkthrough of building a design.

body:
Quick reference for day-to-day Kanvas use: keyboard shortcuts, troubleshooting tips, how to reach help and support, and release notes for Meshery Extensions / Kanvas.
Which plan includes a capability 🔗 Entitlements follow the organization’s plan: Free, Team Designer, Team Operator, and Enterprise. A capability is available only when the plan includes it, the role grants it, the provider supports it, and, when the capability needs a cluster, the deployment can reach one. Current pricing is at layer5.io/pricing.
Capability kanvas.new Meshery you run Author and edit designs Available Available Validate, dry run, deploy, undeploy Shows a prompt Available Connect clusters, Operator mode Shows a prompt Available Share, publish Requires an account Requires an account Component caps, checked on save and import, are Personal 100, Team Designer 200, Team Operator 100, and Enterprise 300. Under the local provider, views, the catalog, sharing, and support requests return HTTP 501 Not Implemented.
Which role can perform an action 🔗 Kanvas checks a permission before it offers these actions. When the user does not hold the key, the toolbar hides the action or shows it disabled, and the action sheet on small screens omits it.
Action Permission Also note Validate and Dry run Validate Design One key controls both. Disabled while the design is empty. Deploy Deploy Design Disabled while the design is empty. Undeploy Undeploy Design Disabled while the design is empty. Share Share Design Also hidden while the design is empty or published. Publish Publish Design Anonymous users get a sign-in prompt instead. Add a comment and reply Add comments Anonymous users get a sign-in prompt instead. Resolve and reopen a comment Resolve a comment @mention someone in a comment View All Users and Discuss any design by leaving review comments Both are required. Without them the composer offers no mention picker. Operator mode None The provider enables Operator mode. When it does not, the Operator switch is disabled. Layer5 Cloud checks Share Design when a design is shared, View Designs when a user reads other members’ private designs, the workspace permissions when designs or views are assigned or removed, and Share Views when a view is shared.
Default roles, from the permission list: User and Team Admin hold Validate, Share, Publish, Clone, and View Designs, and Unpublish only on resources they own. They do not hold Deploy or Undeploy. Workspace Admin, Organization Admin, and Provider Admin hold Validate, Deploy, Undeploy, Share, Publish, Unpublish, Clone, and View Designs. Organization Admin is the Org Admin role. Org Billing Manager and the Academy roles hold none of these. Provider Admin holds every permission.
Anonymous users receive the anonymous role. It holds the same canvas permissions as the User role, plus Screenshot Canvas and View help center. It does not hold the Operator terminal, metrics, component details, Add comments, Resolve a comment, Delete comments, or Lock comments permissions.
Anonymous users can read the comments on a design they open, but cannot add, reply to, resolve, or reopen a comment, and cannot @mention anyone. Adding a comment opens the sign-in prompt. Layer5 Cloud enforces the same boundary on its side: it refuses comment notifications, user search, the online users list, and API token creation for an anonymous session, so no one is emailed on behalf of a guest and a guest cannot look up other users.
Kanvas does not check a permission for individual canvas edits (add, delete, clone, copy, lock, style), except adding and resolving comments, which are checked as listed above. Roles carry keys with those names, but removing them does not prevent the edit. Designer mode allows authoring. Operator mode does not. Live cluster nodes are read-only in every mode. A user edits a design they own or one shared with them.
The Kanvas interface does not check a permission before it opens a terminal session, streams container logs, or runs a performance test. Layer5 Cloud defines Stream container logs, Perform performance test in Operator, and Select performance profile in Operator. By default only Organization Admin and Provider Admin hold them.
A custom role bundles keychains the default roles do not combine, so a group can receive Validate Design without Deploy Design. Only a Provider Admin creates a custom role. On hosted Layer5 Cloud an organization cannot create one itself. On a self-hosted deployment the operator’s Provider Admins can. In Kanvas, a custom role changes what is offered only for the actions in the table above. See Roles.

body:
While you are signed in, Kanvas saves for you. There is no save button you must remember to press before closing the tab: every change you make to a design - adding a component, moving it, editing its configuration, drawing a relationship, renaming the design - is persisted to your account. Kanvas writes pending changes 3 seconds after you stop editing. If a save fails, it retries with a doubling delay (3 seconds, then 6, then 12, and so on) for up to 100 attempts. Any new edit resets that count.
That leaves two things worth knowing: how to tell whether a change has actually landed, and how to deliberately create a second, separate copy.
The save indicator 🔗 The indicator beside the design name reports the state of the design against your account.
Indicator Meaning Cloud with a tick, plus a brief “Saved” Every change is persisted. Hovering shows how long ago the last save completed. Circling arrows, plus “Saving…” A change is in flight. Struck-through cloud, plus “Unable to save. Retrying…” A save failed. Kanvas retries on its own; the message clears once one succeeds. If the indicator sits on “Unable to save” for more than a moment, stop making changes until it clears - your recent edits exist only in the browser until a save succeeds. The usual causes are a lost connection to Layer5 Cloud or an expired session.
Clicking the indicator forces a save immediately rather than waiting for the next automatic one.
Anonymous capture (Sep 2026): the save indicator reads Saving… while the design syncs. Notification toasts from a recent Validate may also appear in this view. Save history 🔗 Hovering the save indicator on a saved design offers View Save History, which opens a list titled “Design Version History”. It is an event log of who changed the design and when. You cannot restore, diff, or export an earlier version from it. If you need a version you can return to, export a copy at that point.
Every save raises the patch number: the first save is 0.0.1, the next 0.0.2, and so on. Autosaves, visibility changes, and catalog data edits all count. There is no way to bump the major or minor number. Cloning and imports reset the version to 0.0.1. Saving sends the whole design and the server overwrites the stored copy. The last save wins. Collaborators editing the same open design are reconciled live in the editor, not at the storage layer.
Save as 🔗 Save as… in the file menu creates a new design from what is currently on the canvas. You give the copy a name, Kanvas stores it as a separate design owned by you, and the canvas switches to that new design - so any further edits go to the copy, not to the original.
Use it to:
take a private working copy of a design someone shared with you, branch a design before making a change you may not keep, turn a design opened from the catalog into one of your own. Save as… is disabled while the canvas is empty.
File menu (hamburger): New, Open, Import, Save as…, Export, Share, View in Operator, Details, and Delete. Signed out 🔗 Anonymous users save normally into a guest account with its own organization and workspace. On sign-in, guest designs migrate to the account. Exporting the design is how you take a file with you.
A new, unsaved design is named “Untitled Design”. Kanvas saves a new design only when it has at least one component, or a name that is not empty and not “Untitled Design”. An empty, unnamed canvas is not saved. Once a design has been saved, it can always be saved again, even after you remove every component. You cannot create a design while your organization scope is set to all organizations. Select a single organization first.
The server rejects a save when the design has more components than your plan allows: Personal 100, Team Designer 200, Team Operator 100, Enterprise 300. These are the seeded values. A deployment can differ. The limit applies to every save, to Save as, to merges, and to URL imports. It does not apply to cloning. A cloned design that exceeds your limit opens normally but fails its first save.
The server answers 403 with the message “Design exeeds maximum limit of N components supported by your current plan” (the misspelling ships) and an upgrade remediation. Kanvas does not show that message. You see only “Unable to save. Retrying…” and the edits stay on the canvas, unsaved. An organization with no active subscription that grants the feature gets “Org is not entitled to adding components to a design”. Other messages: “Failed to reach the cloud. Any changes made may not be saved.” when the server is unreachable (HTTP 503), and “Failed to save Design with name: ” for other failures, including “Design is invalid or empty” when the payload was empty. Closing the tab or switching designs with unsaved changes asks “You have unsaved changes. Are you sure you want to leave?”
See Also 🔗 Sharing Designs: Give other people access to a saved design. Exporting Designs: Take a design out of Kanvas as a file. Publishing Designs: Offer a design to the catalog.

body:
A component is the fundamental building block of a design - it represents one piece of the infrastructure under management, and its configuration is what will actually be applied when the design is deployed. The component configurator is where that configuration is edited.
Kanvas does not ask you to write YAML for this. The form is built from the component’s own definition, as published by the model it belongs to, so the fields you see are exactly the fields that component supports, in the version of the model you have selected.
Opening the configurator 🔗 With a component on the canvas:
Double-click the component, or Right-click it and choose Configure. The configurator opens in a panel beside the canvas. The component stays selected while it is open, so you can see what you are editing.
The header 🔗 Control What it does Component icon Hovering shows the model version the component is using. Version menu Appears when the model has more than one version available. Switching versions rebuilds the form against that version’s definition. Search Filters the form down to matching fields. On a component with many fields this is far quicker than scrolling; if nothing matches, the form says so rather than appearing empty. Help Shows the component’s own description, as published by its model. Expand / collapse Maximizes the configurator to fill the workspace, and restores it. Delete Removes the component from the design. Tabs 🔗 The configurator is organized into tabs. Which are present depends on the component and on your permissions:
Config - the component’s specification. This is where the substantive configuration is done. Labels - Kubernetes labels and annotations for the component, edited separately from the rest of the spec so that metadata does not crowd out configuration. Json Schema - the raw schema the form was generated from, in a JSON viewer. Useful when you want to see exactly what a field expects, and it links out to the component’s entry in the Meshery registry. Relationships - the relationships this component participates in, and the components at the other end of them. Field help and validation 🔗 Each field carries its documentation with it. A ? icon at the right of a field opens a tooltip containing that field’s description, taken straight from the component’s definition - so the guidance you get is the upstream project’s own, not a Kanvas paraphrase. Nested objects and arrays carry the same help on their group headings.
When a value is not valid for that field, a red error icon appears alongside, and its tooltip gives the validation message. The component itself also picks up a validation warning badge on the canvas, so a problem you scroll past in the form is still visible when you close the panel. See Interpreting Component Badges.
Changes take effect as you type 🔗 There is no Apply button. Edits are written into the design shortly after you stop typing, the canvas updates to match, and the design is saved to your account - see Saving Designs. Undo reverses a configuration change like any other edit.
See Also 🔗 Understanding Design Components: What the components on the palette represent. Understanding Tool Modes: Every mouse interaction available on the canvas, including the ones that open this panel. Palette search 🔗 Typing in the palette search box queries the Meshery registry after you pause for one second. Results appear in two groups, Models and Components. An empty result reads “Sorry, no matching records found”. Search matches model and component names only. It does not match labels.

body:
Kanvas offers a Help and Support form for sending a support request to the Layer5 team. You can open it from the Help menu, and from the Get Help action in Kanvas’s troubleshooting panel.
How a support request is delivered 🔗 A support request never leaves your browser for a third party. Kanvas submits the form to Meshery Server, which forwards it to your provider’s support intake:
Kanvas (browser) -> Meshery Server extension proxy -> Remote provider support webhook For Layer5 Cloud that intake is Layer5’s support queue. For a self-hosted Layer5 Cloud deployment it is whatever endpoint the operator has configured - see Customizing Webhooks.
Help and Support requires a remote provider 🔗 Because the submission travels through Meshery Server’s extension proxy, Help and Support only works when Meshery is connected to a remote provider. Under the local provider (None) Meshery Server has no support intake to forward to, and the extension proxy returns 501 Not Implemented.
This puts Help and Support in line with every other Cloud-bound Kanvas capability - sharing designs and views, the catalog, and resource access - all of which likewise require a remote provider.
If Help and Support fails under the local provider: switch Meshery to a remote provider (Meshery UI, Providers in the profile menu, then sign in) and submit the request again. If you cannot switch providers, reach the Layer5 team through the community forum or Slack instead.
Help and Support requires a signed-in identity 🔗 Every support request carries the requester’s name and email so the team can reply. Kanvas resolves your signed-in profile when you open Help and Support, rather than asking you to retype it:
While the profile is being fetched, the dialog shows a loading state and the form is not yet available for input. Once the profile resolves, the form appears, pre-addressed with your identity. If the profile cannot be resolved - an expired or degraded session, for example - the form is not shown and nothing is submitted, because a support request with no way to reply is of no use. If the form does not appear: sign in to your provider again, then reopen Help and Support. If it still does not appear, see Troubleshooting Kanvas.
Type of Inquiry 🔗 Each request carries a Type of Inquiry - one of Support, Community, Account, or Commercial - which the support intake uses to route your request. Support is selected by default. These are the same categories used by the Layer5 Cloud Help and Support form, so a request raised from Kanvas is triaged exactly like one raised from Layer5 Cloud.
If a submission fails, your subject, description, and type of inquiry are preserved so you can retry without retyping them.
Help Center 🔗 The Help Center is a dialog with eight entries. Open it from the canvas context menu or from the help control in the whiteboard dock. It also opens from Get Help in the troubleshooting panel.
Entry What it gives you Documentation These docs, in a new tab. Video Tutorials The Layer5 video library, in a new tab. Quick Tips An in-app tour of placing and configuring components, connecting and grouping them, loading and combining designs, sharing, validating, deploying and undeploying, and collaborating. In Operator mode it covers filtering, health and details, quick operations, performance tests, the terminal, and log streaming. Academy Learning paths in Layer5 Cloud, in a new tab. Discussion Forum discuss.layer5.io. Slack slack.layer5.io. Keyboard Shortcuts A side panel for Designer and Operator. The full list is in Keyboard Shortcuts. Support Opens the support form. The Help Center footer shows the installed Kanvas version and links to that version’s release notes. Every plan includes community support. Standard and Premium support add direct contact with the Layer5 team. The channels are listed in Layer5 Cloud support.

body:
Layer5 Cloud sends email when something happens that involves you: you earn a badge, your role changes, someone comments on your design. Notification preferences decide which of those emails reach you. Preferences belong to your account, so they apply in every organization you belong to.
Email is the only channel. Layer5 Cloud has no per-event choice between email and another channel.
You need the View Profile permission, which the default user role holds. The preferences are on your own account, and you cannot set them for anyone else.
To change the notification preferences 🔗 Sign into Layer5 Cloud. Open your account and the Preferences tab, at https://cloud.layer5.io/account/preferences. How the controls behave:
Everything is on until you turn it off. A new account receives every notification. You opt out of the ones you do not want, and a notification added later is on for you until you turn it off. Preferences save themselves. About one second after your last change, Layer5 Cloud saves it and confirms with “Notification preferences updated”. There is no Save button. Preferences are grouped. The preferences appear under categories and sub-categories. Each category has a switch that turns every preference in it on or off at once. To opt out of all email, turn every category off. A preference suppresses email, not the event. The event still happens and still appears in the audit trail. Only the email is skipped. The categories below are the ones the account page lists. Layer5 Cloud reads the list of available preferences from its own configuration, so a deployment can list more or fewer.
Category Preference Emails you when Acknowledgment Badge assignment and updates A badge is awarded to you or changed. Organization Activity Organization update An organization you belong to is updated. Workspace Activity Team, user, and organization management A team you belong to is updated, or you are added to a team. Workspace Activity Role assignment and updates Your roles change. Workspace Activity Comments on your designs Someone comments on a design you own. Turning this off silences email about comments on your designs. Workspace Activity Participating and @mentions in comments You are mentioned in a comment, or a thread you took part in gets a reply. To stop email from one thread without turning the preference off, mute that thread. See Muting comment notifications.
Preferences that do nothing yet 🔗 Three preferences appear greyed out and unchecked, and cannot be changed: Changes to designs, Deployments in environments, and Weekly summary. Layer5 Cloud does not send those emails today. Do not rely on them.
There is no separate Approval Requests category, and there is no single switch that opts out of every email at once. Turn each category off to stop all email.
Edge cases 🔗 Anonymous accounts never receive organization update email. Layer5 Cloud checks the preference when it is about to send the email. Turning a preference back on does not resend email that was skipped while it was off. If saving fails, the page shows the reason, and your previous setting stays in force. Who receives comment email is described in Managing comment notifications. Profile and sign-in settings are on Setting up a Layer5 account.

body:
Hotfix - custom-domain orgs with anchored-fallback credentials hit 1722 at callback 🔗 Custom-domain orgs without their own BYOC IdP credentials (e.g. exoscale.layer5.io) ran into meshery-cloud-1722 \state validation failed\ immediately after GitHub redirected back to /oidc/callback/github. The W2 state binding stamped the request host (exoscale.layer5.io), but the callback legitimately lands at the canonical host (cloud.layer5.io) because the fallback chain anchors redirect_uri there. The validator’s strict host-binding equality refused the cross-host bounce.
What changed 🔗 OIDCStart now stamps the effective callback host into the state payload, mirroring composeCallbackURL’s precedence:
BYOC (cred.CallbackHost empty) -> stamp req.Host Anchored fallback (cred.CallbackHost set) -> stamp cred.CallbackHost So the state’s host-binding holds whether the callback lands on the same custom domain or on the canonical Provider Org host. body:
Hotfix - production sign-in restored on cloud.layer5.io (v1.0.97 regression) 🔗 Fixes a regression introduced in v1.0.97 where sign-in via GitHub / Google on cloud.layer5.io failed with meshery-cloud-1729 \direct OIDC sign-in without a Hydra login_challenge is not yet supported\ (Cloudflare shows this as 502 from some POPs). The legacy Kratos selfservice OIDC flow initiated the Hydra login challenge internally; W2’s /oidc/start had no equivalent, so the React /login page’s \Sign in with…\ button forwarded to W2 without a login_challenge and OIDCCallback fell into its fail-closed branch.
What changed 🔗 OIDCStart now bounces server-side through Hydra’s /oauth2/auth endpoint when the inbound URL lacks ?login_challenge=, parses the freshly minted challenge out of the 302 Location header, and feeds it into the W2 state binding. The callback then has a valid challenge for accept_login, Hydra returns a code-carrying redirect to /oauth/callback, and HandleRedirect closes the loop via its existing code exchange + cookie issuance. The off-eTLD guard moved ahead of the new bounce so off-eTLD-custom-domain misconfigs surface the correct meshery-cloud-1725 error instead of being masked by a bounce failure. PR: #5392

body:
Hotfix - production sign-in restored on cloud.layer5.io 🔗 Fixes a regression where clicking Sign in with GitHub / Sign in with Google on cloud.layer5.io/login redirected users to the upstream OAuth provider with a redirect_uri of https://cloud.layer5.io/kratos/self-service/methods/oidc/callback/{provider}, which GitHub / Google rejected as edirect_uri is not associated with this application\ after the production OAuth App callback URL was updated to the W2 native path /oidc/callback/{provider}.
What changed 🔗 OrgAuthData exposes a new UseCloudNativeOidc boolean that is true for both registered custom-domain hosts AND for the canonical Provider Org host (SERVER_BASE_URL’s host). The React login / registration pages now gate the W2 cloud-native redirect on this field, so canonical-host sign-in no longer falls through to the legacy Kratos OIDC flow. A new resolveOIDCOrgID(req) helper in the server handlers prefers the middleware-resolved org and falls back to ProviderOrgID when the request lands on the canonical host. Both OIDCStart and OIDCCallback consume the helper so the state binding’s orgId is symmetric across the round trip on the canonical host. Rollout notes 🔗 The Layer5 production GitHub OAuth App’s Authorization callback URL is already https://cloud.layer5.io/oidc/callback/github and this deploy restores canonical-host sign-in without further OAuth App changes.
The staging GitHub OAuth App (1065875) must mirror this with https://staging-cloud.layer5.io/oidc/callback/github for staging sign-in to work after this deploys to staging. If that has not yet been updated, staging will exhibit the same symptom until it is.

body:
Understanding the Layer5 Ecosystem 🔗 5-light-bg Layer5 Cloud is the identity provider and remote provider for Kanvas and Meshery. It owns accounts, organizations, teams, workspaces, roles, and the catalog, and it stores every design and design version. It is available as a hosted service or self-hosted. Kanvas is a visual designer and operator for Kubernetes and multi-cloud infrastructure. It runs as an extension inside Meshery and uses Layer5 Cloud to store, share, and publish designs. What is Layer5 Cloud? 🔗 Layer5 Cloud is the identity, tenancy, and collaboration service behind Kanvas and Meshery. It signs users in, organizes them into organizations, teams, and workspaces, decides what each of them may do, and stores the designs they create and share. Layer5 Cloud runs as a hosted service and as a self-hosted deployment.
Meshery Server, running in your environment, is what talks to your Kubernetes clusters and performs every dry-run, deploy, and undeploy. Kanvas is an extension that runs inside Meshery. Kanvas sends its requests to Meshery Server, which forwards design, catalog, and sharing requests to Layer5 Cloud. Real-time collaboration signaling is the only direct path from the browser to Layer5 Cloud.
Why use Layer5 Cloud? 🔗 Sign-in and identity. Users create an account with an email address and password, with GitHub, or with Google. An organization that configures its own identity providers, including a generic OIDC provider, offers those instead. A signed-in user can link a GitHub or Google account to an existing profile, so either method signs in to the same profile. Email sign-ups verify their address before password sign-in works. After an email sign-up, Layer5 Cloud signs you in immediately, and opening the verification link verifies the address. Tenancy. Organizations own teams and workspaces. A team belongs to the organization it is created in, a workspace can hold any number of teams, and a team can belong to several workspaces. At first successful sign-in, every new user receives a default organization, team, and workspace: they hold the Organization Admin role on the organization, the Team Admin role on the team, and own the workspace. Authorization. Roles, keys, and keychains decide what each user may do. A key is a single permission, a keychain groups keys, and a role carries keychains. Users hold roles within an organization, so the same person can have different permissions in different organizations. Built-in roles cover the provider, organization, team, and workspace levels. See Identity and Security. Design storage and sharing for Kanvas. Layer5 Cloud persists every Kanvas design and every version of it, records who each design is shared with, and keeps the event log. A design belongs to at most one workspace at a time. Real-time collaboration in Kanvas starts with a signaling service that Layer5 Cloud hosts. After participants connect, edits synchronize directly between their browsers. The catalog. Anyone can browse the catalog. A signed-in user with the Clone Design permission can clone a published or public design into their own workspace, download it, or open it in Kanvas on the Meshery Playground. Opening a design in the Playground does not clone it. Remote provider for Meshery Server. Users sign in to Meshery through Layer5 Cloud, Meshery Server registers itself as a connection owned by the signed-in user, and Layer5 Cloud returns a capabilities document that tells Meshery which features to enable for that user. Every new user holds the Kanvas role, which enables the Kanvas extension when their Meshery Server connects. Academy. Academy delivers learning paths, challenges, and certifications, and gives content creators the tools to build and publish their own. What Layer5 Cloud does not do 🔗 Cluster deploy and cluster management stay with Meshery Server. Meshery Server talks to your Kubernetes clusters through Meshery Operator and MeshSync, and performs every dry-run, deploy, and undeploy. Kanvas runs inside Meshery. Kanvas sends its requests to Meshery Server, which forwards design, catalog, and sharing requests to Layer5 Cloud. Real-time collaboration signaling is the only direct path from the browser to Layer5 Cloud. Concepts explains how the building blocks relate, including how Layer5 Cloud, Meshery Server, and Kanvas divide the work.
Plans 🔗 Layer5 sells four plans: Free, Team Designer, Team Operator, and Enterprise, each with monthly and annual billing. In subscription and entitlement records the Free plan is named Personal. Entitlements follow the organization’s plan. Current prices are on the pricing page.
Layer5 Cloud enforces one plan limit: components per design. The recorded limits are 100 on Free, 200 on Team Designer, 100 on Team Operator, and 300 on Enterprise. Saving or importing a design over the active plan’s limit is refused with Design exeeds maximum limit of N components supported by your current plan. When an organization holds more than one active subscription, the highest component limit among them applies. An organization with no active subscription cannot save or import a design: the request fails with HTTP 500 and Org is not entitled to adding components to a design.
Other recorded quantities (relationships per design, image size, designs per workspace, workspaces per organization) are listed by GET /api/entitlement/features and are not enforced. For workspaces per organization on the Free plan, the plan records disagree: the monthly billing record sets 1 and the annual billing record sets 10. Authorization is by permission key. An action your role does not grant is refused with HTTP 403 even when the plan includes the capability. See Subscriptions and billing for how a subscription is started, upgraded, and canceled.

body:
To create integrations, retrieve data, and automate your cloud native infrastructure, build with the Layer5 Cloud REST API.
Every endpoint lives under /api on the host of your Layer5 Cloud deployment. Hosted Layer5 Cloud uses https://cloud.layer5.io/api. A self-hosted deployment uses https://<your-cloud-host>/api.
Authenticating with the API 🔗 In order to authenticate to Layer5 Cloud’s REST API, you need to generate and use a security token. Visit your user account’s security tokens and generate a long-lived token. Security tokens remain valid until you revoke them, and you can issue as many as you need.
A token belongs to your user account, not to an organization. One token reaches every organization you are a member of. What a token can do is the same as what you can do: every guarded endpoint checks that you hold the required permission in the organization the request runs in. See Default Permissions.
When a request has no Authorization header, Layer5 Cloud reads the browser session cookie instead. Scripts and integrations always send the header. A request with a missing or invalid credential receives HTTP 401. The body is JSON, {"message": "user must be logged in to perform this operation"}.
To authenticate with the API, pass the token as a bearer token in the Authorization header. For example, in cURL:
curl <protocol>://<Layer5-cloud-hostname>/api/identity/users/profile \ -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" Replace <protocol> with http or https depending on your Layer5 Cloud instance. Replace <Layer5-cloud-hostname> with the hostname or IP address of your hosted Layer5 Cloud instance. For example, https://cloud.layer5.io. Replace the path with the API endpoint you want to access. Replace <token> with the security token you generated. Specifying Organization Context 🔗 API Tokens are User-Scoped Layer5 Cloud API tokens are scoped to your user account, not to a specific organization. This means a single API token provides access to all organizations you are a member of. For users who belong to multiple organizations, you need to explicitly specify which organization your API requests should operate on.
This is similar to how GitHub Personal Access Tokens work, where a single token grants access to all repositories and organizations the user has access to.
A guarded request runs in one organization. Layer5 Cloud resolves the organization from these sources, in this order:
The request’s host. A request that arrives on an organization’s custom domain runs in that organization, and the sources below are not consulted. Requests to the deployment’s own address skip this step. The X-Current-Orgid request header. The organization saved in your user preferences. The organization saved in your browser session (browser clients only). Header names are case-insensitive. The first source that holds a value wins.
Condition Result The value is the ID of an organization you belong to The request runs in that organization. The value is not a valid ID, or names an organization you do not belong to Layer5 Cloud ignores it and runs the request with no organization scope. This is not an error by itself. The endpoint decides what to return. The value is all The request spans every organization, but only for callers who hold the View All Organizations permission (Provider Admin by default). For everyone else Layer5 Cloud ignores all. A Provider Admin names an organization they do not belong to The request runs in that organization. Check the header name Layer5 Cloud reads X-Current-Orgid only. A header with any other name, including layer5-current-orgid, has no effect, and the request silently falls back to your saved organization. Using the X-Current-Orgid Header 🔗 Include the X-Current-Orgid header with your organization’s ID to specify the target organization for a request:
cURL JavaScript Python curl -X GET "https://cloud.layer5.io/api/environments" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer <Your-Token>" \ -H "X-Current-Orgid: <Your-Organization-ID>" const token = "Your-Token"; const orgId = "Your-Organization-ID"; async function listEnvironments() { const res = await fetch("https://cloud.layer5.io/api/environments", { method: "GET", headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}`, "X-Current-Orgid": orgId, }, }); const data = await res.json(); console.log(data); } listEnvironments(); import requests url = "https://cloud.layer5.io/api/environments" headers = { "Authorization": "Bearer <Your-Token>", "X-Current-Orgid": "<Your-Organization-ID>" } res = requests.get(url, headers=headers) print(res.json()) Setting Organization and Workspace Preferences 🔗 To make an organization the default for every request that omits the header, save it in your user preferences:
cURL JavaScript Python # Set organization and workspace preferences curl -X PUT "https://cloud.layer5.io/api/identity/users/preferences" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer <Your-Token>" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "selectedOrganizationId": "<Your-Organization-ID>", "selectedWorkspaceForOrganizations": { "<Your-Organization-ID>": "<Your-Workspace-ID>" } }' const token = "Your-Token"; async function setPreferences() { const res = await fetch("https://cloud.layer5.io/api/identity/users/preferences", { method: "PUT", headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}`, "Content-Type": "application/json", }, body: JSON.stringify({ selectedOrganizationId: "<Your-Organization-ID>", selectedWorkspaceForOrganizations: { "<Your-Organization-ID>": "<Your-Workspace-ID>", }, }), }); const data = await res.json(); console.log(data); } setPreferences(); import requests import json url = "https://cloud.layer5.io/api/identity/users/preferences" headers = { "Authorization": "Bearer <Your-Token>", "Content-Type": "application/json" } payload = { "selectedOrganizationId": "<Your-Organization-ID>", "selectedWorkspaceForOrganizations": { "<Your-Organization-ID>": "<Your-Workspace-ID>" } } res = requests.put(url, headers=headers, data=json.dumps(payload)) print(res.json()) selectedOrganizationId is the default organization. The key is case-insensitive. selectedWorkspaceForOrganizations maps an organization ID to the workspace that receives the designs you save in it. When an organization has no saved workspace, Layer5 Cloud uses the first workspace available. A preference key that the request does not mention keeps its stored value. A key the server does not recognize, such as selectedOrganization or selectedWorkspace, is ignored. You cannot change your badges through this endpoint. API Example 🔗 The following example demonstrates how to retrieve information from the Academy REST APIs.
Get the total number of registered learners in Academy 🔗 Use the Layer5 Cloud API to retrieve the total number of registered learners. The Academy curricula endpoint is public. It needs no token. It returns curricula, each with its registration count. The path is /api/academy/curricula.
cURL JavaScript Python Golang curl -s "https://cloud.layer5.io/api/academy/curricula" \ | jq '[.data[].registration_count] | add' async function getTotalLearners() { const res = await fetch("https://cloud.layer5.io/api/academy/curricula"); const data = await res.json(); const total = data.data.reduce((sum, path) => sum + path.registration_count, 0); console.log(total); } getTotalLearners(); import requests url = "https://cloud.layer5.io/api/academy/curricula" res = requests.get(url) data = res.json() total = sum(item["registration_count"] for item in data["data"]) print(total) package main import ( "encoding/json" "fmt" "io" "net/http" ) type Path struct { RegistrationCount int `json:"registration_count"` } type Response struct { Data []Path `json:"data"` } func main() { url := "https://cloud.layer5.io/api/academy/curricula" req, _ := http.NewRequest("GET", url, nil) client := &http.Client{} res, err := client.Do(req) if err != nil { panic(err) } defer res.Body.Close() body, _ := io.ReadAll(res.Body) var response Response if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &response); err != nil { panic(err) } total := 0 for _, path := range response.Data { total += path.RegistrationCount } fmt.Println(total) } The result is a single number, the total of registration_count across the curricula returned.
Pagination 🔗 List endpoints that paginate accept these query parameters.
Parameter Default Behavior page 0 Zero-based page number. A negative value becomes 0. pageSize 10 Items per page. The maximum is 100. A larger value becomes 100, and zero or a negative value becomes 10. order Endpoint-specific Sort field and direction, for example updated_at desc. search None Filters items by text. The response carries the current page, the page size, the total count, and the array of items.
Errors 🔗 An error response is identified by its HTTP status code. The body takes one of three shapes, depending on the endpoint.
Shape Where you see it Example JSON with message Authentication failures and some middleware refusals {"message": "user must be logged in to perform this operation"} JSON with error Permission refusals and endpoints that report structured errors. May also carry code, severity, probableCause, and suggestedRemediation. {"error": "You do not hold the permission this action requires in this organization", "code": "..."} Plain text Endpoints that report a short message, for example a malformed request body malformed request body Status Meaning 400 The request is malformed or a required parameter is missing. 401 The credential is missing, invalid, or expired. 403 You do not hold the permission the endpoint requires in the organization of the request. 500 The server could not complete the request. Branch on the status code first, then parse the body defensively. The generated REST API Reference documents 401 responses as plain text, but the authentication layer answers with JSON.

Take and renew claims Take a claim on a resource of your organization with one of your own connections, and renew it. Release claim Release a claim you hold and record its outcome.
